Sports.title: Leandro Paredes receives 10-match ban as Argentina punished for World Cup final brawl
Sports.content:
Three Argentina players have been banned for their part in a brawl at the end of last month’s World Cup final against Spain, but they have only been fined for displaying a Falkland Islands banner after the semi-final win over England.

Leandro Paredes has been given a 10-match ban and a $90,000 (£66,000) fine by Fifa’s disciplinary committee, while Nahuel Molina was given a seven-match suspension and fined the same amount.

Thiago Almada was given a one-match ban and a $30,000 (£22,000) fine, while from coaching staff Roberto Ayala was banned for three matches and fined the same amount. Spain’s Gavi has also been given a one-match ban and a $30,000 fine.

The Argentinian football association (AFA) has been fined $321,000 in relation to the displaying of a banner at the end of the England game. It read “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” which translates as “the Falkland Islands are Argentinian”. The fine also covered breaches by Argentina supporters of Fifa’s anti-discrimination regulations at other World Cup matches.

For the discrimination offences, the AFA has been ordered to play the country’s next home match at 50% capacity, with a 50% capacity restriction at a further match suspended. Fifa said $100,000 of the fine was also suspended.

The banner was condemned by UK politicians at the time it was displayed, with Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey calling for the players who held it up to be suspended. Uefa had banned two Spain players – Rodri and Álvaro Morata – after they sang about Spain’s claims to Gibraltar after their Euro 2024 triumph.

On 6 August, the AFA announced that the date of the semi-final win over England – 15 July – would be commemorated as National Football Teams Day in the future.

Sports.title: Uefa and Concacaf discuss joint Nations League in latest challenge to Fifa
Sports.content:
Uefa and Concacaf have begun talks about setting up a combined Nations League tournament featuring all 96 European and North and Central American and Caribbean countries, in another direct challenge to Fifa.

The Guardian has learned that having come together to push for Gianni Infantino’s removal in the light of the World Cup sell-off controversy, the two confederations are now working on creating their own biennial tournament, which could launch as early as 2028 after the next European Championship.

Although discussions are at an early stage, it is understood the new competition would mirror the current multi-league format used for the existing Nations Leagues by Europe’s governing body and Concacaf, the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football. It would be followed by a knockout phase, a final-four tournament to determine the champions.

League A would feature the top teams in Europe, including Spain, France, England and Germany, playing competitive league fixtures against the highest-ranked nations in Concacaf such as Mexico, the United States and Canada.

Uefa and Concacaf launched Nations League competitions in 2018, with the confederations staging fixtures in the same international windows, so the mechanics required to set up a joint tournament are already in place.

Under the draft plans the league phase would be played during the existing September, October and November international breaks, followed by knockout matches in March and finals in June.

As the fixtures would take place during international windows that have already been agreed, it is unclear whether the new tournament would need to be ratified by Fifa, although given the world governing body is in the midst of an existential crisis with Infantino facing a leadership challenge that may be a moot point.

With serious discussions having begun only in the past few weeks, the number of teams in each league has yet to be determined, but all 96 members of Uefa and Concacaf would be involved and much of the revenue pooled, generating significant additional income for smaller nations.

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino is under pressure with Uefa and Concacaf pushing for his removal and now planning a combined Nations League tournament. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

The commercial appeal of the bigger European teams playing regular competitive matches in North America and Canada would be considerable, while there would also be major benefits for Mexico, whose football federation (FMF) is known to be frustrated by what it sees as the financial limitations of playing within Concacaf.

The FMF has held initial discussions about leaving to join the South American confederation, Conmebol, in a move that would need to be ratified by Fifa, but the prospect of lucrative matches against European opposition could lead to a change of heart.

The proposed new format would replace rather than add to existing international fixtures, while games would be played in geographical blocks to reduce travel.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) is also understood to have expressed interest in joining a global Nations League at a future date, and the competition structure being discussed would be flexible enough to accommodate them. The AFC does not currently operate a Nations League, however, so that would be a more long-term aspiration.

Uefa and Concacaf have been working together for some time, but have become even more closely aligned since the World Cup sell-off plan emerged last month.

Both confederations have made it abundantly clear that they regard Infantino’s position as untenable as a result of his role in the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, and are working together to propose an alternative candidate to stand against him in the presidential election next March.

Uefa declined to comment, although one source with knowledge of the proposal confirmed discussions are under way.

Concacaf declined to comment directly, but highlighted the confederation’s longstanding commitment to collaboration, which has led to guest teams participating in the Concacaf Gold Cup.

A historically strong relationship with Conmebol has resulted in many South American teams taking part in the Gold Cup, as have South Africa, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

Sports.title: Crystal Palace agree Disasi loan and tell Manchester City that Wharton is not for sale
Sports.content:
Crystal Palace have agreed a deal with Chelsea to sign Axel Disasi on loan and are expecting further interest in some of their key players in the final week of the transfer window, having informed Manchester City that Adam Wharton is not for sale.

Palace have been searching for a replacement for Maxence Lacroix after selling the France defender to Chelsea and are also understood to have approached Xabi Alonso’s side over a potential move for Josh Acheampong. But with Chelsea not willing to allow the England Under-21s international to leave Stamford Bridge, Palace have opted to bring in Disasi instead. The 28-year-old, who spent the second half of last season on loan at West Ham, is set to complete his medical on Friday.

Palace are also hoping to bring in a midfielder before the deadline and have expressed an interest in signing Kévin Danois from Auxerre and Monaco’s Lamine Camara. But it is understood the Conference League winners are determined to keep Wharton after City made an inquiry about the England midfielder this week. The 22-year-old has three years left on his contract at Selhurst Park and it is thought Palace would demand a sizeable fee to consider selling him. Liverpool and Chelsea have both also shown interest in Wharton in the past, with the latter said to be monitoring his situation should City make a bid for Enzo Fernández.

Pierre Sage is hoping Wharton will stay for another season. “We sold big players and now I think it’s not the moment to do that,” said Palace’s manager as he prepared for their Premier League opener against Everton on Saturday. “Adam can play at a big club but I think one year with us, one year with a new dynamic, will be good for him and we need him.”

Sage delivered the same message about Ismaïla Sarr after Palace turned down a bid of about £26m from Galatasaray for the Senegal forward. The Turkish side are expected to return with an improved offer and could face competition from their Istanbul rivals Fenerbache for last season’s top scorer. “We will keep him,” said Sage. “He’s a really important player for the club and for us. He will be able to play this weekend.”

There is, however, a strong possibility that Daniel Muñoz could depart after Palace signed Anan Khalaili last week, and given his fellow new recruits Óscar Mingueza and Zavier Gozo can also fill the right-wingback role. The Colombia defender has entered the final two years of his contract and is thought to be valued at about £25m, with Everton, Nottingham Forest and Tottenham having been linked with him in recent days.

Sports.title: Manchester United’s midfield rebuild leaves Carrick with no excuses
Sports.content:
Ed Woodward to MUTV in July 2015: “When people see Bastian Schweinsteiger on the team sheet, that’s going to send some shivers down the spine.” This prediction by Manchester United’s then executive vice-president, about Louis van Gaal’s new midfield signing, proved to be badly off‑target as the World Cup-winner’s career at the club proved to be a disappointment.

Two years after Woodward’s bullish statement, Schweinsteiger departed for Chicago Fire with a paltry 35 appearances and two goals for United on his CV, having been forced to train for a while with the youngsters by José Mourinho, Van Gaal’s successor. Here, in microcosm, is the story of virtually all midfield recruits by United for a generation. The hope at the club is that this trend changed this summer, with the arrivals of Youri Tielemans for £35m from Aston Villa and Andrey Santos for £48m plus £2m in add-ons from Chelsea, with the manager, Michael Carrick, also closing in on Brighton’s Carlos Baleba for a fee in the region of £70m.

You have to go back to Carrick’s own £18m transfer from Tottenham in 2006 for the last elite-level midfielder bought by United who arrived with his peak years ahead of him and went on to be a consistent force for many years, a strange dereliction of duty for a lineage that boasts Roy Keane, Paul Scholes, Paul Ince, Bryan Robson and Nobby Stiles, alongside other A-list acts.

Since Carrick, Paul Pogba – purchased by Mourinho a decade later for a club-record £93.2m – possessed the highest ceiling, but the Frenchman was unable to return even seven- or eight-out-of-10 displays in most games. Casemiro, who departed Old Trafford in May, came from Real Madrid in 2022 as a five-time Champions League-winner but, at 30, his best years were firmly behind him, and only the first and last of his four seasons at United could be rated as high level.

View image in fullscreen Manchester United have been linked with a £70m swoop for the Brighton midfielder Carlos Baleba. Photograph: Jeff Mood/ProSports/Shutterstock

Cite any other signing who has patrolled United’s midfield since Carrick and you are naming mediocrity in a United shirt, at best: Fred, Morgan Schneiderlin, Ander Herrera, Sofyan Amrabat, Daley Blind and Manuel Ugarte among those on that list. The exception is a home-reared player – Kobbie Mainoo. And even he, who as a teenager scored the winner in United’s 2024 FA Cup final triumph against Manchester City and started England’s 2-1 Euros final loss to Spain that summer, was discarded by Ruben Amorim, before Carrick’s mid-January appointment, after the Portuguese’s sacking, saved his United career.

So we arrive at the start of a new campaign and Carrick’s move to end this poor engine-room policy reaches Baleba. If the 22-year-old is acquired, he will join Santos, another No 6, and Tielemans, a No 8 who will compete with Mainoo, in a central cadre that has legs, skill, aggression and knowhow. Mason Mount has also shown to be another viable midfield option during pre-season. The 27-year-old operated with accomplishment as an attacking midfielder before sustaining his latest injury in a friendly draw with Paris Saint-Germain this month.

It is the latest setback for Mount, but Carrick has brushed aside any concerns regarding his robustness. “First of all Mason is a top player – we have seen that he was one of our best players in the first games,” the manager said. “He was outstanding and has picked up a bit of a knock. But there are no dramas. He has missed some football over recent years and he wants to be fit and be in full rhythm and we want to help him. Mason will be back soon.”

United travel to Hull on Saturday before hosting Ipswich a week on Sunday. Games against two promoted teams represent a favourable launch to Carrick’s first full campaign in charge, albeit he branded as “ridiculous” the view that it was an easy start. Yet factor in how a trip to Everton is United’s third game before Manchester City arrive at Old Trafford on 13 September and this is undoubtedly a golden chance for United to plant a flag as potential title contenders.

Reviving United amid the chaos of Amorim’s departure and finishing third last year was a fine effort by Carrick. Yet when he took over, the team were already out of both domestic cups and not in Europe. That left 17 games for the then caretaker to navigate. Now Carrick has a full programme of Premier League, Champions League, Carabao Cup and FA Cup fixtures before him: a litmus test of his side, as well as of the 45-year-old.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A squad with the requisite depth of quality is beginning to form. If Baleba is added alongside a left-back – Newcastle’s Lewis Hall and Arsenal’s Myles Lewis‑Skelly remain on the radar – by 1 September, then Carrick will have been bolstered by four new major signings. There remain question marks regarding the centre-back unit but ultimately the manager can have no excuses.

View image in fullscreen Michael Carrick has had a lot to think about this summer. Photograph: Grzegorz Wajda/Sopa Images/Shutterstock

Of Hull being an unknown quantity, Carrick said: “That is the beauty of the new season, for teams coming up there tend to be a few changes, that is the challenge playing against them – we are fully aware of that. Mentally and physically we have done a lot of work”. The last comment applies especially to the surgery undertaken to United’s midfield. At 12.30pm on Saturday, at the MKM Stadium, the picture of how good this has been will begin to emerge.

Sports.title: Aston Villa’s Rachel Daly: ‘It’s given me more of a focus: club football is my one job’
Sports.content:
A year after taking up golf, Rachel Daly has already reached a handicap of 19. “I think that’s too generous, I was playing really well in the summer,” she point outs before politely declaring that further questions about her pastimes are out of bounds. “I’m not that exciting, to be honest,” Daly says. “I walk the dogs, play golf. I don’t do a whole lot. I don’t lead a very exciting life.” Instead, Daly wants to talk about the new Women’s Super League season, which is more than fair enough.

Coincidentally, by next summer, 19 will be the number of seasons Daly has played at the top level, ever since breaking into Leeds’ first team as a 16-year-old in 2008, and therefore it feels reasonable to disagree with her view that a former Olympian, who played 84 times for England and was the WSL’s player of the season only three years ago, does not lead an exciting life. Yet there is another number on Daly’s mind as she discusses her role as Aston Villa’s captain.

“I’m the oldest in the team by a country mile,” the 34-year-old says, sitting down at Aston Villa’s Bodymoor Heath base, where she trains alongside 20-year-olds such as Georgia Mullett and Mia McAulay, a summer signing from Rangers. “A lot of the youngsters look up to me. It’s a nice feeling. It shows that they respect me and they value me, which is nice. And equally so do I [respect them]. I’m kind of a person that believes everyone should have a voice in the building. If I can reflect that to the wider group, then they can feel comfortable being able to communicate.

“I like to hear their experiences. It’s very different from when I was at their age, how I was experiencing football. They’re all very privileged where they’re at right now. When I was younger, we were paying to play, we were in men’s kits, the whole stereotypes and all that, but it’s true, that’s exactly what was happening. I try to give them my perspective of where I was at their age. I think it helps them a little bit to understand where the game has come from. They’re a really good bunch.”

Daly is now heading into her fifth season at Villa, having arrived there from Houston Dash shortly after starting every game of England’s triumphant 2022 Euros campaign. She had spent six years with the National Women’s Soccer League side and clearly likes being settled. “I like to set my roots at places. I don’t like to jump about. I [like] that familiarity of being at the same place. Villa has a big place in my heart.

“I said when I first signed here that I wanted to be part of the journey. I’ve stayed and been part of that journey and seen how we’ve moved and how we’ve progressed. I like to commit to a club and see what I can do there and give it my all. I’m really happy to be here and it feels like home.”

View image in fullscreen Rachel Daly has a leadership role at Aston Villa and is the club captain. Photograph: Aston Villa/Aston Villa FC/Getty Images

During her time at Villa, Daly also helped England reach a World Cup final in Sydney in 2023, before announcing her retirement from international football the following April. That meant her watching 2025’s Euros triumph, including the tense drama of penalties, as a nervous fan. “It’s awful actually, I much prefer playing than watching,” Daly admits. “I was just like, ‘just win, please!’” Reflecting on her decision to call time on her Lionesses career, having scored 16 senior international goals, Daly says: “I made that decision purely for me. I needed to do that at the time of my life. For club football, it’s given me more of a focus: ‘That’s my one job’. Recovery-wise, obviously, I’m not getting any younger, so it gave me more time, I got my international breaks back. It’s about spending time with my family. I didn’t want to miss out on my nephew growing up and stuff like that. So it was the right decision at the right time for me.”

“I do think I feel fresher,” Daly adds. “It’s taxing on your body being away for 10 days every month. Getting that time back and mentally just resetting – the most positive thing I’ve felt is just being able to breathe and get that time back with my family. I missed a lot of [family] time when I was in America.” Asked how she likes to use her free time during international breaks now, she says: “Because of the demands of being a professional footballer and the environment you’re in, it’s nice to just do nothing. I like what I like. It’s just been nice to kick back and just chill a little bit.”

On the pitch, Daly is determined to do the exact opposite and has a laser-like focus on ensuring Villa improve on last season’s ninth place. “We weren’t happy with the way we finished,” she says, recalling Villa’s run of four straight defeats at the end of the campaign. “There’s no denying that it’s the best league in the world for a reason and it’s not just us that are investing. There are a lot of clubs investing. We need to improve on where we finished last year. And for us, it’s kind of a bit of a transition, rebuilding year. There’s a lot of big players that left last year and there’s a lot of new faces in the door. A lot of young players, which is exciting. But [the aim] is building on how we left last year.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The WSL is entering a new phase of its development, with two extra teams entering the league this season. “It excites me,” Daly says. “The league has been kind of at a steady place for quite a while but we need growth, we need change, we need to have more teams in the league, we need to expand. And I think it came at a really good time. There’s no downside to it. More games means more fun.”

View image in fullscreen Rachel Daly has scored 16 times for England and was part of the Euro 2022-winning side. Photograph: Nigel Keene/ProSports/Shutterstock

The first two games of Villa’s campaign look tricky; away to Chelsea on 5 September before hosting Manchester City, the defending champions, eight days later. “Yes, September will be tough, starting against Chelsea and City is not an easy feat,” says Daly, who has never played at Stamford Bridge. “It’ll be a good test for us. We’re in a good spot so it will be interesting to see how that month goes, but I back us all the time. If you want to be the best, you’ve got to play the best and I think there’s no better place to start than playing Chelsea.”

Villa’s last trip to Chelsea in March ended in a seven-goal thriller, the hosts winning 4-3. If anything similar occurs this time around, the WSL campaign will be off to a roaring start. “It’s exciting,” Daly says. “Big hitters early doors. Lets see what happens.”

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 20: Tottenham
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 6th (NB: this is not necessarily John Brewin’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 17th

Prospects

Tottenham’s hopes for the season can be measured by what went wrong last season. And the season before that. This time last year, the arrival of a fresh, enthusiastic face in Thomas Frank gave considerable grounds for optimism. Surely Spurs would not be as bad in the Premier League as they had been in 2024-25? They proved to be worse. Despite a decent enough Champions League group stage, European football did not provide salvation for an ill-fitting manager or the unconvincing hierarchy around him.

That Frank is almost a forgotten figure owes much to the Igor Tudor interlude, a misadventure that resembled a disaster movie. Tottenham were on the brink of relegation until the season’s final days, a saga that became irresistible to rubberneckers. Roberto De Zerbi’s appointment was a much-needed corrective, the change in direction Spurs supporters clamoured for during so many years of their club never paying top dollar, of cutting corners. The Italian’s high wages were not his only demands. Fuller control than his predecessors, far more than he enjoyed at Brighton and Marseille, and a proper transfer spend on readymade players were also demanded. He has received them, though the lack of a top-level striker is glaring.

Thus, the unusual sensation of Tottenham being among the transfer window’s biggest spenders. Buying Jan Paul van Hecke, Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali, with Savinho and Omar Marmoush expected to also arrive from Manchester City, resembles the type of outlay rarely seen since Terry Venables was collecting Paul Gascoigne and Gary Lineker at White Hart Lane in the late 1980s or the influx of foreign talent in the mid-1990s – Jürgen Klinsmann, Ilie Dumitrescu and all that: a flash of glamour that is old-school Spurs. Andy Robertson’s addition as an experienced head is a further pointer towards a different Tottenham, one where success is expected and not promised, a very different form of optimism. Cristian Romero has departed, a player of talent whose foibles often betrayed his teammates, endemic of the Spurs era he played in.

Off-field picture

Finishing 17th two seasons in succession is bad for the bank balance. The club’s 2025 accounts revealed that the £34.7m garnered from winning the Europa League was wiped out by a £38.9m shortfall in Premier League income. Champions League football last season will help, with £71.6m trousered, but there are no European funds to feed off this season. The international break in September allows Tottenham Hotspur Stadium to welcome Jay-Z, having hosted the veteran heavy metal band System Of A Down in July. Two NFL regular season matches will be staged in October. Such revenue streams cushion Spurs, as does an August share issue that raised £100m.

Owner-fan relationship

The removal of Daniel Levy was what many Spurs fans had desired, but it also created a vacuum. The family trust of the former majority shareholder, Joe Lewis, took the residual heat. In January, Lewis’s daughter, Vivienne, was confronted by a fan demanding that Frank be sacked and that she sell up. The Lewis trust has doubled down. Levy’s 29% previous share is reduced by his missing the deadline for that August share issue; the two parties are reported to be battling over an NBA Europe franchise. Vinai Venkatesham, a chief executive who came under heavy fire, admitted in May “a complete reset” was required. Supporters will wait to gauge the success of the brave new world.

The manager

De Zerbi’s coaching is admired across the football spectrum, Pep Guardiola a confirmed fan, though breakdowns in relationships at both Brighton and Marseille offer caution. Will he be remembered solely for saving Spurs from relegation or can he offer progress in a fashion not seen since Mauricio Pochettino arrived in 2014? He has offered notes of realism to temper the excitement of the spending spree. “We need to create a clear playing style and give a soul to this team,” the Italian said in pre-season. “So many talk about ‘projects’, but very few manage to see them through.” He has been handed as blank a canvas as is available at any major club.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen João Pedro (left) and Dário Essugo (right) try to stop Spurs’ Sandro Tonali in his tracks during the 2-1 victory over Chelsea in their Sydney Cup friendly, in which Tonali opened the scoring. Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PA

“The gaffer was Italian, I knew him,” was among the reasons Sandro Tonali offered for choosing Tottenham when a number of other suitors came calling. “I was already watching Tonali when he was playing for Brescia, my hometown club and the team I support,” explained De Zerbi. “At the age of 18, he already looked like a veteran.” With Tonali 26, Spurs have signed a peak-age player who, the season before last, was among the very best midfielders in English football, though his final season at Newcastle was mixed. A fee of £100m could not be refused.

Stat attack

Tottenham were the only club in the Premier League who overachieved their xG in attack by at least four while also underachieving by that margin or more in defence. It was up front where the biggest discrepancy occurred, with Spurs scoring 7.91 goals more than their chances implied they deserved. They might have been playing Championship football this season had this not happened.

Set for a breakthrough

Much is expected of Mikey Moore, though he is likely to go out on loan again after a season at Rangers. Antonin Kinsky was the victim of one of the horrors of the Tudor reign, subbed off after 17 minutes against Atlético Madrid, only to be trusted by the new manager as relegation was avoided. His save from Leeds’ Sean Longstaff was highly significant in the clamber to safety. Kinsky is set to be first choice this season after the departure of Guglielmo Vicario. “He forces you to believe in yourself,” said Kinsky of De Zerbi, who in turn said: “He has great personality, strong character.”

World Cup impact

Full-backs were Tottenham’s leading men in the United States. Djed Spence has departed for Inter but Pedro Porro remains, after signing a new deal amid interest from Manchester City. Porro scored twice, including in Spain’s semi-final defeat of France. As a world champion, the 26-year-old received a guard of honour on his return to his club’s training ground, having beaten the Argentina team of the now-departed Romero in the final. Among Tottenham’s nine players in North America, the new central defensive pairing of Van Hecke and Micky van de Ven was kept apart, the latter playing left-back as the Dutch disappointed.

Sports.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for as the new season kicks off
Sports.content:
1 Nwaneri out of Arsenal picture

While Myles Lewis-Skelly looks likely to remain at the Emirates, the same can’t be said for Ethan Nwaneri. The 19-year-old was outstanding in his breakthrough season for Arsenal in 2024-25 but barely featured last season and was sent on loan to Marseille. That didn’t really work out and Arsenal are now exploring another temporary move to ensure Nwaneri gets regular football this season. Milan, RB Leipzig, Dortmund and Fulham are all thought to be interested, with Nwaneri unlikely to feature on the bench for Friday’s opener against Coventry as a result. Whether Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus are available remains to be seen as Arsenal attempt to find suitors for the Brazil duo. Ed Aarons

Arsenal v Coventry City, Friday 8pm (all times BST)

2 New United pair down for Tigers test

Manchester United’s summer transfer business has focused on recruiting in central midfield. It will be interesting to see who Michael Carrick selects in two key roles for the first game of the season. Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans have been present for more of pre-season than Kobbie Mainoo, who did not play a minute for England at the World Cup and was a late returner to Carrington after a holiday. Carlos Baleba surely will not have arrived in time to start at Hull. Mainoo is in the best position in the long term but if Carrick decides to ease him into the season, it would be intriguing to see how Santos and Tielemans team up, the stress test for a new partnership that could provide the perfect balance of defensive awareness and ability to move the team up the pitch. Will Unwin

Hull City v Manchester United, Saturday 12.30pm

3 Swapped pair face former clubs

Neither Everton nor Crystal Palace have enjoyed a particularly scintillating summer of transfer activity but combined to make headlines with a swap deal between Dwight McNeil and Brennan Johnson. The pair will face one another – and their former clubs - on the first weekend of the season, eager to prove what their worth to their new teams. McNeil was rarely a regular on Merseyside but had a positive second half to last season, ironically after a move to Crystal Palace fell through at the last minute. Johnson did not settle at Selhurst Park, unable to crack the code that would get him into the starting lineup on a weekly basis, after moving from Spurs. A fresh start should reinvigorate the duo and there is no better way to further boost the mood than beating a former employer. WU

Everton v Crystal Palace, Saturday 3pm

4 Can Ipswich copy Black Cats’ success?

Ipswich clearly learned a lot from what Sunderland did a year ago, as they went out and bought a lot of players. The Black Cats quickly moulded their 19 acquisitions into a successful unit but at least they had the positive of a head coach in Régis Le Bris who had his feet under the table. Gary O’Neil is the new man at Portman Road and he has 12 signings – at time of writing – to potentially use for the opener. The record arrival, Emersonn, who has moved to Portman Road from Toulouse, is the most eye-catching of those who have been acquired. The Brazilian has an underwhelming career goalscoring record and a few question marks hanging over his head. Even though it is their first game, Ipswich need to pick up points at home, and to do so require a striker who can cause problems for defenders. How quickly Emersonn adapts will be critical for the Tractor Boys’ success this year. WU

Ipswich Town v Sunderland, Saturday 3pm

View image in fullscreen Emersonn is one of a number of big-money signings made by promoted Ipswich this summer. Photograph: Keeran Marquis/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

5 Glasner’s tough Diomande ready for debut

August is the season for debuts and no one will be more satisfied than Oliver Glasner when Ousmane Diomande steps over the white line at the City Ground. Glasner wanted the Ivorian centre-back to replace Marc Guéhi at Crystal Palace, six months before the England defender departed for Manchester City. Diomande, a £34m buy from Sporting, is expected to line up in a back three for Nottingham Forest against Leeds, when the Austria midfielder Xaver Schlager, who played for Glasner at Wolfsburg, could also make his Forest bow. Diomande is a quick and physical defender but another aspect of his appeal is his aerial power at set pieces. “They’ve both played Champions League football and they are used to competing for titles,” said Glasner. “They can add this winning mentality.” Ben Fisher

Nottingham Forest v Leeds, Saturday 3pm

6 Serene Senesi can bring calm to Spurs

Cristian Romero has taken his maverick brand of defending to Atlético Madrid, upsetting neutral Premier League watchers. His compatriot Marcos Senesi has arrived to shore up things at the back as Roberto De Zerbi desperately tries to steer Spurs away from a third straight season of battling relegation. The all-action Romero had his qualities as a leader and defender but never felt dependable, which is what most want from a centre-back and captain. Senesi impressed during his time at Bournemouth, rarely making headlines but proving himself a calm presence at the back. The Argentinian is good on the ball and will be more adventurous in possession than his countryman. He is yet to be sent off in three seasons as a Premier League player – Romero was dismissed twice in 2025-26 alone, not to mention a one-match ban and a fine for his behaviour towards a referee. His calmness will improve Spurs. WU

Brentford v Tottenham, Saturday 5.30pm

7 Villa head south besieged by problems

It is surely not how Unai Emery envisaged the countdown to Aston Villa’s season-opener at Brighton on Sunday – and certainly not as he enjoyed the afterglow from the club’s Europa League triumph over Freiburg in May. The manager has an extraordinary number of problems. Take the midfield where the new signings João Gomes and Johan Manzambi are injury doubts. Note: Amadou Onana is a long-term casualty while Youri Tielemans has been sold. It goes on. Emery is about to lose Ezri Konsa to Arsenal – in a summer where Villa have also sold Morgan Rogers and Lucas Digne. They are trying to move on Emi Martínez, while the future of Ollie Watkins is uncertain, with Al-Hilal circling. For the cherry on top, the rampaging 17-year-old striker Brian Madjo is a fitness concern. Emery’s teamsheet will be very interesting. Will he pitch the new goalkeeper, Zion Suzuki, who only signed on Wednesday, straight in? David Hytner

Brighton v Aston Villa, Sunday 2pm

8 Maresca must win to silence City noise

Is Enzo Maresca already under pressure after Manchester City’s 3-0 schooling by Arsenal in the Community Shield? Maybe not, but if the Italian’s new team go down at home to Bournemouth on Sunday, you do not have to be a soothsayer to picture the scrutiny that will follow. Maresca and City are enduring a difficult transfer window, with Rodri’s departure to Barcelona the headline, a dizzying blow that has to be shaken off. The new Bournemouth coach, Marco Rose, has faced City six times in the Champions League with Leipzig and Mönchengladbach, and is sure to order his visitors to go for the jugular at the Etihad. City are vulnerable but Maresca can remedy this with a win of any sort. This, after all, is the job many felt he was the obvious choice for. Jamie Jackson

Manchester City v Bournemouth, Sunday 2pm

View image in fullscreen Anything but a win for Manchester City at home to Bournemouth will increase scrutiny on Enzo Maresca. Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/EPA

9 King Kev remembered at Newcastle

Kevin Keegan was supposed to have been the guest of honour at St James’ Park on Sunday, but his death from cancer in July means this meeting of two of his old clubs will turn into a tribute to one of English football’s enduring heroes. Keegan’s family will be present to witness an outpouring of love for the former Liverpool and Newcastle forward and (twice) Magpies manager. Once the game kicks off, all eyes will be on Alexander Isak, a St James’ Park old boy whose decision to force a £125m move to Anfield last summer did not go down well on Tyneside. The Sweden striker, making his first return to Newcastle, has much to prove at Liverpool, and now has a new head coach to impress in Andoni Iraola. Newcastle too have a new face in the home dugout, where Matthias Jaissle will occupy the technical area for so long inhabited by Eddie Howe. Louise Taylor

Newcastle v Liverpool, Sunday 4.30pm

10 Former Madrid managers meet in capital

Real Madrid’s two head coaches from last season meet at Craven Cottage, with the focus on Xabi Alonso, rather than Álvaro Arbeloa. The Fulham man, however, may have more to prove in the Premier League. His managerial career has been less prominent than that of his Basque rival – and he has clearly insisted on snapping up talent from the Bernabéu. Gonzalo García and César Palacios have made the trip over from the Spanish capital with Arbeloa. It shows great faith from the former Liverpool defender but it does put extra pressure on the trio, their fates now permanently intertwined. All three need a positive start to show they merit being in the Premier League. Otherwise, it would be very easily to criticise them individually and collectively. WU

Sports.title: Argentina's World Cup stars LET-OFF without serious punishment for Falklands banner against England - as two of their players get banned for total of 17 matches over final fighting
Sports.content:
Argentina have escaped without major punishment despite calls to ban their 'idiotic' stars who carried a banner claiming the Falkland Islands belong to their country following their World Cup semi-final victory over England last month.

FIFA today slapped Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes with a massive 10-match ban over a fight at the end of the World Cup final against Spain - with team-mate Nahuel Molina hit with a seven-game sanction.

But the tournament runners-up were let-off when it came to their Falklands protests. FIFA have imposed a two-match partial stadium closure, reducing the crowd size for Argentina's next two home matches to 50 per cent. However, one of those matches is suspended. They have also been hit with £235,000 in fines, £73,000 of which is suspended.

The banner, first displayed in the crowd before being handed down to the players after they beat England 2-1, read 'The Falkland Islands are Argentine' in Spanish.

Despite FIFA's ban on political flags, now-departed Tottenham captain Cristian Romero, Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez and ex-Spurs midfielder Giovani Lo Celso celebrated with the controversial sign after the final whistle. Captain and star player Lionel Messi was also seen dancing alongside the banner.

Argentina's Leandro Paredes has been banned for 10 matches over the World Cup final fight

Nahuel Molina has been handed a seven-match ban for his role in the post-match brawl

UK Secretary of State for Business and Trade, Peter Kyle, said at the time that it was 'entirely inappropriate' to wave the banner, praising England for acting with dignity in 'real contrast with what we saw with the Argentina team'.

And Tory shadow minister Andrew Griffith said: 'Labour's Chagos surrender has made us look weak, and British territory up for grabs. The Falklands are British. Whoever won the football. This idiotic display from the Argies was clearly against FIFA rules. They should be punished.'

Argentina have been condemned for their thuggish antics throughout the tournament, prompting FIFA to investigate their behaviour following the final whistle of last month's showpiece where they were beaten 1-0 by Spain.

Paredes grabbed Spain's Eric Garcia by the neck before punching Gavi in the face and pushing him to the ground in appalling scenes at full time.

The 32-year-old will now miss Argentina's next 10 matches and has also been fined £65,000.

Molina was another involved in the fracas, hitting Spain captain Rodri in the torso as he ran past, prompting the midfielder to square up to his rival. FIFA have handed Molina a seven-match ban.

Meanwhile, Argentina's Thiago Almada and Spain's Gavi will serve one-match bans for their role in the unsporting scenes.

Argentina players were criticised for displaying this banner after beating England

The fines, though, will do little to put a dent in the £25million prize money they received for finishing runners-up in North America.

Twelve years ago, Argentina players carried the same banner at an international friendly and were fined just £20,000. There were calls for them to face tougher sanctions this time.

A total of 255 British servicemen were among the 907 people who died in the 1982 Falklands War, which saw UK armed forces retake the islands after an Argentine invasion.

Britain first landed on the uninhabited islands in 1690 and claimed them for the Crown in 1765. It has maintained a permanent presence there since 1833 - 47 years before Argentina became a fully unified state following its declaration of independence from Spain in 1816.

The last official referendum of Falkland Islanders was held in 2013, when 99.8 per cent of voters chose to remain a British Overseas Territory.

Sports.title: Jack Draper ruled OUT of US Open as former British No 1 continues to tackle problematic bone bruising injury in his arm which forced him to miss Wimbledon
Sports.content:
Jack Draper ruled OUT of US Open as former British No 1 continues to tackle problematic bone bruising injury in his arm which forced him to miss Wimbledon

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Jack Draper will miss the US Open in the latest blow to the former world number four.

Draper is continuing to battle a bone bruise in his dominant left arm and, after two dispiriting matches in the US, he has concluded he needs more time to recover.

The news, which comes only a couple of hours after world number one Jannik Sinner announced he would miss the tournament with a knee injury, means Draper will not have played in a single grand slam this year.

It has been a disastrous last 12 months for the 24-year-old, who was ranked in the world’s top five last summer but is now down at 143.

His arm problems forced him out after Wimbledon last year for seven months, aside from a US Open appearance where he pulled out ahead of the second round.

Jack Draper will not play in New York after failing to overcome his bone bruising injury

Draper then appeared to be back on track, only for a knee problem to surface in the spring and force him out of the French Open.

He made another return at Eastbourne ahead of Wimbledon, but more pain in his arm prompted him to make the difficult decision to miss his home grand slam and things have only gone downhill since.

Draper finally returned to action in Canada earlier this month but broke down in tears during the third set of a defeat by France’s Terence Atmane before losing the final five games to young Spaniard Martin Landaluce in Cincinnati last week.

Speaking to the Guardian after that match, Draper said: 'It’s a difficult place to be right now. It’s got to a point with me where it’s taken probably one of my biggest qualities, my fighting spirit.'

The former US Open semi-finalist has changed his racket and strings in an effort to recover from the injury, while he continues to tweak his service motion, but so far the alterations have not taken the pain away.

'I think that’s the toughest part,' he said. 'It’s like there are no right answers. You have to figure it out. It’s not as simple as taking time off and it’s going to go because it doesn’t. I’ve tried it.'

Draper’s low ranking meant he would have had to go through qualifying in New York barring a late wild card, but he joins Sinner and Emma Raducanu in sitting out the tournament.

Arthur Fery’s run to the Wimbledon semi-finals has been an outstanding bright spot in what has been a disappointing season for British tennis, with Draper and Raducanu again blighted by injury.

One bit of positive news this week has been the return to court at the National Tennis Centre in London of Sonay Kartal, who has been sidelined since March with a back injury and will also sit out the US Open.

Cameron Norrie, who has overtaken Fery to reclaim the British number one spot, will be the only seeded British player in singles in New York, with Fery, Katie Boulter and Jan Choinski also securing direct entry.

Sports.title: George Russell takes Dutch Grand Prix sprint race pole in Zandvoort - ahead of fellow Brit Lando Norris
Sports.content:
George Russell takes Dutch Grand Prix sprint race pole in Zandvoort - ahead of fellow Brit Lando Norris

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

George Russell, who needs a gulp of oxygen more than any of his competitors in the contest for the Formula One world title, claimed pole position for the sprint race at the Dutch Grand Prix.

The British driver achieved the accolade 0.041 of a second ahead of his compatriot and defending champion Lando Norris of McLaren.

Charles Leclerc was third for Ferrari with Lewis Hamilton a slightly disappointing seventh best in the other red car, a place ahead of Max Verstappen, who this week signed a new deal with Red Bull, worth £70million a year plus bonuses.

But, best of all for Russell, Kimi Antonelli, his Mercedes team-mate and nearest rival for the world crown, qualified fifth.

Russell and Antonelli are separated by 59 points at F1’s post-summer resumption in Zandvoort, with 12 rounds remaining if the season works out as planned comprising races in the Middle East in late November and early December, war-permitting; 11 otherwise.

George Russell celebrates his sprint race pole in the Netherlands

Speaking at Holland’s seaside race venue less than an hour out of Amsterdam, Russell said: ‘It’s great to be back here after the break. It’s a circuit I love. It needs a lot of commitment.

‘It was a tough end to the first half of the year and I’m really happy to come back.

‘The lap felt good. It all came together nicely. It’s always difficult in sprint qualifying with just one shot on the soft tyre. The track always takes a step, the grip takes a step.

‘McLaren look quick, Ferrari look quick but I’m glad to pull it off when it mattered.

‘It is only sprint qualifying. The big points are on Sunday so I will try to carry this momentum into tomorrow.’

Russell, 28, has just proposed to his Spanish girlfriend Carmen Montero Mundt. He was thrilled she said ‘yes’, which his team principal Toto Wolff believed may have helped lift his man’s spirits and fortunes after a stop-start season. He won in Australia on the first day of the campaign but has not done so other than in Austria three months later.

‘George is coming back,’ said Wolff. ‘I think he feels so much pressure is off his shoulders after she accepted his marriage proposal!

‘Some solid work on the day and from day to day. He put the dots together and had a very good lap.

‘Kimi lost 20 points (of downforce) with a hole in the floor, but we managed to patch it up and it looked like it was completely intact afterwards.

‘The gaps are so close and he made a little bit of a mistake at Turn 11, pushing too hard on the entry, and it can go quickly.

‘On the long run Ferrari looked strong. We didn’t have that pace.

‘But it’s the baby race. The important session is qualifying tomorrow for the Grand Prix proper.’

There are only eight points up for the winner of the sprint, but nibbling into that bounty would still be a welcome bonus for husband-to-be George.

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola names Liverpool's new vice-captain as Alisson - but WON'T allow him to wear the armband on the pitch to combat Premier League rule
Sports.content:
Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson has been the victim of Premier League rule-changes – as he has been named a vice-captain but is likely to never wear the armband.

Rules that came into play last season stipulate only the team captain is permitted to approach the referee to discuss major decisions or flashpoints in the game.

As it would not make sense for Reds shot-stopper Alisson to run the length of the pitch to debate, for example, a penalty shout, he is likely to never wear the armband.

Virgil van Dijk is club captain and the Brazil No 1 has been named as vice-skipper, to replace outgoing Andy Robertson, alongside fellow experienced pro Joe Gomez and Dominik Szoboszlai.

'I explained to Alisson especially that it's not going to be possible that he wears the armband because with the new rule I think there is a big limitation if a goalkeeper wears the armband,' said Iraola.

Alisson is Liverpool's new vice-captain but is unlikely to ever wear the armband for them

Andoni Iraola is wary of Premier League rules which only allow captains to speak to referees

'Because basically, if something happens in the opposition box the referee has to explain to the captains what's happening, all the decisions.

'I had one season with (goalkeeper) Neto in Bournemouth and then you have to start every game to say a different player that can act as a captain, and this is not viable.

'But I wanted him to feel like we value him. I've had enough time and we will have more time to get to know each other, but I had to explain the decision about the armband to Ali.

'Because he is a keeper and, unfortunately, they are putting the rules in a way that there are a lot of disadvantages to having a keeper as a captain.'

Of Premier League clubs, only one has a goalkeeper as skipper: Crystal Palace with Dean Henderson.

Sports.title: Joe Root's second-coming as England Test captain starts with a bang at fortress Headingley - as dismal Pakistan made to pay by destructive hosts, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH
Sports.content:
The dressing-room kettle had not yet been switched on for tea on the third day of this first Test when England were celebrating a crushing victory and a pristine start to the second coming of Joe Root.

Their bowling heroes, once more, were Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue, who backed up their five-fors on Wednesday with three more wickets each as Pakistan were dismissed for 135, to go with their first-innings 171. In all, they survived 85.4 overs, the equivalent of a less than a full day’s play. They were as dismal as England were destructive.

Robinson finished the match with eight for 80, and Tongue – who collected his three wickets in six balls after lunch – with eight for 89, both career-bests.

If Jofra Archer had started the rout by removing both openers, and finished it by persuading Mohammad Abbas to sky a slash to Dan Lawrence at backward point, it was these two, in their differing styles, who condemned the tourists to defeat by an innings and 103 runs.

For the first time in the game, the Leeds weather behaved itself – but while it never rained, for Pakistan it continued to pour. Robinson was all loping accuracy and both-ways menace, Tongue 10mph quicker and a nightmare to line up thanks to an action that goes beyond the perpendicular and obliges batsmen, especially right-handers, to play at balls better left alone.

When Archer and Gus Atkinson are back to their best, England will have a seam attack to conjure with, and there was an understandable spring in Root’s step as he encouraged Robinson and Tongue to lead the team off the field with a gentle shove in the back.

Man-of-the-match Ollie Robinson recorded career-best figures at Headingley

And Josh Tongue also returned his own career-best numbers and proved too hot to handle for the Pakistan batsmen all week

Robinson, by a sliver, won the match award, though no one would have complained if they had done to the medal what they did to the ball two days earlier and sawn it in half.

That followed meaningful runs for Jordan Cox and Lawrence, reinventing themselves at No 3 and No 6 as England reached an above-par 409, and an almost flawless display in the field.

And if there was any regret for Root as he discussed his first Test win as captain since seeing off India here five years ago, it was surely that Headingley is now off the rota until 2029.

This is not merely Root’s home ground, but England’s new spiritual home: a seventh win in succession was a national record. The Australians, who have lost their last two Tests here, must still be chortling at the thought they won’t have to visit the place next summer as they go in search of a first series win in England since 2001.

It is an act of self-harm the ECB may yet come to regret. ‘I’d love to play as many games here as possible,’ said Root, before diplomatically suggesting he should ‘stay in his lane’.

For now, though, there was simply relief at a job impeccably done, from the moment Robinson trapped Azan Awais with the game’s first ball. On a pitch which rewarded accurate bowling as much as it did judicious strokeplay, England were superior in all departments.

Pakistan’s awfulness made it difficult to draw wider conclusions. One suggestion that this is the worst team they have sent to these shores in 50 years has gone down badly in Lahore and Karachi, yet it’s hard to think of a rival for the tag.

Where once they would rise above their unfathomable internal politics by producing classy, stylish batsmen, reverse-swinging fast bowlers and world-class leg-spinners, they are now deficient in all three categories.

Only Abdullah Shafique, in the first innings, passed 50, while their military-medium seamers spurned helpful conditions on the second day. Mohammad Ali looks as hittable now as he did when he cost 5.5 an over on debut against England at Rawalpindi in December 2022. The fielding was a car crash. It was desperate stuff.

Jofra Archer launched a few lusty blows with the bat to take the game well out of Pakistan's reach...

Before claiming three wickets in the second innings to complete the rout

They have now lost 19 of their last 30 Tests, and need to avoid defeat next week at Lord’s to avoid tipping over into negative historical territory: after this game, they have lost as many Tests (153) as they have won.

Pakistan had begun their second innings 238 behind, but for the second time in the game lost a wicket before scoring a run, Imam-ul-Haq unable to sway out of the way of a brute from Archer which brushed the glove en route to Jamie Smith.

Archer then had Awais caught at leg slip for nine, a feather in Root’s tactical cap, though not the last: when Saud Shakeel worked Tongue uppishly behind square on the leg side, Root had positioned Lawrence there especially for the stroke.

Stephen Fleming, England’s incoming coach and a lover of unusual fields during his 80 Tests in charge of New Zealand, must have enjoyed that.

It was an excellent start to Joe Root's second tenure as England captain

In between, Robinson removed Shafique, the man likeliest to detain England, with a ball that squared him up and took the edge, and later benefited from two sharp catches at third slip by Cox.

Tongue had Shan Masood caught at first slip, then pinned Salman Agha leg-before. Later, asked whether Babar Azam might return from his hand injury in time for Thursday’s second Test, Agha replied with a smile: ‘I’m more than happy to hand the captaincy on to Babar Azam.’

For the first time in a while, the gallows humour was provided not by England, but by their opponents. Progress comes in all shapes and sizes.

Sports.title: England first Test ratings: Pace duo get top marks but who lands just a 4/10 for moment of madness in victory over Pakistan?
Sports.content:
England first Test ratings: Pace duo get top marks but who lands just a 4/10 for moment of madness in victory over Pakistan?

Unlock more of the best of our cricket coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

Ben and Baz who? England got Joe Root's second coming as captain off to a flier with a walloping of Pakistan at Headingley to quash any yearnings for Bazball.

After bowling Pakistan out for 171 in the first innings – with Josh Tongue and Ollie Robinson sharing the wickets – they ran up 409 before bowling out the tourists for just 135 in 37.3 overs. So, who were the standout performers and who has work to do under the new/old skipper?

Richard Gibson was at Headingley to run the rule over Root's team.

Ben Duckett: 4/10

Defeated all ends up by a jag-backer from Pakistan seamer Mohammad Abbas, and embarrassed himself by a review that showed the ball to be hitting middle stump three-quarters up.

Ben Duckett wasted a review after being given out lbw in England's only innings

Emilio Gay: 5

Punchy response to a pair against the same opponents in last week’s warm-up fixture, but opener failed to fully cash in on favourable conditions making only 33, and was dismissed just when he was beginning to motor.

Jordan Cox: 7

Essex man played with impressive tempo in an unfamiliar role at No 3, picking off boundaries in clumps, and absorbing pressure when Pakistan bowled well. Out for 73 and will also be disappointed not to go on to a bigger score against a tiring attack.

Jordan Cox played with impressive tempo in an unfamiliar role at No 3 on his way to 73

Joe Root: 8

Took his England record number of Test wins as captain to 28, leading the side decisively in the field either side of a typically authoritative half century. Rotated his bowlers well but hardly had need to flog them either.

Harry Brook: 8

England's No 5 batted with typical flamboyance, albeit against a poor Pakistan attack, but a lackadaisical moment on 91 cost him a hundred when he was caught in the crease. Caught smartly in the slips.

Dan Lawrence: 6

England were already in credit when the Surrey man arrived at the crease, making this the gentlest of starts for his fourth incarnation as a Test cricketer. Another who will feel he could have gone on to get a three-figure score after falling for 51.

Jamie Smith: 6

A soft dismissal for England's wicketkeeper, although excusable given he was left to bat with the tail. Glovework was sound, including during sustained spells stood up to the stumps.

Jamie Smith kept well - and was particularly impressive standing up to the stumps from Ollie Robinson's seam bowling

Gus Atkinson: 6

Paceman didn’t strike until the penultimate dismissal of the match, but generally kept things tight as the others in the four-pronged seam attack reaped the rewards. Figures of one for 51 probably don't do him justice.

Ollie Robinson: 9

Set the tone with a wicket from the first ball of his return and didn’t let up with his skilful probing, taking eight in a Test for the first time and taking home half the match ball as a memento.

Ollie Robinson set the tone with a wicket from the first ball of his return to the team and didn’t let up with his skilful probing

Jofra Archer: 6.5

Began erratically up the hill, lasting just two overs in his first spell on the opening morning, but provided Root with new-ball venom at the start of the second innings when he took two quick wickets.

Josh Tongue: 9

Ran in hard throughout, breaching the 90mph barrier and completed what was his career-best Test haul of eight for 89. Erratic on occasions but when he got it right, it was very right.

PAKISTAN: Azan Awais: 2, Imam-ul-Haq: 6, Shan Masood: 5, Abdullah Shafique: 7, Saud Shakeel: 2, Salman Ali Agha: 3, Mohammad Rizwan: 5, Ali Usman: 7, Khurram Shahzad: 4, Mohammad Ali: 4, Mohammad Abbas: 5.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
