We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak The biggest-ever split within Poland’s main right-wing opposition party is a serious self-inflicted wound, signalling a more fragmented conservative landscape and complicating the right’s path back to power. While it provides a tactical boost for the Tusk government, there is still every chance of a conservative comeback if the right-wing parties cooperate effectively. Radical-right challengers At the end of last month, the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party, Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, saw the biggest split in its 25-year history. The rupture was the culmination of months of increasingly open and bitter factional conflict over the party’s future direction. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right. However, it lost power following the October 2023 parliamentary election, which led to the formation of a coalition headed up by Donald Tusk, leader of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party. Since last autumn, PiS has seen its polling numbers decline to the party’s lowest level of support for 15 years. At the same time, it has been challenged by two radical right competitors: the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and the ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which together began to match, or even exceed, PiS’s level of support. Responding to declining support At the heart of this conflict was a bitter clash between longtime party leader Jarosław Kaczyński and Mateusz Morawiecki, who served as PiS prime minister from 2017 to 2023 but grew increasingly impatient with the former’s dominance. Two main factions emerged centred on a bitter dispute on how the party should respond to declining support and political competition on its right flank. The hardline traditionalist-conservative faction, often referred to as the “butter-makers” (maślarze), was more Eurosceptic and advocated a clearer right-wing agenda that included pushing ahead with radical state reconstruction and promoting a conservative vision of national identity and traditional values. In their reading, PiS lost support to its right-wing competitors because it was not radical enough and the solution was to sharpen its ideological profile and double down on hardline rhetoric. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 This group gained influence in party structures and when, in March, Kaczyński designated one of its key figures, former education minister Przemysław Czarnek, as the party’s prime ministerial candidate in the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, this was widely seen as a clear signal favouring the traditionalist-conservative faction. Morawiecki and his allies in the modernising-technocratic faction, often called the “scouts” (harcerze), also had strong conservative values and at times were very critical of Poland’s post-1989 establishment. However, they advocated a strategy of stressing economic competence, pragmatic governance and boosting Polish prosperity over hardline rhetoric on moral-cultural issues as a more effective way of appealing to voters less influenced by traditional institutions such as the Catholic church. Although they were also critical of Brussels overreach, Morawiecki’s faction preferred to avoid escalating conflict with the EU and argued that PiS had to broaden its appeal to younger, urban, more centrist-conservative Poles who found radical cultural rhetoric off-putting. Programmatic differences and personal ambitions The conflict became so destabilising because, although rooted in genuine programmatic and strategic disagreements, personalities and individual ambitions also played a major role. While Kaczyński maintained formal control of the party, his advancing age escalated debates over PiS’s direction and leadership, and these tensions intensified after the party failed to translate its presidential candidate Karol Nawrocki’s surprise summer 2025 election victory into broader momentum. For his part, Morawiecki grew increasingly impatient and frustrated as hardliners sidelined him, while his supporters were afraid that they would be excluded from PiS candidate lists at the next election. These long-simmering tensions came to a head in April, when Morawiecki announced the formation of Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), a think tank-like platform focused on economic development The association was widely interpreted by Kaczyński and PiS hardliners as a direct challenge to party unity and the leader’s authority. The leadership ruled that Development Plus violated the PiS statute, which explicitly prohibits members from joining political organisations that conflict with the party’s goals. While Morawiecki insisted that it was simply a modest intra-party policy forum, by registering an organisation with dozens of parliamentarians, he gave his faction a formal institutional shell that could potentially act as a launchpad for his own rival breakaway party. Initially, Kaczyński and Morawiecki came to a compromise agreement whereby Development Plus would work within an official party expert group. However, in July the situation escalated when the PiS leadership issued an ultimatum banning members from participating in internal political factions (clearly targeting Development Plus) and instructing parliamentarians to sign loyalty declarations confirming that they were not involved in any such groupings. Most complied, but 40 parliamentarians affiliated with Development Plus refused to do so, accusing the leadership of political blackmail. Ultimately, Kaczyński announced that, by refusing to sign, Morawiecki and his allies had effectively left the party, while Development Plus framed it as expulsion over policy differences caused by “plotters” surrounding the party leader. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 An even more fragmented right The loss of 40 deputies means that PiS is no longer the largest parliamentary caucus, thus losing procedural advantages, committee control and visibility. The departing group includes many experienced and talented politicians, particularly in the economic and foreign policy fields. The split also reduces PiS’s funding, staffing, and in some regions local organisation, as well as creating the risk of demoralisation and further defections. Even if the Polish right secures a parliamentary majority at the next election, PiS’s relative influence could be greatly reduced. Although Kaczyński’s formal party leadership remains unquestioned, the split signals to the broader right that his authority is waning and undermines his claim to be the undisputed hegemon and central broker on the right; he is increasingly now one leader among several. It also further erodes the model that Kaczyński has built over many years as the main ideologue and ultimate arbiter of internal PiS factions. In earlier crises, this personal authority and control gave him leverage to keep everyone on board so that disagreements were managed internally, and even disillusioned figures usually stayed in, or returned to, the party. Indeed, by adding a fourth distinctive player, the PiS split further compounds the divisions on the Polish right that have deepened since the last election, transforming what was once a relatively consolidated “big tent” bloc into a multi-polar competitive field. For sure, polls conducted after the split show the combined right-wing vote as competitive overall, but even if this level of support remains stable, or even increases slightly, it is now divided across more options. This is significant because Poland’s proportional electoral system uses the d’Hondt counting system that favours larger groupings. It also creates the risk that smaller right-wing parties such as Morawiecki’s new grouping could fall below the 5% parliamentary representation threshold, so their votes are excluded from seat allocation. All of this makes it harder for the right to translate raw voter support into political power. Moreover, even if the right-wing parties win a combined parliamentary majority, post-election coordination becomes much more complex with four (or more) actors whose leaders’ rivalries, different priorities and historical animosities complicate forming a stable coalition government. Nawrocki’s role will be crucial In the light of this, Nawrocki has emerged as a critical unifier with crossover appeal across the fractured Polish right. His presidential election victory showed that he could attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists and consolidate a broad right-wing coalition, including the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. As president, he operates outside direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative unifying figure on the right, which gives him much greater moral and symbolic stature than a partisan leader immersed in day-to-day machinations. Nawrocki has also used his constitutional powers and standing, including a legislative veto that the government lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, to position himself assertively as a powerful counterweight to the Tusk administration, and is currently Poland’s most popular politician. Nonetheless, Nawrocki’s potential to act as a possible right-wing unifier and broker is limited. For sure, he can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 However, Nawrocki has no formal unifying mandate and his success ultimately depends on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Without broader cooperation, even his efforts will only mitigate, not eliminate, the damage from a divided right, and personal and ideological rivalries currently run deep and cannot be easily overridden. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally above the fray and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, he also lacks the control over party organisational machinery needed to micro-manage and enforce messy backroom deals. Pivotal but not transformative? Initial polling conducted since the split suggests that Morawiecki’s new grouping would likely clear the 5% threshold and enter parliament with a small-to-medium-sized fraction; according to Politico Europe, it is currently averaging around 6% support. Although this could make it a pivotal player in coalition talks, it does not suggest that the grouping can dramatically reshape the country’s political landscape. Moreover, its support appears to be drawn mainly from PiS’s traditional electoral base, so it is simply further fragmenting the existing right-wing vote rather than drawing in a significant number of new voters who hitherto supported the governing coalition parties. For sure, Morawiecki‘s project has advantages that many newcomers lack, notably its leader’s very high name recognition and a sizeable bloc of high-profile, political heavyweight allies, much larger than any previous PiS breakaway faction. His grouping immediately became the third largest parliamentary fraction, giving it visibility, funding, and organisational backbone. However, although there are some rare exceptions that usually involve major figures with significant resources breaking from established parties, it is a familiar pattern in post-1989 Polish politics for a brand new “startup” party to show an early bounce, benefiting from initial media coverage, only to fade or disappear as voters drift back to more established groupings or abstain at the next election. Sustaining momentum requires local organisational infrastructure, reliable funding, rapid professionalisation, and a clear identity, which new parties often lack. Indeed, to be successful a new startup should really attract at least 10% support initially simply because of its “newness”. Over the years, PiS breakaway politicians have established new parties that either quickly disappeared from the political scene or were eventually reintegrated into the grouping. Temporary relief for Tusk From a short-term tactical perspective, the PiS split is a welcome political gift for the Tusk government, shifting the media focus away from criticisms of its record and recent scandals and controversies. It has for example, blunted the opposition’s ability to maintain a sustained assault over a scandal involving high earnings for, and mismanagement by, a KO-connected doctor, alleged VIP access and potential patient harm at the Warsaw South Hospital, which had previously dominated the summer news headlines. The ruling coalition is likely to survive until next year's election, but its prospects are hampered by a weak domestic record, writes @AleksSzczerbiak The government has therefore made security key to its reelection narrative, but that also carries risks https://t.co/w2UeNaTwAO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 1, 2026 However, the PiS split has not resolved the deeper image and performance problems that have dragged down the Tusk government’s approval ratings. The administration struggles with perceptions of slow delivery on promises while facing a hostile president, and if these problems persist, or new controversies reignite strongly once the PiS drama cools, the government will very quickly find itself back on the defensive. The PiS split only provides temporary relief; to win the next election, the ruling coalition needs to improve its own standing, not rely on opposition mistakes. World.title: Polish NGOs urge PM’s “right-hand man” to withdraw constitutional court candidacy
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A group of Polish civil society organisations has urged a former government minister to withdraw his candidacy to become a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, saying his close ties to the prime minister could undermine confidence in the court’s independence. In a joint statement, the nine organisations say that restoring the legitimacy of the court, which has been in crisis since 2015 following illegitimate judicial appointments made by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, requires not only addressing legal irregularities but also rebuilding public trust. “The existence of the Constitutional Tribunal as an organ of judicial power only makes sense if it is an independent arbiter,” they say. 🔴Wspólnie z innymi organizacjami apelujemy do dr. M. Berka o rezygnację z kandydowania do TK, a do Sejmu o wybór osoby niezależnej politycznie. Droga do praworządności to nie „odbijanie” Trybunału, ale odbudowa jego autorytetu. Przeczytajcie nasz apel, link w komentarzu ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/LPlbk39lNr — Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka (@hfhrpl) August 20, 2026 The appeal follows Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s announcement that Maciej Berek, who until recently served as a government minister and whom Tusk has described as his “right-hand man”, would be put forward as a candidate for the Constitutional Tribunal. The choice has drawn particular attention because Tusk came to power promising to “depoliticise” the court after the previous PiS government appointed former politicians as judges. “Regardless of the extent to which the tribunal has become politicised, the way to reform this institution cannot be for it to be ‘recaptured’ or ‘taken over’ by another ruling majority,” the NGOs write in the statement. The organisations, including the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, the Institute of Public Affairs and the Stefan Batory Foundation, say Berek’s close ties to the current political leadership could cause his appointment to be perceived as political, regardless of his legal qualifications or personal integrity. “Not only must courts and tribunals operate independently and impartially, but citizens must also recognise and have confidence in that independence and impartiality. This is not possible when judges are appointed whose links to the government are immediately apparent,” the organisations add. “We therefore call on Dr Maciej Berek to withdraw his candidacy in the interests of the independence of the constitutional judiciary.” The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law. State pollster @CBOS_Info found 61% now hold a negative view, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017 https://t.co/P3fbTTbS5C — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 The organisations also argue that Berek’s nomination goes against a principle that the current ruling coalition sought to introduce: that anyone who has held political office within the previous four years should be barred from appointment to the tribunal. Berek was a government minister until last week. The coalition’s proposal was included in a bill approved by parliament in 2024. However, the Constitutional Tribunal itself later ruled the provision unconstitutional after former President Andrzej Duda, an ally of PiS, referred the legislation for review. “Although this law has not come into force, it would be reasonable for the Sejm to adhere to the standard it has adopted,” they said, referring to the lower chamber of the parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 However, the selection of Berek, whose candidacy was put forward by MPs from Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has exposed divisions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from centre-right to left. “We were supposed to be different from PiS; we were supposed to do things differently, not exactly the same way,” Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s (Lewica) parliamentary caucus, told Polsat News. Paweł Śliz, leader of the centre-right Poland 2050’s (Polska 2050) caucus, said Berek would make an excellent Constitutional Tribunal judge were it not for his recent role as a government minister. “I consider him an excellent, outstanding professional; I value his experience and expertise. However, my position on this matter is unequivocal. I will not compromise my principles,” he told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The chief justice of the constitutional court has refused to accept four new judges appointed by parliament but whom the opposition-aligned president has refused to swear in. The decision deepens an unprecedented standoff over Poland's top court https://t.co/B02DKA3uBL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 9, 2026 Given that the government has a majority of just nine in the 460-seat Sejm, it would only require a small number of MPs from Tusk’s coalition opposing Berek’s nomination for him to lose the vote. Last week, Tusk said that he “understands” concerns from some coalition partners but that he would “try to convince those who have doubts”. However, even if Berek is approved by the Sejm, the law states that new TK judges must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. It remains unclear what the president would do in the case of Berek. Presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz told PAP on Thursday that “there are serious doubts” about Berek’s formal qualifications to become a Constitutional Tribunal judge. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though he was never a member of the PiS party). ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland has summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) have discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból. “Partnership requires mutual respect,” declared foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for [the] IDF’s excessive use of force[,] are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations.” Partnership requires mutual respect. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for IDF’s excessive use of force are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations. https://t.co/9H0nhiDE4H — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 20, 2026 The incident in question took place in April 2024, when Israeli drones struck a convoy delivering humanitarian aid from World Central Kitchen (WCK), a major international food relief NGO. The attack killed seven aid workers, including Soból. The incident caused outrage in Poland, whose government demanded that Israel fully explain the circumstances. The IDF expressed “sincere sorrow” over the deaths and pledged to carry out a “thorough and transparent” investigation. On Wednesday this week, the IDF announced that it had closed the case after determining “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident”. The IDF said that its troops had identified a gunman on one of the trucks in the convoy. It also claimed that WCK had hired an armed security force to protect the convoy without coordinating that with IDF authorities and that the convoy deviated from the route previously agreed with the IDF. However, the IDF also acknowledged that it had mistakenly identified several individuals as being armed. It added that attempts to contact WCK representatives over a half-hour period while the convoy was on the move were unsuccessful. The IDF noted that, after the incident, two military officers were removed from their positions while three others were reprimanded. But it found that there was no basis for any further action. ⚖️ IDF prosecution rules on five FFAM cases: The IDF says its General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism has completed reviews of approximately 150 exceptional wartime incidents since the beginning of the war and transferred them to the Military Prosecution. Decisions… pic.twitter.com/H5g4qOu5e2 — Israel Realtime (@IsraelRealtime) August 19, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s foreign ministry issued a statement saying that it was “greatly disappointed to receive the information provided about the discontinuation of the proceedings by the Israeli military authorities”. It announced that it had summoned the Israeli ambassador in order to “communicate a critical assessment of the actions taken to date to clarify the causes and course of the tragedy”. It also noted that Polish prosecutors are still conducting their own investigation and that the foreign ministry had informed the Israeli ambassador that they “expect the Israeli side will provide the relevant Polish authorities with all necessary explanations and materials requested”. “The circumstances of the tragedy should be fully investigated and [we] do not accept that the perpetrators are avoiding legal and moral responsibility,” concluded the ministry, adding that “the families deserve adequate compensation”. We strongly condemn the Israeli military prosecutor’s account of the deaths of our seven colleagues on April 1, 2024. And we fundamentally disagree with their decision about criminal investigations into the IDF airstrikes that killed our team. Read our full statement here:… — World Central Kitchen (@WCKitchen) August 19, 2026 The IDF’s findings were also condemned by WCK itself, which called them “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. It added that, “at the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody”. The NGO repeated its demand for an independent investigation into the incident, “because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct”. On Friday, the UK, Canada and Australia, whose citizens were also killed in the strike, issued a joint statement calling the IDF’s decision to drop the investigation “shameful” and another example of the lack of accountability for incidents in Gaza. Joint statement from the foreign ministries of Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom on Israel closing the investigation into strikes on the World Central Kitchen convoy in Gaza on 1 April 2024 ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/V3CZe286tN — Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (@FCDOGovUK) August 21, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: New official tasked with promoting Poland criticised over error-strewn, potentially AI-generated report
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing errors and which shows signs of being generated by artificial intelligence. The document mislocated major Polish cities and included bizarre language mixing Polish and English. It was marked as being part of a project financed by the sport and tourism ministry, though the ministry itself has denied that claim. The opposition has called on prosecutors to investigate potential misuse of public funds. ⁉️ Czy “Markę Polska” ma nam wygenerować sztuczna inteligencja? ⁉️ Czy Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki zapłaciło 200 000 złotych w ramach zadania publicznego za raport wygenerowany przez AI? ⁉️ Czy mogę prosić Panią Minister prof. @b_mroz_gorgon o odniesienie się do tych pytań… pic.twitter.com/lM2AY88oAh — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 The official in question, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, is a professor at Wrocław University of Economics who was appointed three weeks ago as the government’s plenipotentiary for the promotion of Poland’s brand, a newly created position. She was presented at a press conference by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. However, this week, journalists and commentators began highlighting cases of bizarre errors from a report, titled A Self-Portrait of the Poles (Polaków Portret Własny), published last year with Mróz-Gorgoń named as the author, in her position as president of a think tank called Marka Polska (Brand Poland). The report contained some glaring errors, such as describing the city of Katowice as being in “north central” Poland (whereas in fact it is in the south) and Wrocław as being in the “northwest” (when it is actually in the southwest). Geografia – czyli gdzie leżą Katowice A propos miast jest też ciekawy chochlik lub też, jakby to powiedział ktoś złośliwy, klasyczna halucynacja AI. Przy opisie badań FGI miasta opisane są w następujący sposób (zdjęcie poniżej): 👉 Olsztyn – północny wschód 👉 Szczecin -… pic.twitter.com/SF6XBRfhWS — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 Other parts contain strange analysis, such as noting that “after World War Two, Germany did not build its brand on the Holocaust”. The text also features unusual language, including random use of words in English, some of which have been turned into Polish ones. It is also regularly features words written in capital letters. One sentence, for example, refers to “INSTABILNOŚĆ” and “REZILIENCE”, presumably meaning “instability” and “resilience”, but neither of which is a Polish word. Another section claims that 95% of Poles born after 1990 are “polilingwalni” (an invented Polonised version of “polylingual”) who speak “angielski fluent”, a strange linguistic mix that means they speak English fluently. As well as the unusual language, the very claim that 95% of young Poles speak fluent English, as well as that many additionally speak Mandarin, has been questioned by many commentators. The report also contains bizarre errors in footnotes, which are numbered randomly (on one page, three consecutive footnotes are numbered “41, 517, 6”) and some of which are completely empty. A number of expert commentators have suggested that the text contains clear indications that it was generated by AI, a claim supported by evidence from programmes that check texts for AI-generated content. AI czy nie AI, oto jest pytanie Czytając ten raport kilkukrotnie, trudno mi było pozbyć się wrażenia, że nikt poważny, a szczególnie naukowiec z tytułem doktora habilitowanego, nie wygenerowałby dużych części raportu, za który zapłacili podatnicy, w jakimś LLM. No bo przecież… pic.twitter.com/jyTexgmeXS — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 As well as bearing Mróz-Gorgoń’s name as author, the report also features on its front cover the logo of the sport and tourism ministry. The first page then includes a note saying that the project was carried out under an initiative co-financed by the ministry. After the issue began to draw attention and criticism on Thursday, the ministry issued a statement saying that the report was not ordered by them, was not part of any agreement to which the ministry was a party, and that no request to use the ministry’s logo was submitted. However, a social media post last November by deputy sport and tourism minister Piotr Borys shows him attending an event to present the report. He thanked Mróz-Gorgoń for coordinating the project and inviting him to the presentation. 📚W Akademii Leona Koźmińskiego odbyła się prezentacja raportu „Polaków Portret Własny”, przygotowanego Think Tank Marka Polska. To wyjątkowe wydarzenie poświęcone premierze badań dotyczących DNA Marki Polska. 🧬To pierwsze tak kompleksowe badanie, które pokazuje, kim jesteśmy… pic.twitter.com/jb7KdCJTPM — Piotr Borys (@piotr_borys) November 26, 2025 On Thursday evening, Mróz-Gorgoń herself addressed the controversy in an interview with Polsat News. She said that the report was actually a “work in progress” that “should never have appeared in the public space”. However, she still defended the work, saying that “the research was conducted reliably” and “the conclusions stand up to scrutiny”. But she also admitted that the writing of the report had been “aided by artificial intelligence”. In separate remarks to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), she said that “we used AI tools solely for transcription, summarising and text editing; they did not design research content or draw conclusions…We worked according to social science methodology, diligently and without cutting corners”. Meanwhile, on the Marka Polska think tank’s website, where the report had been published, it was initially changed on Thursday to being marked as a “draft version” before later being deleted entirely. Od raportu i deklaracji, że “praca badawcza [została] przeprowadzona zgodnie z zasadami nauk społecznych, rzetelnie i merytorycznie, w oparciu o opisaną metodologię”, przez “work in progress”, aż do “Oops! That page can’t be found”. Myślę, że to słowo “Oops!” jest najlepszym… pic.twitter.com/OaSTxkwKwa — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 On Thursday evening, the main opposition party, Law and Justice (PiS), announced that it was submitting requests to both prosecutors and the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (ABW) to investigate the use of around 200,000 zloty (€46,380) in state funds for the project that the report was allegedly part of. PiS has also called on Mróz-Gorgoń to resign or to be fired. On Friday, a deputy digital affairs minister, Dariusz Standerski, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that “all the circumstances surrounding the creation of this report will be clarified”. The controversy around Mróz-Gorgoń comes just days after the sport and tourism ministry was involved in the launch of a new advertising campaign designed to encourage tourism to Poland, but which many commentators have argued was poorly conceived and executed. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland tests 250 km/h train speeds for planned cuts to intercity journey times
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A speed of 253 km/h (157 mph) has been reached by a Pendolino train during tests carried out as part of preparations to speed up rail connections between Poland’s major cities from next year. The plans will see the journey time between Warsaw and Kraków cut to well under two hours. “Polish rail is accelerating – and 250 km/h is just the beginning,” declared the infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak, alluding to plans for Poland to later begin running trains at speeds of up to 320 km/h. Osiągnęliśmy 250 km/h na Centralnej Magistrali Kolejowej❗🚅 Dzisiejsze nocne testy systemu GSM-R na linii nr 4 zakończyły się pełnym sukcesem. Oznacza to, że pociągi pojadą tą trasą z rozkładową prędkością 250 km/h już w przyszłym roku❗ Pozwoli to znacznie skrócić czas… pic.twitter.com/ndXvePZP4t — PLK SA (@PKP_PLK_SA) August 18, 2026 The tests on the GSM-R data transmission system, a communication standard designed to be used at very high speeds, were carried out on Monday night. Trains will be able to run on Poland’s Central Main Line (CMK), which connects Warsaw with Kraków and Katowice, at a scheduled speed of 250 km/h from December 2027. That will cut the expected journey time between Warsaw and Kraków, the country’s two largest cities, by around half an hour to 1 hour and 52 minutes, reports rail news service Portal Kolejowy. It will also be possible to travel from the capital to Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, in around three hours. The fastest current connection is 3 hours and 30 minutes. Reaching the target speed of 250 km/h was a “very important moment for Polish rail”, said Maciej Kaczorek, a board member of PKP Polskie Linie Kolejowe, the state railway infrastructure manager, quoted by news website Money.pl. Poland has been operating Pendolinos, built by France’s Alstom, since 2014. The trains are designed to run at speeds of up to 250 km/h, but currently operate at a maximum of 200 km/h in Poland and run on routes connecting Warsaw, Kraków, Wrocław and the Tricity area. However, this week’s tests are not a record rail speed in Poland. In 2013, a Pendolino reached 293 km/h during a test on the CMK a year before the high-speed trains commenced passenger services in the country. A Polish Pendolino high-speed train has begun running in the Czech Republic for the first time. The Prague-Bohumín service will run until June as part of a certification process that Polish operator PKP Intercity hopes will lead to a Warsaw-Prague route https://t.co/hmUNd7ft0E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026 Speaking to Rynek Kolejowy, deputy infrastructure minister Piotr Malepszak said that it had “taken too long” for the network to be adapted to allow regular speeds of 250 km/h. The current government, which took power in December 2023, has much broader plans for expanding high-speed rail travel in Poland, including building 2,700 km of tracks capable of carrying trains at 320 km/h. In December 2025, state rail operator PKP Intercity launched a tender for 20 such trains. They would cut the journey time between Warsaw and Gdańsk, on Poland’s Baltic coast, to around 100 minutes – from 2 hours 25 minutes currently – by 2040, Malepszak told the Polish Press Agency in June. Passenger numbers on Poland’s rail network have been booming in recent years. In the first half of 2026, a record 44.7 million passengers travelled with PKP Intercity, more than 10% up on the previous year’s record and some 45% higher than three years earlier. Poland has launched a tender to buy 20 trains that can reach speeds of 320 km/h (199 mph), making them the fastest ever to travel on Polish tracks. World.title: Polish government proposes middle-class tax cuts funded by increased rates for wealthiest
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has unveiled plans to reduce income tax rates for an estimated 3.5 million people earning around or slightly above average salaries. The costs of the cuts would be covered by increasing the tax rate for large companies and individuals with the highest earnings. The changes, which Prime Minister Donald Tusk says are intended to “provide relief and assistance to the growing middle class”, would come into effect from next year – when the government is facing re-election. However, the proposals still require approval from parliament, where Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, has a majority, and President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of bills. 📊 Nowa skala PIT będzie lepiej dopasowana do rosnących wynagrodzeń. Do 130 tys. zł pozostaje stawka 12%, między 130 a 150 tys. zł pojawi się 24%, a 32% zacznie obowiązywać dopiero powyżej 150 tys. zł. 💰 #WięcejWPortfelu pic.twitter.com/1S2MpSkVoC — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 19, 2026 The main elements of the proposed changes, which were outlined by Tusk and finance minister Andrzej Domański on Wednesday, are an increase in the earnings threshold at which the lowest rate of income tax is paid and the introduction of a new rate between the lowest and highest earnings brackets. Currently, there are two income tax brackets: the first taxes earnings of up to 120,000 zloty (around €27,800) at a rate of 12%; the second taxes earnings above that level at a rate of 32%. There is also a tax-free allowance for earnings of up to 30,000 zloty. Meanwhile, anyone who earns more than 1 million zloty a year pays an additional “solidarity levy” (effectively a third tax bracket) of 4% on income above that amount. Under the new proposals, the threshold for the first 12% tax bracket would be raised to 130,000 zloty. For earnings between 130,000 and 150,000 zloty, a new tax bracket of 24% would be introduced. Then earnings above 150,000 would be taxed at 32%. Tusk noted that, since his government took office, wages in Poland have increased by around 30%, bringing increasing numbers of people into the higher tax bracket. According to figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, in June this year, average monthly earnings at companies employing more than nine people were 9,401.58 zloty, the equivalent of almost 113,000 zloty a year. “We’re not talking about millionaires here; we’re talking about a growing middle class…on whose shoulders the financing of state security, defence spending, etc. rests to a large extent,” said Domański. “We want to change this…so that those who work hard to earn their average wage can clearly feel the relief,” added Tusk. “And we want this to be financed by the wealthiest companies and the wealthiest individuals, who have the lowest tax burden.” The number of ultra-wealthy individuals in Poland has more than doubled since 2021, a faster rate of growth than anywhere else in the world, according to a new study https://t.co/MNKgmjzn2U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 Therefore, in order to finance the middle-class tax cuts, Tusk and Domański announced that the government would seek to increase corporate income tax from 19% to 22% for firms and tax capital groups that generate annual revenues above €50 million. Meanwhile, the solidarity levy for individuals earning over 1 million zloty a year would be increased by one percentage point, to 5%. “I am absolutely convinced that this will make our tax system more equitable,” declared Tusk. However, he also conceded that raising the income-tax-free amount from 30,000 to 60,000 zloty – as his Civic Platform (KO) party promised to do within its first 100 days in office – would not be possible for budgetary reasons, in particular the need to finance high defence spending. Poland has introduced a new type of account that will allow individuals to invest up to 100,000 zloty (€23,200) tax free. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build savings and channel money into the domestic financial market https://t.co/1xDHHJGYKX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 14, 2026 The prime minister said that the planned tax changes would be discussed further this week at a cabinet meeting devoted to next year’s state budget, which is currently being prepared. The relevant legislation will subsequently be submitted to parliament, with the aim of bringing it into force in 2027. However, Tusk acknowledged that there is a strong possibility of a veto by Nawrocki, who has blocked dozens of government bills, including fiscal measures. In December, Nawrocki vetoed an increase in the tax on alcoholic and sweet drinks. Last month, he effectively blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits by sending it to the constitutional court for review. However, he did approve a law increasing the corporate income tax rate for banks. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 Next year’s budget will be closely watched given that Poland’s fiscal situation has become increasingly problematic in recent years. In 2024, the European Union placed Poland under its excessive deficit procedure, requiring Warsaw to commit to measures to bring down the deficit. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. Given that Poland will hold parliamentary elections in autumn 2027, it is unlikely that either the government or Nawrocki – who will be supporting the right-wing opposition – will be keen on any fiscal measures that either raise taxes or reduce spending in areas such as social policy and defence. Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland launches tourism campaign featuring Lewandowski, Eisenberg and Rubik
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to promote itself internationally and attract more tourists from “key European markets” and the United States. The new initiative, which has the slogan “Poland. More than you expected”, features global Polish icons such as football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, and Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, who received Polish citizenship last year. A series of videos, the first of which was released Tuesday, will aim to present Poland as “modern, safe, diverse and authentic”, as well as “defying stereotypes”, says sports and tourism minister Jakub Rutnicki. Commissioned by his ministry and launched by the Polish Tourism Organisation (POT), the campaign will be conducted in Germany, Spain, Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States. The first video promotes Warsaw, Poland’s capital, and features Lewandowski, Rubik and Eisenberg appearing near the city’s landmarks. Polish actor Nikodem Rozbicki, meanwhile, plays the role of renowned 19th-century Polish composer Fryderyk Chopin. In the 30-second spot, Chopin’s character declares that Warsaw is “where my heart is” – a reference to the fact that Chopin’s heart, preserved in cognac, was brought back to the city from Paris by his sister shortly after his death in 1849 and is now immured in a pillar in the city’s Holy Cross Church. Lewandowski, who recently joined US football team Chicago Fire, tells viewers that Poland offers “more than you expected”, a reference to the campaign’s main slogan, which suggests to viewers that Poland may surprise them positively. “Research shows that people who have visited Poland rate it much more favourably than their previous perceptions or media reports suggested,” notes POT in its press release. Magdalena Krucz, the head of POT, adds that she believes the campaign “will be as surprising to audiences as Poland itself is to tourists who come to us for the first time”. However, the slogan is not new: it has been used by POT to promote Poland since 2021. The new campaign will also feature Nobel Peace Prize winner and former president Lech Wałęsa, who led the Solidarity movement that brought down Poland’s former communist regime. POT notes that he remains “one of the most recognisable symbols in the world of the fight for freedom and democracy”. The music is arranged by Radzimir Dębski, better known as Jimek, a Polish composer and conductor who has regularly performed with US rap legend Snoop Dogg. Polish-American NBA star @JeremySochan has joined a campaign to promote Poland as a tourist destination. His appearance has been received positively, but Sochan responded directly to one commentator who said a black person shouldn't be advertising Poland https://t.co/KXDok7IAXP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 15, 2024 Poland has experienced a tourism boom in recent years. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation, behind only Malta. The biggest tourist draw is the historic city of Kraków, which was last year named the best city break destination in Europe by members of British consumer association and magazine Which? for the fifth time. This year, Time Out magazine rated Kraków the 16th best city in the world. However, the country has a wide range of tourist-friendly destinations, including long, sandy beaches on the northern Baltic coast, mountains in the south, the lake district of Masuria, as well as many historic cities and modern museums and galleries. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 The city of Lublin in eastern Poland, which will be a European City of Culture in 2029, last year welcomed a record 2.2 million visitors, including over half a million from abroad. The city is known for its rich Jewish history, and featured prominently in the 2024 Oscar-nominated film A Real Pain, directed by and starring Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Lublin and the nearby town of Krasnystaw. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP within a decade, from about 5% now. The strategy includes creating a “Polish brand” through which internationally recognised athletes, artists, historical figures and products are showcased more prominently. Last month, the government appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. The city of Lublin in eastern Poland welcomed a record 2.2 million visitors in 2025. That included 506,000 from abroad, which was also the highest ever figure, with Brits, Israelis and Americans the most common foreign visitors https://t.co/6yMrRcf6ml — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 28, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Warsaw Uprising veteran and activist Wanda Traczyk-Stawska dies aged 99
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Wanda Traczyk-Stawska, a veteran of the Warsaw Uprising against Nazi-German occupation during World War Two, has died aged 99. Traczyk-Stawska, who survived imprisonment in German camps after the uprising, in her later years became a vocal advocate for the rights of women and disabled people. “Warsaw has lost someone extraordinary,” wrote Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, announcing her death on Wednesday. “A heroine, a soldier…but above all a teacher who, throughout her life, taught us what matters most: courage, dignity, and responsibility for our fellow human beings.” Odeszła Pani Wanda. Trudno w to uwierzyć. Warszawa straciła kogoś wyjątkowego – Bohaterkę, żołnierkę Powstania Warszawskiego, Honorową Obywatelkę miasta. Ale przede wszystkim nauczycielkę, która przez całe życie uczyła nas tego, co najważniejsze: odwagi, godności i… pic.twitter.com/uSNcsZ7c1P — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) August 19, 2026 Traczyk-Stawska, born in Warsaw in 1927, was only 12 years old when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. She initially became involved in the Grey Ranks (Szare Szeregi), an underground resistance movement associated with the Polish scouting movement, participating in sabotage operations. She later joined the Home Army (AK), Poland’s main resistance force, and, at the age of 17, served as a riflewoman and liaison during the Warsaw Uprising, taking the nom de guerre “Pączek” (meaning “Bud”). Traczyk-Stawska was seriously injured while fighting in the uprising. After the revolt was defeated, she was taken prisoner and subsequently held in various prisoner-of-war camps in Germany until the end of the war. After returning to Poland, Traczyk-Stawska earned a degree in psychology and began working as a teacher of disabled children in Warsaw. At the same time, she became an active figure in commemorating the uprising and its participants. In her final years, Traczyk-Stawska also became politically active. In 2018, she visited parliament to support a protest by disabled people and their carers, who were seeking more state support. Two years later, at the age of 93, she and another female uprising veteran, Hanna Stadnik, joined the mass Women’s Strike protests that broke out in response to the introduction of a near-total ban on abortion under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. “We women will not relent this time,” she told broadcaster TVN at the time. “In the uprising, we fought for our freedom, because there is no dignity without freedom. If we are currently treated like incubators, we have the right to fight for our dignity…We will fight – unarmed, but to the last woman – not to be treated like objects.” Traczyk-Stawska was also among a group of female Uprising veterans who that year criticised PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński for wearing, during a speech condemning the Women’s Strike protests, a badge featuring the anchor symbol that was used by the Home Army during the war. She was also an advocate for women’s rights more broadly. In 2023, in a speech at the 79th anniversary of the uprising, Traczyk-Stawska noted that, “at the beginning, the generals shouted: ‘Why do we need so many women?'” But, by the time the uprising ended, “we had been given the same rights as boys. And we won’t get rid of these rights. Because everyone, whether a man or a woman, is a citizen of this country and has equality written into the constitution”. Her speech then became overtly political, saying that “this [PiS] government needs to be completely changed, as it doesn’t remember that women have their own position enshrined in the constitution. That we are equal to men.” In both the 2020 and 2025 presidential elections, Traczyk-Stawska expressed support for the candidacy of Trzaskowski, who is a deputy leader of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party that is PiS’s main opponent. However, in both elections, Trzaskowski lost to PiS-backed candidates. Odeszła Wanda Traczyk-Stawska ps. „Pączek” – Bohaterka, Patriotka, wzór odwagi i niezłomności. Pokazywała, że prawdziwy patriotyzm to budowanie wspólnoty, empatia i otwartość na świat. Cześć Jej pamięci! 🕯️🤍 Najgłębsze wyrazy współczucia dla Bliskich. pic.twitter.com/nY0ijDSBlJ — Monika Sikora ⚡️ (@Moni_Sikora) August 19, 2026 Following news of Traczyk-Stawska’s death, many prominent figures paid tribute to her, in particular from the current KO-led ruling coalition. “Farewell, heroine,” wrote KO leader and Prime Minister Donald Tusk, sharing a photo of himself with Traczyk-Stawska and quoting one of her statements: “Do not stand, do not watch when evil happens, but react immediately, for that is your duty.” While she had fought against German occupation, Traczyk-Stawska later called for reconciliation. In her 2023 speech, she called Germany “our best neighbour” and said that the two countries must now “stand together”, including supporting Ukraine against Russian aggression. World.title: Tesco Teams Up With Wolt. Can Express Delivery Save Its Czech Business?
World.content:
Tesco will launch a new express delivery service in Prague in September, working with Wolt to deliver orders within 40 minutes.

The service, called Tesco Hned, will initially be available from selected Tesco stores in the Czech capital.

The launch comes as speculation continues over a possible sale of Tesco’s Central European operations and the British retailer’s future in the Czech Republic.



Tesco Hned is designed for customers who need groceries and other everyday products quickly rather than as part of a larger planned shop. Orders will include food, drinks, cosmetics, household products, pet supplies and other goods.

The company says its standard online shopping service will continue to focus on larger orders, while the new option is aimed at customers who need a few items immediately.

Tesco has already tested the service at six Prague stores. It plans to extend Tesco Hned to another 22 locations in the coming weeks.

Delivery will be provided through Wolt, giving customers access to Tesco products through the courier company’s platform.

Tesco faces questions over its future

The new service comes at a difficult time for Tesco in Central Europe.

According to the Financial Times, Tesco’s British owners are considering selling their operations in the region, including the Czech Republic. The Schwarz Group, which owns Lidl and Kaufland, and Polish retailer Biedronka have reportedly been mentioned among potential buyers.

Tesco has not announced plans to leave the Czech market, and the launch of Tesco Hned suggests the company continues to invest in its services.

World.title: New Budget Airline to Launch Direct Flights from Prague to Santiago de Compostela
World.content:
A new budget airline is set to launch direct flights between Prague and Santiago de Compostela in Spain, giving travellers from the Czech capital a new low-cost option for visiting Galicia and the famous Camino de Santiago.

Fly2Galicia plans to begin operating flights from Santiago–Rosalía de Castro Airport to eight European destinations from December 1, 2026.



Prague is among the international destinations, alongside Brussels, Munich, Venice and Milan.

Tickets are already on sale, with fares from Prague to Santiago de Compostela starting at €51.

The new route could be particularly attractive in 2027, when Santiago de Compostela will celebrate a Holy Year. The occasion is expected to bring increased numbers of pilgrims completing the Camino de Santiago, one of Europe’s best-known pilgrimage routes.

There is, however, one detail to note: Fly2Galicia will not operate the initial flights itself. The airline says the routes will be operated by another European carrier, which has not yet been named.

The new service comes as airlines continue to expand connections between Central Europe and Spain. Wizz Air has also announced new flights to Santiago from Rome and Warsaw starting this December.

What to see in Santiago de Compostela

For travellers arriving from Prague, Santiago’s historic centre is the main attraction. Its UNESCO-listed Old Town combines Romanesque, Gothic, Baroque and Neoclassical architecture, with the Cathedral of Santiago at the heart of the city.

The Mercado de Abastos is another popular stop, offering fresh seafood and local produce. Galicia is also known for Albariño, a white wine that pairs particularly well with the region’s seafood.

Santiago can also serve as a base for exploring Galicia, with trips to A Coruña, Vigo and the Rías Baixas wine region, as well as the area’s beaches and islands.

World.title: Russell Crowe to Perform in Prague for the First Time in May 2027
World.content:
Oscar-winning actor and musician Russell Crowe will bring his band, The Gentlemen Barbers, to Forum Karlín on May 23, 2027, for their first-ever Prague concert.

Russell Crowe is best known for his roles in Gladiator, A Beautiful Mind and A Good Year, but long before Hollywood, music was a major part of his life.

On May 23, 2027, the Oscar and Golden Globe winner will bring that side of his career to Prague for the first time, performing with his band The Gentlemen Barbers at Forum Karlín.



You can get your ticket here.

The concert will also mark the opening night of the band’s European tour.

The Gentlemen Barbers have been developing their sound over the past four years, although many of the musicians have worked with Crowe for decades. The lineup includes drummer Dave Kelly and trumpeter Stewart Kirwan, both former members of Thirty Odd Foot of Grunts, as well as musicians who have collaborated with Crowe on later projects.

The band also features pianist Stu Hunter, guitarist Chris Kamzelas and bassist James Hazelwood. Irish singer Lorraine O’Reilly, known for her powerful, raspy vocals, has performed with Crowe since they first met while recording a duet for the Bible Code Sundays album Walk Like Kings.

The result is a band that moves between R&B, gospel, country, dark waltzes and singalong anthems, with storytelling at the centre of its music.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by JV Classics (@jvclassics)

“There is an attitude about this band. It’s got a groove. We do a lot of story songs, but we also know we are here to blow out cobwebs and give the audience a good night,” Crowe says.

For Crowe, music has remained a constant alongside his film career. He began performing in bands, touring and releasing records before moving into musical theatre and eventually film. He has continued to perform throughout his decades in Hollywood, despite his demanding acting career.

“I love playing in pubs. It’s what I did growing up. Even though my day job has a huge claim on my time, I’ve never not played music,” he says.

Russell Crowe’s Indoor Garden Party & The Gentlemen Barbers takes place on May 23, 2027, at 8 p.m. at Forum Karlín in Prague.

World.title: Students in Czech Republic Face Higher Rents as Housing Costs Rise
World.content:
Students looking for private accommodation in Czech university cities this year are facing higher rents, with prices for some types of housing up by as much as 14 percent compared with 2025.

The increase comes as demand for student accommodation reaches its annual peak ahead of the winter semester.

Data from several Czech property platforms show that the busiest period started earlier this year, meaning students who have not yet found accommodation may face a more limited and expensive selection in September.

Those unable to secure a place in a student dormitory generally have three alternatives: renting a small apartment alone, taking a private room in a shared apartment, or renting a bed in shared accommodation.



The most expensive option is usually a small one-bedroom apartment with a kitchenette, typically around 30 square meters. According to the REMAX network, monthly rents for these apartments range from more than CZK 7,000 in Ústí nad Labem to around CZK 14,000 in Prague.

Prices have not increased evenly across the country. Brno recorded the sharpest rise, with rents for small apartments increasing by 12 percent year on year.

Prague saw a 4 percent increase, while rents in Hradec Králové and Pardubice rose by almost 9 percent. Olomouc was one of the few exceptions, with prices falling by slightly more than 2 percent.

Rent is not the only expense students need to consider. Utilities, water and maintenance charges can add another CZK 1,000 to CZK 2,000 a month, according to property platforms.

Private rooms offer a cheaper alternative

Many students instead rent individual rooms in shared apartments, with properties ranging from smaller 2+kk and 2+1 layouts to larger 4+kk and 4+1 apartments. Czech property portal Sreality.cz puts the average cost of a private room in university cities at between approximately CZK 5,700 in Opava and CZK 11,500 in Prague.

In Prague, private rooms listed on Sreality.cz were around 10 percent more expensive than during the same period last year. Prices in Brno, meanwhile, remained roughly unchanged.

Shared housing remains the cheapest option

For students on a tighter budget, sharing an apartment and renting a bed rather than an entire room remains the least expensive choice. The more people share a property, the lower the individual housing costs tend to be.

Even this option, however, has become more expensive. According to UlovDomov.cz, the cost of renting a bed has increased by several hundred Czech crowns compared with last year.

Prague remains considerably more expensive. A bed in a two-bedroom apartment costs almost CZK 5,500, about CZK 1,200 more than a bed in a three-bedroom apartment.

World.title: 58 Years Since Warsaw Pact Troops Invaded Czechoslovakia
World.content:
On August 21, 1968, Soviet troops and their Warsaw Pact allies invaded Czechoslovakia to bring an end to that country’s brief period of political liberalization, called the Prague Spring.

People still recall waking up on that fateful morning to find that Soviet-led Warsaw Pact tanks had rolled into the country, crushing all hope of implementing the democratic reforms of the Prague Spring. Shocked citizens took to the streets in protest of the invasion.

About 500,000 troops were involved in the invasion and occupation, during which 137 Czechoslovaks died and some 500 were wounded.

One of the key battles was for the control of Czech Radio, similar to the one that took place at the end of the Second World War.

The invasion ended the political and economic reforms led by Alexander Dubcek and reasserted dominant Soviet and Communist authority in Czechoslovakia.

It also helped establish the Brezhnev Doctrine, which Moscow said allowed the U.S.S.R. to intervene in any country where a communist government was under threat.

Within the following year, resistance faded, Dubček was removed from office, his reforms were undone, and a more Soviet-controlled government was installed.

World.title: Prague’s Groovy Market Fest Returns After a Successful Debut
World.content:
A new urban festival is aiming to become a regular fixture on Prague’s cultural calendar after attracting 1,200 visitors to its first edition in Riegrovy sady.

Groovy Market Fest, held on August 1, brought together food, design, music and local brands in a format inspired by European city markets.

According to the organizers, around 85% of visitors were tourists or foreign residents of Prague, highlighting the event’s appeal beyond the Czech-speaking audience.



The festival will return to Riegrovy sady on September 5, with further editions planned for October, November and December.

From Barcelona to Prague

Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food culture.

Their interest in international gastronomy also led them to compete in Spain. In 2025, they won first place in the Cooking The Street competition, where their dish was judged by a professional panel that included chefs Beñat Ormaetxea and Jon Kepa Aurrecoetxea.

After returning to Prague, they decided to develop their own event, drawing inspiration from markets such as Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market.

The First Edition

Food Garden focused on gastronomy, while Palm Street featured local products and handmade goods. The Design Zone presented Czech brands working in fashion, design and art.

Rather than filling the site with as many vendors as possible, the organizers selected a smaller number of participants. They say the approach was intended to create a more coherent experience for visitors.

Music was another part of the programme, with live performances and DJ sets throughout the event. Visitors could also attend a masterclass focused on preparing the festival’s signature Groovy cocktail.

Additional editions are scheduled for October 3, November 7 and December 5, all at the same location.

Tickets for upcoming editions are available through GoOut.

World.title: Faster Than the Metro. New Bus is Now Linking Prague 8 and Prague 6
World.content:
A new bus service running through Prague’s Blanka tunnel has begun operating, offering a direct connection between the northern part of the city and Dejvice.

Bus line 145 connects Čimice and Kobylisy in Prague 8 with Hradčanská and Dejvická in Prague 6. The journey takes around 15 minutes, according to Prague’s public transport authority ROPID.



The same trip by metro requires a change between lines C and A in the city centre and takes around 22 minutes.

Including the time spent walking through stations and using escalators, the journey can take about half an hour.

The first day of operation brought mostly positive results, with many buses arriving on time or even ahead of schedule. The real test will come during regular weekday traffic, when congestion around Prague is heavier.

Where the new bus runs

In the direction from Čimice to Dejvice, line 145 serves:

Sídliště Čimice – Čimice – Libeňská – Řepínská – Podhajská pole – Čimický háj – Písečná – Služská – Kobylisy – Okrouhlická – Vychovatelna – Hradčanská – Vítězné náměstí – Dejvická

The return route follows the same corridor in the opposite direction.

The key feature of line 145 is its use of the Blanka tunnel, allowing buses to avoid the city centre and provide a direct connection between Prague 8 and Prague 6.

The new route is expected to make commuting easier for residents of Čimice, Kobylisy and surrounding neighbourhoods, while providing an alternative to the metro for journeys towards Dejvice and Hradčanská.

World.title: Leo Express to Launch Direct Prague–Brno Trains in December
World.content:
Leo Express is set to begin operating direct trains between Prague and Brno in December, marking the private carrier’s first direct connection between the two cities.

The company has already been serving passengers in the South Moravian Region, but its trains have so far bypassed Brno.

Over the past year, travellers from towns such as Hodonín and Břeclav have been able to use Leo Express services to reach Prague, travelling via Přerov and Olomouc.



The new Prague–Brno service will change that, putting the carrier directly on one of the Czech Republic’s busiest rail routes.

There is, however, one limitation for passengers travelling to Prague.

Leo Express trains do not serve Prague Main Station. In Prague, passengers must use Praha-Libeň station, which may be less convenient for those travelling to the city centre.

Leo Express was founded by businessman Leoš Novotný and has operated passenger trains in the Czech Republic since 2012.

The company has gradually expanded its network in the Czech Republic and abroad, competing with established operators such as České dráhy and RegioJet.

The Prague–Brno connection is expected to become another important part of the company’s Czech network from December.

World.title: Hungary split in two: More than 10°C separates the hottest and coolest parts of the country
World.content:
Hungary is experiencing a striking weather divide on Friday, with temperatures varying by more than 10°C between the country’s coolest and hottest regions. A wavy frontal system is bringing heavy showers and thunderstorms to western and northern Hungary, while the southeast is sweltering in temperatures approaching 40°C.

21°C in the west, almost 39°C in the southeast

The contrast was already clear around midday and remained pronounced throughout the day. According to Időkép, the highest temperature recorded on Friday was 38.7°C near Kötegyán in Békés County, while the instruments at Kendig Peak in the west showed just 21.36°C. The national average was around 32°C.

The sharp contrast is being driven by the frontal system crossing the country. While sunny and mostly dry conditions prevail across much of the southeast, cloudier and stormier weather is affecting the west and north.

Storms and torrential rain expected

HungaroMet forecasts several waves of showers and thunderstorms moving from southwest towards northeast across northern and western parts of the country.

Thunderstorms may bring strong or locally severe wind gusts, hail and intense rainfall. Conditions are particularly favourable for severe storms in Transdanubia, where storm systems could develop with very strong winds, larger hail and torrential downpours.

The weather service has issued warnings for thunderstorms in western and northern counties, as well as for torrential rain in four western counties. Heat-related warnings are also in place in four counties in the Southern Great Plain. Thunderstorm activity is expected to decrease towards late evening, although another, weaker band of showers and thunderstorms may arrive from the west later at night.

If you missed it: Severe storms threaten several regions in Hungary, heat to peak today

Weekend brings cooler temperatures

Temperatures will fall to between 21 and 30°C by late Friday evening. Saturday will be noticeably cooler, with daytime highs generally between 25 and 33°C. Sunday morning will bring temperatures of around 13–20°C, while afternoon highs are expected to reach 24–31°C.

The heat will gradually return in the following days, with daytime temperatures rising again in some parts of the country. HungaroMet currently expects highs of 28–34°C on Thursday. For now, however, Hungary remains divided between stormy, significantly cooler conditions in the west and another spell of intense summer heat in the southeast.

World.title: Hungary’s PM Magyar reveals what moved him to tears on 20 August
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has revealed which moment of this year’s 20 August national holiday left the strongest impression on him, highlighting a meeting with 160 young people from child protection institutions.

In a Facebook post on Friday, Magyar described the national holiday as a long, memorable and heartwarming day, but said that meeting the young people shortly before the evening fireworks was by far its most emotional moment.

‘Heartbreaking and uplifting’

The 160 young people had been invited to the Karmelita Palace, where they watched the fireworks from the terrace while enjoying food and refreshments. Magyar said he briefly sat down with the young people on the grass and spoke with them before the fireworks began.

He described seeing the young people as both “heartbreaking and uplifting”, noting that although they had faced difficult circumstances, they were smiling and enjoying the national holiday.

The prime minister also made a pointed political reference to the location, saying that the young people were having a picnic in the same place where, a year earlier, “those in power who had abandoned them and believed themselves untouchable” had celebrated.

“I thought to myself that there is justice. Love ultimately conquers everything,” Magyar wrote.

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

A 16-hour national holiday

Magyar also recounted his packed schedule on 20 August, saying that he left the main entrance of Parliament at 8 AM for the swearing-in ceremony and returned to the same location 16 hours later, at midnight, to bid farewell to tens of thousands of young people celebrating.

His programme included the raising of the national flag, the swearing-in ceremony for newly commissioned officers, an air show and the presentation of state awards. He also attended the national meeting of TISZA Islands, which he said brought together around 10,000 supporters, as well as the procession carrying the Holy Right at St Stephen’s Basilica.

The evening programme included a large-scale drone show and light display, along with Hungarian carnival events at three locations. Yet, despite the packed programme, Magyar said his meeting with the 160 young people was the moment he would remember most from this year’s national holiday.

World.title: Polish bus driver speaks out after deadly Hungary crash: ‘No words can ease the families’ pain’
World.content:
The Polish coach driver involved in the deadly bus crash on Hungary’s M3 motorway has expressed his condolences to the victims and their families through his lawyer, saying he is aware of the immense weight and consequences of the tragedy.

In a statement released on Thursday evening, lawyer Dániel Gerván told the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) that his client understands that no words can ease the loss suffered by the victims’ families. The driver has been deeply affected by the crash and is receiving professional help to process what happened, his lawyer said.

Investigation still at an early stage

Gerván stressed that the criminal proceedings are still at a very early stage. In view of the ongoing investigation, the defence is not currently releasing further details about the circumstances of the crash.

The lawyer added that the family would share further information with the public through their legal representative in the future. The driver has been detained and is being investigated on suspicion of causing a fatal mass accident through negligence. A court ordered his detention earlier this week.

Photo: MTI

Twelve people died in M3 motorway crash

The tragedy happened in the early hours of 16 August near Mezőkeresztes, when a Polish coach carrying pilgrims left the road and overturned onto its side. There were 59 people on board, including 57 passengers and two drivers. Twelve people were killed, while dozens of others suffered injuries.

According to prosecutors, three people sustained life-threatening injuries, while another 20 suffered serious injuries expected to take more than eight days to heal. Eight others were also injured. The injured passengers were taken to hospitals in Miskolc, Debrecen, Nyíregyháza and Eger. The first group of around 20 injured passengers returned to Poland on Monday evening.

Read more details: 12 killed in devastating bus crash on Hungary’s M3 motorway

Driver allegedly fell asleep at the wheel

According to the prosecutor’s office, the driver was not in a condition to operate the coach safely because of fatigue and allegedly fell asleep while driving. The bus subsequently left the carriageway via the emergency lane and overturned on a sloping section of land.

Initial police information indicated that the driver may have fallen asleep. According to Telex, investigators estimated from the scene that he may have been asleep for between two and four seconds, although a vehicle engineering expert, Sándor Boncsér, said that even less time could be enough for a 24-tonne coach to become uncontrollable if its driver falls asleep.

The investigation is continuing, and the exact circumstances that led to the crash have not yet been established with complete certainty.
