National average rainfall is already more than 400 millimetres. (Supplied: Richard Norris)

August rainfall is looking particularly impressive for an El Niño year.

Through 27 previous Pacific warm phases since 1900, the nation's average August rain is a paltry 13mm.

But during the next five days, a mammoth cloudband will engulf the southern two-thirds of the country as a stream of tropical moisture arrives off the Indian Ocean.

For parts of South Australia, Victoria and New South Wales, the system will ensure one of the wettest Augusts on record.

Patchy rain will initially spread across Western Australia this weekend, before reaching SA on Monday and eastern states on Tuesday and Wednesday.

A second band may then follow from south-west WA on Wednesday to eastern states next weekend.

As a result, most of south-east Australia and parts of WA can expect between 15 and 50mm before the end of the month.

For some towns in northern SA it has already been the wettest August on record, including at Arkaroola where 97mm easily exceeds the previous record of 72mm from August 1973.

Rain is ahead this week for the southern two-thirds of Australia. (ABC News)

Simmering Indian Ocean supplying moisture

It is a reasonable call that winter rainfall predictions across Australia were a little off the mark.

The outlook issued by the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) in late May heavily favoured a dry season, but away from the east coast and south-west WA the season has turned out wetter than normal.

The winter outlook offered little hope of a wet season, but frequent rainbands have brought above-average rains to much of inland Australia this winter. (ABC News)

So why isn't 2026 playing by the rules when Pacific warming, the heartbeat of El Niño, is on track to become the strongest on record？

Firstly, not every event is the same, there is always natural variability in weather, and history has proven the strength of an El Niño is not proportional to impacts on Australia.

But despite this expected variability, a trend has emerged on how El Niño is affecting Australia — we are getting wetter.

The graph below illustrates the shift, with yearly totals during El Niño years early last century ranging from 320mm to 445mm, while the past 20 years have brought between 437mm and 482mm, with 2026 on track to pass 500mm.

This is mostly an influence of climate change which is causing Australia's annual average precipitation to steadily climb.

However, this increase is enhanced in El Niño years which opens up the possibility that climate change may be indirectly altering how El Niño affects Australia's weather patterns.

Another key factor is the Pacific Ocean is just one of multiple influences on Australia's climate variability.

One possibility which could be negating El Niño this year is what is happening off the west coast — waters across the central Indian Ocean are currently simmering.

Waters across the Indian Ocean are currently about 1 degree Celsius to 2C above average, and are forecast to warm further into spring. (ABC News)

"Warmer waters can increase atmospheric moisture, providing favourable conditions for rainfall-producing weather systems such as north-west cloud bands and frontal systems that can draw tropical moisture across inland Australia," BOM senior climatologist Zhi-Weng Chua said.

Wet spring and summer a possibility, but heat could break records

The winter season is when El Niños have historically had the greatest impact on rainfall across Australia.

During 16 past moderate-to-strong events, Australia's winter rainfall has decreased by an average of 32 per cent compared to neutral years, but that figure drops to 20 per cent in spring and just 2 per cent in summer.

Since winter has not brought widespread drought, the 2026 unprecedented El Niño may leave Australia relatively unscathed.

And the BOM's latest spring modelling is very confident the western half of Australia is in for a wet spring.

Spring is tipped to be wet across much of WA and the NT, and drier than average along the eastern seaboard, the BOM says. (ABC News)

The outlook is mixed for eastern states from near-even odds of it being wetter or drier in parts of Queensland and NSW to an 80 per cent probability of below-median rain in pockets of Victoria and Tasmania.

What is far more certain is our mild winter should transition into a scorching spring and summer.

"El Niño events typically favour warmer-than-average conditions across … the southern two-thirds of Australia," Mr Chua said.

But warmer than average could be an understatement since modelling is tipping southern Australia will bake in mean temperatures up to 3 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels during the coming months.

"Exceptionally warm surrounding oceans … may also be enhancing the forecast warmth signal," Mr Chua said.

"Together, these factors are occurring against a backdrop of elevated global and regional temperatures, increasing the probability of an unusually warm spring."

World.title: 'Shameful': Australia, UK, Canada slam Israel over probe into aid killings
World.content:
Australia, the UK and Canada have condemned as "shameful" Israel's decision to close an investigation into the death of seven aid workers killed in Gaza in 2024.

The World Central Kitchen employees -- Australian Zomi Frankcom, three Britons, a dual US-Canadian national, a Pole and a Palestinian -- died in a drone strike on their vehicle convoy after overseeing the unloading of a food aid shipment.

Israel's military called the incident a "tragic mistake".

Zomi Frankcom's family disappointed by IDF decision Zomi Frankcom's brother says the decision to announce the outcome of the IDF investigation on World Humanitarian Day was an insult.

"In the more than two years since, we have been pressing for Israel to swiftly and thoroughly consider the case and hold those responsible to account," the three nations said in a joint statement.

"The announcement by the IDF (Israel Defense Forces) on 19 August 2026 that it would not pursue criminal investigations into this strike, without further explanation, is shameful," it said.

The incident in April 2024 sparked global outrage and renewed calls to ensure the safety of aid workers in Gaza.

"Announcing this decision on World Humanitarian Day, while the world honoured the courage and sacrifice of humanitarians, was particularly egregious," the joint statement added.

The Israeli military acknowledged a series of errors at various levels of command, but a preliminary investigation concluded on Wednesday that there was no "reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct".

"Israel extends its condolences to the families of the seven World Central Kitchen aid workers … who tragically lost their lives under deeply regrettable circumstances," Israel's foreign ministry posted on X on Friday.

'Deeply offensive'

It said the decision not to launch a criminal probe "was made by Israel's independent military prosecution authorities on the basis of strict professional and legal considerations".

"We remain committed to the safety of humanitarian personnel, compliance with international humanitarian law and preventing such tragedies from recurring," it added.

The US-based World Central Kitchen condemned the decision not to launch a criminal investigation, calling it "inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive".

It demanded an independent commission to investigate the airstrikes "because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct".

On Thursday, Australia expressed outrage at the closure of the investigation and summoned Israel's ambassador to the country.

AFP

World.title: How much does it cost to fight Pauline Hanson? Labor has options
World.content:
If you have a spare $5, $10 or even $42, the Labor Party has a proposition for you: help stop Pauline Hanson.

The varying price tags are attached to a stream of digital fundraising pitches that offer a window into how Labor is approaching the electoral threat posed by One Nation.

But a look beyond the requests for loose change and a more sophisticated strategy is emerging.

The varying price tags are attached to a stream of digital fundraising pitches that offer a window into how Labor is approaching the electoral threat posed by One Nation. (Instagram)

Labor is increasingly trying not to simply attack One Nation, but to bind Hanson and the Coalition together in voters' minds as partners in a shared agenda.

"One Nation and the Coalition are on a unity ticket to undermine universal super," one ad featured on Instagram asking for a $10 donation this week begins.

For the more spendthrift Labor supporter, a sponsored post claims One Nation is "rising" and the "hard truth" is the Liberals can "only form government with Pauline Hanson".

"If everyone seeing this ad donated just $5 today, we'd have the resources to take on One Nation and the Coalition," it says.

A different post addressed to "everyone who wants to stop One Nation" asks for a $30 donation to Labor to help train party volunteers.

Labor's digital marketing strategy is clear.

First highlight Hanson's record on issues of workers' rights, pay and conditions.

Then, warn the Coalition does not have the numbers to govern without One Nation. Increasingly, Labor is trying to argue its two opponents have a shared policy agenda.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said he was "genuinely worried" about the future of super "in the hands of the Liberals, the Nationals and One Nation". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A shifting political agenda

This all played out in a fundraising text message sent to ALP supporters ostensibly addressed from Treasurer Jim Chalmers asking for a $42 donation because Liberal frontbencher Andrew Bragg "wants to scrap your super" and Hanson is "backing him".

This missive caught the attention of Hanson, who replied on X with the rebuttal Chalmers was "full of shit" as One Nation was not looking to end super.

When this column asked Chalmers for a response, he said he was "genuinely worried" about the future of super "in the hands of the Liberals, the Nationals and One Nation".

"They do not support universal superannuation and preservation at its core," he said.

Loading Instagram content

Bragg's appearance at the National Press Club last week provided the impetus for this latest example of the time-tested practice of a political party seizing on a news story to animate their supporters and raise funds.

Hanson's suggestion people be allowed to dip into their super when struggling with cost of living only galvanised Labor's argument its opponents wanted to raid Australians' retirement savings.

This month Labor's digital ads were framed around superannuation, last month it was Hanson's uncomplimentary comments about paid parental leave.

But as politically potent as those issues may be, One Nation hasn't taken these attacks lying down.

After Labor asked supporters for a $27 donation to help fight Hanson in June, One Nation launched its "Fire the Liar" campaign in response and raised more than $4 million in just five days.

The amount of what's known as "earned media" — ie free publicity — Hanson's fundraising campaign attracted was quite unprecedented by Australian political standards.

Despite this, Hanson has either plateaued or slipped a little in the polls following scrutiny on some of her policy positions.

But as Labor moves against one populist idea, another rises in its place.

Yesterday superannuation, today slashing the tobacco excise under the highly contested notion it would quash the illicit cigarette market.

Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie, whose own federal seat of Canning overlaps with parts of Secret Harbour, criticised what he has felt was a lack of effort from his state colleagues. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A test around the corner

While many are looking to the Victorian state election in November as the first real world contest between Labor and a historically popular One Nation, there is another test coming sooner.

Next Saturday residents in the WA state seat of Secret Harbour will vote in a by-election triggered by the retirement of the local Labor member.

The outer-suburban string of coastal towns south of Perth form exactly the sort of electorate where a mix of mortgage pressure, rapid population growth and voters willing to look beyond the major parties could prove a winning combination for One Nation.

Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie, whose own federal seat of Canning overlaps with parts of Secret Harbour, certainly thinks so, criticising what he has felt was a lack of effort from his state colleagues.

"We should always strive to win, and we should signal that ambition to our voters," he told the Australian Financial Review this week.

Labor is increasingly trying not to simply attack One Nation, but binding Pauline Hanson and the Coalition together in voters' minds as partners in a shared agenda. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Hanson's key advantage

Labor is at an incredibly high water mark in WA and increasingly sound far from confident about retaining Secret Harbour themselves.

The not-so-subtle pivot from Labor sources in recent weeks has been to talk up the by-election as the source of an important "lesson" for how preferences might flow in future contests with the Liberals and One Nation.

Though not totally ruling out their chances, the shifting view inside Labor that the seat could fall to One Nation also raises the stakes for Hanson.

One Labor source told this column Secret Harbour was "exactly the type of seat" One Nation could win.

"Where if not there?" they said.

Perhaps that pressure was a factor in Hanson's recent staunch defence of WA's GST deal, which has been quite the change in tune to her critical remarks of the past.

Hanson's GST conversion is a reminder of a key advantage she holds compared to arguably most other politicians.

She is often able to jettison a previous position no longer deemed politically useful without any blowback from voters.

Labor is clearly getting more deliberate about how it fights One Nation, from the issues it chooses to prosecute to the way it increasingly links Hanson to the Coalition.

But Hanson is adapting too and historically has had considerable freedom to tailor her pitch to the political moment.

World.title: Israel's impunity has been virtually unaffected by collective concern
World.content:
Records of the village of Qusra, just south of Nablus in the Occupied West Bank, go back to Ottoman tax registers of 1596. There has been documentation of its existence and that of its inhabitants ever since.

Documenting a place, and a community, and the events that occur there, is always important.

But documenting Qusra has made it one of the stand-outs in the wider story of Israeli actions against Palestinian people which, amid the noise of Donald Trump's chaotic war against Iran, have only escalated in 2026.

Earlier this month, Israeli settlers besieged three houses in Qusra telling the families that lived there they had to leave because the settlers were going to take their land.

The settlers cut off the water and electricity to the houses. They blocked the roads.

Such actions are not unusual in the West Bank. Nor are they by any means the worst that happen there.

The West Bank community of Qusra has been the site of repeated settler attacks on Palestinian residents. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

Coverage of Qusra easier than of Gaza

Last month settlers set fire to the village's newly constructed mosque after an earlier clash in another village in which four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers died, after a group of settlers entered an area of the West Bank for an "unauthorised hike", according to the Israeli military.

But the besieging of the three houses and their 15 inhabitants — which has continued with the UN allowed to deliver supplies — struck a chord in the international community, and particularly in the United States.

That was possibly because one of the houses that has now come under siege belongs to a Palestinian-American, Loai Ridi.

But it is mostly because the international media have been able to document what has been going on in real time, in real pictures.

The contrast with Gaza could not be more stark.

In Gaza, where the international media has not been allowed to independently enter since October 7, 2023, the killing of more than 70,000 people according to the Gaza Health Ministry, the wounding of many more, and the continuing appalling living conditions of around two million people on a small strip of land where the majority of buildings have been flattened, occupies a strange space in history where what we see and what are told bear little resemblance to each other.

The lack of international media access leaves it in a situation in which almost every event is contested, but the Israeli ban prevents the media from testing and filtering out false claims and information.

These Israeli statements reduce horrific events to the language of bureaucratic failure. Whether incidents are investigated at all, or go on to be a criminal investigation, they rarely result in any real accountability even if there is a fault admitted.

Israeli Ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman said there was no intention to kill innocent civilians and that while he could "express deep sorrow and grief" for the families he would not apologise over the deaths as that would have "legal ramifications". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Israel clears soldiers over Australian aid worker

This week Australia expressed outrage at the findings of an internal IDF report which found "serious failures" in the process that led to the killings of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and six colleagues in April 2024.

The IDF said "the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct".

Wong has 'no confidence' in IDF report Foreign Minister Penny Wong says she has 'no confidence' in the IDF investigation that cleared Israeli soldiers of criminal wrongdoing in the killing of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom.

The humanitarian aid group for which Frankcom worked, World Central Kitchen, said that "at the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody".

"It had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team's movements, identities and activities in advance," it said.

"The military investigation conflates different timelines and events, muddies the story and shifts the blame for the IDF's illegal conduct."

Israeli Ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman said there was no intention to kill innocent civilians and that while he could "express deep sorrow and grief" for the families he would not apologise over the deaths as that would have "legal ramifications".

"There are a lot of haters of Israel in Australia," he added. "We have seen this time and time again."

The credibility of the IDF account was not helped by a reminder of two other notorious incidents at the time the findings were released.

The IDF announced it would be launching criminal investigations into the now globally famous incident in which a five year old girl, Hind Rajab, was left talking to emergency services in January 2024 from a car where she was surrounded by the bodies of her six dead relatives, after an IDF strike, only to eventually die, along with two paramedics killed by Israeli forces in an ambulance that was supposed to be on a negotiated path to rescue her.

The IDF said it would also launch a criminal investigation into the killing of 15 Palestinian paramedics in March 2025 in Rafah.

Postmortems of the dead paramedics, whose bodies had been retrieved from a mass grave that had also buried their vehicles, revealed they had been killed at close-range with "specific and intentional" bullet wounds in heads and hearts.

But given the IDF's record of failure to bring people to account, and the time that has already passed since these events took place, there is already deep scepticism about the likely outcome.

For example, The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) — set up in the little girl's name to pursue legal action against those responsible for violence against Palestinians — said in a statement that has "no confidence in the Israeli military's reported decision to open criminal investigations into the murder of Hind Rajab, six members of her family, and the two Palestinian Red Crescent paramedics" or into the targeted killing of the 15 Palestinian paramedics.

"These reported investigations, even if they do occur, should not be mistaken for a genuine step toward justice", the Foundation said.

"As numerous Palestinian and international legal and human rights organisations have documented for years, Israel's internal investigations into the criminal conduct of its own soldiers are fundamentally flawed and cannot be regarded as credible mechanisms of accountability."

Wreckage of one of three World Central Kitchen vehicles destroyed in the strikes. (Reuters: Ahmed Zakot)

US criticises Israel over West Bank

Back in the West Bank this week, the IDF has played what would be politely called an ineffective role in ending the siege in Qusra.

The events seem to have been one of those lightning rod moments to galvanise public criticism of Israel and its actions in the West Bank.

That most notably came from the US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee.

The evangelist is a longstanding supporter of Israeli settlements in the West Bank and follows the Israeli practice of calling the area by the biblical names of "Judea and Samaria" — to assert the traditional Hebrew ownership of the lands.

Yet Huckabee this week condemned the besieging settlers at Qusra as "Israeli terrorists" and said the siege was inexcusable.

But as the siege was occurring in front of the world's media, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his cabinet ministers attended ceremonies in the West Bank to promote massive new settlements across the illegally occupied territory.

Israeli settlement plans in West Bank Israeli plans to press ahead with the controversial E1 development would effectively break the West Bank in two and make Palestinian statehood impossible, according to critics of the project.

Australia was one of 21 countries, along with Britain, France, Italy, Canada and Germany to sign a joint statement calling Israel's particular approval of a major settlement project which will effectively cut the West Bank in half — and further separate it from east Jerusalem "unacceptable and a violation of international law".

A group that monitors and maps conflicts and protests, ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data) says it has recorded more than 80 incidents involving settlers in Qusra since the beginning of 2026, "making it one of the three locations most affected by settler violence in the West Bank".

"These incidents included property theft and destruction, razing lands, physical clashes with Palestinians, and shootings at Palestinians — one of these shootings killed a Palestinian on 14 March," the group said in a statement.

Across the West Bank, it says it has recorded "300 incidents of land seizures between 1 January and 14 August, which is already higher than the 267 incidents recorded throughout 2025".

"In such incidents, settlers established outposts, built roads, placed tents and mobile rooms on Palestinian land, or seized homes, leading to more daily friction and violence between settlers and Palestinians."

The United Nations recorded more than 2,200 Palestinians displaced by settler violence and access restrictions in the first half of 2026 alone.

All these actions by Israel, a country whose ambassador to Australia told the National Press Club in March this year "will always be a beacon of hope".

Israel's enemies, Newman said, "seek its destruction for what it represents; a modern democracy, Western civilisation, and a national home for the Jewish people. There is no other country in the Middle East that upholds the same democratic ideals of Australia as Israel does."

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee warned Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank not to steal property owned by Palestinian ​Americans. (Reuters: Ronen Zvulun)

Netanyahu goes from Trump whisperer to Trump ignorer

Are any of Israel's actions likely to change?

The answer to this has usually been that it is really only the United States that can apply any external pressure to Israel to change its actions.

But there is an election coming in Israel.

Donald Trump also now shows little interest in the fate of the Palestinians, particularly with his Board of Peace plan blown up by the Israelis.

Netanyahu long boasted to his country that he was the Trump Whisperer. Now he is just the Trump Ignorer.

There are still actions taken by the US which are clearly read as sops to Israel.

The US, for example this week sanctioned the president of the International Criminal Court and a prosecutor tasked with investigating crimes committed by Israel during its war on Gaza.

But it was the language used by the US secretary of state Marco Rubio in unveiling the new sanctions that was the most troubling.

In another time, it would have sounded positively unhinged for a senior American official to describe an international court as a "corrupt and fatally politicised supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate".

But not in these times.

Loading

Israel's ongoing impunity

Israel's actions in Gaza and the West Bank reflect a sense of impunity which only continues to grow.

It is equally reflected in its actions in the region.

'Israeli terrorists' target villagers' homes in days-long siege Palestinians in a small West Bank village have spent almost a week under siege from Israeli settlers, with members of the community accusing the Israeli military of complicity in the saga.

This week Israel launched air strikes on a Syrian air base just 70 kilometres from the Turkish border.

The Syrian foreign ministry condemned the attacks and described them as an "unjustified act of aggression, a flagrant violation of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a dangerous escalation that threatens security and stability in the region".

But, beyond the 'buffer zones' and incursions in Syrian territory that Israel has been making for some time (along with those which have effectively claimed about 20 per cent of Lebanon), the target of the strike on the air base was actually Turkiye, which Israel claims has breached an agreed status quo by taking steps to establish a military presence in Syria by letting Turkish troops deploy near the air base.

On Wednesday, Netanyahu said in a political podcast that Israel will "not tolerate a Turkish military presence, which moves to the south, because it threatens us".

Like actions in the West Bank, the US has condemned the Israeli air strikes on the base as an "unnecessary escalation" and insisted the new Syrian government is not the threat the Netanyahu government argues it is.

Once again it is being ignored.

Once again that raises the question of what other countries, like Australia, really need to collectively do — rather than just speak firmly to ambassadors.

Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

World.title: Batteries send power prices up in midnight charging mystery
World.content:
In the wee hours of a cold night last month, as most West Australians slept in their beds, a strange thing happened in the state's biggest and most important electricity system.

About 1am, prices on the spot market started to soar.

They had been hovering at an elevated level of roughly $120 per megawatt-hour but suddenly began to climb to extreme highs of more than $350/MWh.

Driving that jump in prices was no catastrophic loss of a high-voltage power line or a major coal-fired plant.

It was a spike in demand and it was coming from an unexpected source.

The surge was coming from batteries, the very things supposedly designed to prevent just such a breakout in prices.

Why it happened — in the middle of the night when there was seemingly no obvious reason — is still unclear.

But experts say the episode highlights how the way batteries are managed will determine their impact on prices as Australia transitions away from fossil fuels.

A midnight mystery

One person who has been seeking answers is Marcus Freese, an analyst at Modo Energy.

He says a few things are known based on publicly available data.

For one, the batteries that charged between 1am and 2am on July 12 were all owned by the state-owned WA power provider Synergy.

Freese says the effect was significant.

Combined, Synergy's four big batteries added more than 30 per cent to demand for power from the grid at a time when prices were already high.

"The market was not tight because of demand or renewable output," Freese wrote in a report.

"Underlying demand was unremarkable for the time of day, in line with the July average for that hour, and wind generation was close to its July average.

"The price rise instead coincided with Synergy increasing charging from 229 (megawatts) to 640MW, which added around a third to system demand at the overnight trough."

Synergy built its first battery three years ago. (ABC News: Glyn Jones)

Freese says it is not the first time Synergy has materially pushed up prices in the market through the "coordinated charging" of its battery fleet.

He says it appears to make little sense as a tactic.

Not only does it push up prices that will ultimately be borne by everyone, Freese says it is not even profitable for Synergy's batteries.

In this case, on July 12, he says Synergy's battery fleet lost $383,000 across the day.

Over the last 13 months, Freese says Synergy has lost more than $100/MWh on 54 days, while it's earned more than $100/MWh on just 31 days.

By contrast, the company which owns WA's other two mega batteries, French firm Neoen, has made money much more often than not.

"We've now observed this dynamic across April, June, and July," Freese noted.

"Synergy's coordinated charging adds material load (demand) at the wrong time, lifts prices, and then buys into the spike it helped create."

Big bets on batteries

The events in WA are being watched closely by energy observers across the country.

More than anywhere else in Australia — and, by some measures, the world — the state has led the charge into big batteries as a way to balance an electricity system turning towards renewable energy.

From practically nothing three years ago, the amount of large-scale battery capacity in WA's main grid has risen to about 1400 megawatts.

Collectively, those batteries regularly meet more than 20 per cent of demand for power at peak times and can sometimes provide more than a third.

Batteries are a key part of plans for WA to exit coal-fired power in coming years. (ABC News: Daniel Mercer)

Michael Sarich, a senior vice president of global energy consultancy Rystad, says WA has bet big on batteries, partly because of a very real vulnerability.

Its main electricity grid is an island, cut off from the rest of the world and unable to tap imports when times get tough.

Those batteries, he says, are aimed at safeguarding that system.

Sarich says the daily flood of rooftop solar was previously pushing daytime prices — and demand for power from the grid — to ever lower levels.

But when the sun set and the solar panels stopped generating, he says prices were rising to highs that were even more extreme.

Bills hit by power price whiplash The benefits of extremely low energy prices during the day are "washed away" by extremely high ones after dark. But there is light at the end of the tunnel.

Sarich says batteries had flattened this price curve by soaking up excess renewable energy at times of surplus and discharging in times of scarcity.

"The role the batteries have done really well is meet that evening demand, which is why you're seeing the price curve is a lot flatter across the day," he explains.

"But the other thing you need to remember is batteries are not really generators. They're really just moving demand around throughout the day."

Battery behaviour compounds winter woes

The strengths and weaknesses of batteries have been brought into sharp relief in WA in recent months.

In its most recent snapshot of WA's "wholesale electricity market", or WEM, the market operator noted batteries had indeed smoothed prices in the three months to June 30.

Those prices, however, had flattened out at record high levels of almost $120/MWh.

According to the Australian Energy Market Operator, coal plant and wind farm outages partly caused the price pain.

But so too did increased battery charging during the middle of the day and overnight, AEMO noted.

Sarich says these factors ran headlong into other inconveniences.

He says demand for electricity in winter is simply higher, while output from wind and solar is almost invariably lower.

For Sarich, winter, not summer, is now the biggest test of electricity systems and the people who run them.

He says WA, like the rest of the country, is moving to a system powered by renewable energy.

As such, it needs to be able to cope with extended periods in winter where the wind does not blow and the sun does not shine.

"Our view is over the next few years that wholesale prices are going to remain elevated because fundamentally it's all about supply and demand," Sarich says.

"You need to have enough supply from whatever source you've got."

Sarich says WA's safety net at the moment is gas-fired power, a relatively pricey form of power.

But he also notes that batteries are increasingly "mirroring" the behaviour of gas plants when they offer to supply their power to the market.

Batteries charge ahead as gas 'sputters' Falling battery costs and a data centre-fuelled dash for gas have overturned decades of accepted wisdom: gas is no longer the cheapest way to meet peak power demand.

And at times of scarce supply, as has been the case in WA over much of the winter, this meant the prices offered had more often than not been high.

Bizarrely, energy traders not authorised to speak to the ABC also noted gas generators had fired up at times to meet the demand created by Synergy's batteries.

One such energy trader described the events as "crazy".

"The other key thing is there's only a very small number of these batteries," Sarich says.

"So, they've got this sort of dominant position."

With Synergy's two remaining coal plants due to be retired next year and in 2029, Sarich says the need to build enough capacity to replace those units is becoming urgent.

He's optimistic it will, pointing to a slew of wind projects under construction or in the pipeline.

Synergy would not be drawn on why its batteries were all charged at times when spot prices were high. A spokeswoman said they were a relatively new technology whose capabilities would be monitored and refined.

She said "safe, reliable and lowest-cost" energy systems needed diverse sources of supply.

Batteries offered flexibility that would allow greater amounts of renewable energy "while enhancing system reliability through rapid response to changing system conditions".

Growing pains, growing tensions

WA's Energy Minister, Amber-Jade Sanderson, also declined to comment on Synergy's trading behaviour.

However, she did not back away from the state's plans to close its coal plants and make the switch to a heavy dependence on green power.

"We've always said that the most reliable and affordable energy mix for the future is renewables backed by batteries and gas," Ms Sanderson said.

The minister blamed outages — planned and unplanned — at coal plants and a wind farm undergoing expansion for the high prices in recent months.

"This demonstrates why we need more renewables to keep prices down," Ms Sanderson said.

She stressed that households and small businesses in WA would be shielded from any pain in the wholesale market because the government regulated prices for those customers.

Amid the upheaval, Marcus Freese from Modo Energy says scrutiny needs to be applied to a battery fleet that now in a powerful position.

He notes batteries are now setting the prices in WA's main grid, whether charging or discharging, more than 90 per cent of the time.

Given this power and the inadequacy of current regulations, Freese says there is a risk Synergy could use batteries to push up wholesale prices to benefit the utility's fleet of other coal, gas and wind generators.

He argues this may have been the case in recent months, saying Synergy's batteries "paid $7.3 million to charge whilst its generation earned $18.4 million" across more than 70 high-price charging days.

"A high charging offer increases the price paid by the battery, but it can also increase the price earned by generation in the same portfolio," Freese wrote.

Looking ahead, he says WA's battery fleet and the way it is managed will evolve.

Indeed, he says it has already changed dramatically in the past year.

Revenues from batteries trading energy had plunged, he notes, led by Synergy's losses.

So, too, had revenues for system strength and security services.

Nowadays, he says, WA batteries earned most of their money for simply being there through so-called capacity payments.

These are paid to generators or batteries as a type of insurance for making reliable capacity available when the system needs it.

While a capacity market exists in WA, it does not in the national electricity market, which covers Australia's eastern seaboard.

On the eastern seaboard, batteries earn the lion's share of their revenues by trading energy — or the "arbitrage" between low and high prices — in the wholesale market.

Freese says WA's experience suggests batteries could have a counterproductive effect on prices if they are not managed carefully.

"In a market with wide spreads and a clear daily arbitrage window, how you charge matters as much as when you discharge," Freese wrote.

WA battery boom Western Australia in particular is proving to the world that grid-scale batteries are no longer a complementary technology but can play a central role in power grids.

Sarich says batteries are playing a crucial role in helping to keep the lights on by storing energy as the share of renewable generation grows.

But their role in driving down prices is a different matter.

"I don't necessarily believe they will lower prices," Sarich says.

"And the reason for that is they're not providing more generation.

"You kind of need to think of them as an enabler.

"It's sort of like the cost you need to pay to enable more wind and solar, which is adding more generation, and that will push the price down.

"Once you add these sort of batteries, they provide the role of making the whole system work better."

World.title: Fiddler on the Roof features an usher turned actor in starring role
World.content:
When Ellen Ebbs took to the stage for the first time as an actor in Fiddler on the Roof at Theatre Royal Sydney, she found it difficult to hold back tears.

Ebbs, 24, was performing in the same theatre where she used to work as an usher.

"It's literally the theatre I work [in] five times a week," Ebbs told ABC News.

" I clean those stalls, I work on the bar, I work with the cocktails … I've been in that theatre, like, 200 times, but always from the other side. "

Ebbs has made her main stage debut in the Australian production of the award-winning and critically acclaimed Fiddler on the Roof starring Troy Sussman as Tevye, Alexis Fishman as Golde and Sigrid Thornton as Yente.

Loading Instagram content

The musical is set in 1905 in the tiny village of Anatevka.

Tevye, a Jewish milkman, has five daughters, which means a visit from the matchmaker.

But he's forced to reckon with his proud traditions against the backdrop of a changing world and the will of his children.

Fiddler on the Roof is internationally hailed as one of the greatest musicals of all time, with a score featuring If I Were a Rich Man, Tradition, Matchmaker and Sunrise, Sunset.

'A crazy full-circle moment'

Ebbs plays Tevye's daughter, Hodel, alongside stage sisters Freya Boltman as Tzeitel, and Caity Plummer as Chava.

Ellen Ebbs is making her main stage debut in Fiddler on the Roof. (Supplied: Daniel Boud)

As a former usher in that same room, as soon as Ebbs looked out at the audience, the emotions took over.

"As soon as I stepped on stage, I literally started crying," Ebbs said.

"It was just such a crazy full-circle moment, and I think it hit me in that moment, seeing the stage from that point of view, and looking at the stalls that I've worked at.

"It was such a pinch-me moment."

From the Foyer to the stage

Ebbs started working as an usher at Theatre Royal Sydney in February 2025.

Her first shift was on opening night of Hadestown starring Christine Anu.

"I remember [my] first shift. I was like, 'Wait, I'm getting paid to watch theatre?' I was like, 'This is such a hack! What the heck?'

" Every shift, getting to watch all these actors that I look up to, it was just like a free masterclass every shift. "

Ebbs enjoyed chatting to patrons about what they thought about each show.

Ellen Ebbs used to clean the stalls at the same theatre she's now starring at. (Supplied)

Her co-workers were other young creatives working as ushers, including aspiring actors, directors and writers.

She says they've all been super supportive of her transition to the stage.

"The support from Theatre Royal has actually melted my heart," Ebbs said.

"On opening night, there was a big bouquet of flowers in my dressing room, and they had a massive card that was signed by every usher and bartender."

She says she was greeted by staff in the foyer on opening night.

"They all just started screaming and cheering my name, and clapping, and my besties were crying," Ebbs said.

"And I was like, 'This is literally like a movie.'

"It was so beautiful, and just seeing how excited they all [were], and that's something I realised: every single show, I'm going to have someone supporting me, because I have the ushers.

"They've been very, very supportive."

Getting with the program

Ebbs graduated in Musical Theatre in 2024 from the Western Australian Academy of Performing Arts (WAAPA) after being bitten by the acting bug early in life.

"I feel like I was one of those kids that I didn't really see myself doing anything else," Ebbs said.

"My parents met doing amateur musicals.

"So, I definitely got my love for theatre and musicals from them."

Ellen Ebbs's responsibilities included making coffee and cocktails. (Supplied)

Ebbs always felt "free" on stage, but as the youngest of four children, and with both parents working as psychologists, Ebbs didn't realise acting could be a job.

Whenever she went to a show, however, she would read the program and notice that so many of the actors had graduated from WAAPA.

"I was like, 'What the hell is this WAAPA place?'" Ebbs said.

"I remember being, like, 10 and being like, 'Okay, well, the people that are up there went here, so I'm going to go there, because then I can get up there.'

"So that kind of started my dream of going to acting school and going to WAAPA."

'Truly magic show'

In Fiddler on the Roof, Ebbs plays the defiant second-oldest daughter.

"Hodel is so strong-minded, very intelligent, very witty, and isn't afraid to go against the grain," Ebbs says.

"It is truly magic this show.

"I feel so honoured and so, so grateful to be a part of this show."

Hodel is a headstrong character. (Supplied: Daniel Boud)

She didn't anticipate finding her feet so quickly.

"Because this is my first main stage production, I was a bit, obviously, intimidated, coming into it," Ebbs says.

"I was like, 'Right, okay, I don't really have any credits to my name, and I'm coming into this with theatre vets, like Troy, like Alexis, like Sigrid.'

"And I … wasn't sure what the vibe was going to be, but day one of rehearsal, I was blown away by how humble the room was.

"Everyone is so down-to-earth, and there's no power hierarchy at all.

"Everyone's just here to work, and also to support each other, and I think with a show like Fiddler, where it tackles some heavy themes and very emotional themes, it's so important to have a company that has each other's back."

One of Ellen Ebbs's favourite parts of the show is singing Matchmaker with her on-stage siblings. (Supplied: Daniel Boud)

She says her favourite part of the show is watching Sussman sing If I Were a Rich Man, and she also gets a kick out of singing Matchmaker with the other daughters.

"The way that Jordan [Fein] has directed it to be this feminist anthem … it's like this kind of punk rock anthem," she says.

"And singing that with [Caity and Freya] every night fills me with so much joy, and shout out to them, because they're amazing."

Fiddler on the Roof is currently playing at Theatre Royal Sydney and will soon tour Brisbane, Melbourne and Perth.

World.title: Claudia Karvan on The Secret Life of Us finale that was never filmed
World.content:
Claudia Karvan was 10 years old when she first stepped into a starring role in 1983's Molly, and the Order of Australia recipient hasn't stepped back since.

By the time she scored her first AFI (now AACTA) award in 1996 for a feature role on hospital procedural TV series GP, Karvan was already a household name thanks to star turns in feature films such as Redheads and The Heartbreak Kid, which went on to inspire the long-running and recently rebooted teen series Heartbreak High.

Claudia Karvan and Alex Dimitriades in The Heartbreak Kid. (Supplied: IMDb)

She was three seasons into starring in ground-breaking Australian drama The Secret Life of Us (for which she picked up her first Logie Award) when co-creator John Edwards pushed her to begin directing episodes, the catalyst which took Karvan from actor to film and TV all-rounder.

Over the next 15 years, Karvan would co-create three shows, Love My Way, Spirited and Bump, often wearing multiple hats of actor, producer and screenwriter.

The multi-hyphenate was on the Logies Awards stage again last week, accepting the Best Supporting Actress for her extraordinary work on SBS's Homebodies, a short-form miniseries written by and loosely based on the experiences of AP Pobjoy. Karvan told ABC she was proud to lend her voice to the first trans-led project to be awarded at the Logies.

Claudia Karvan accepts the Silver Logie Award for Best Supporting Actress for Homebodies with co-star Luke Wiltshire. (Getty: James Gourley)

After more than two decades of keeping multiple plates spinning at once, Karvan is slowing down the pace with her latest role in SBS's The Airport Chaplain, alongside Australian icon (and her former co-star) Hugo Weaving and The Pitt breakthrough star Shabana Azeez. Featuring a cast of airport employees, the workplace drama revolves around empathetic-to-a-fault airport chaplain Tobias, played by Weaving.

So, you've got two hours to kill before a flight. Where are we most likely to find you at the airport?

The bookshop.

What has your relationship been to chaplains throughout your life. Did you have one at your school?

I did. I went to SCEGGS Darlinghurst, which is an Anglican school, and I loved singing in the choir and singing the hymns, but I never used the chaplain in the way people use Hugo's character. I'd never even heard of an airport chaplain.

It's a fascinating role to perform, and they have them in airports all around the world, and in fact, they even have an airport chaplain international convention, a conference that you can go to.

How has your relationship to religion and faith changed over your life?

I think I only temporarily believed in God in fifth grade for a little bit. I went to a couple of Christian camps, which was so much fun. We played lots of games, and we read from the Bible, and it all just felt like jolly hockey sticks.

It was the comfort that I needed, but when I told my dad that I was religious, he just laughed, and he went, "Pfft." When he laughed, I was sort of like, "Hmm, yeah, you're probably right."

I'm not someone who has faith in a monotheist God. I do read a lot of Buddhist philosophy, though, and I often call on things that I've learned from people talking about Buddhism, or podcasts, or meditation books, or Leonard Cohen. I wouldn't describe myself as a Buddhist, but I do have a deep amount of respect for the discipline of Buddhism and the theory behind Buddhism. I think it's really revelatory. I love it.

Claudia Karvan and Hugo Weaving in The Airport Chaplain. (Supplied: SBS)

Where do you think a chaplain's role should be in 2026? Should it just be contained to an airport?

Look, I wouldn't want to tell anyone how to live their lives.

Like, I think if you've got faith and if that's what you need, it's a wonderful thing. We've got to be tolerant of all the ways people move through the world; we all move through the world very differently. Variety and diversity is what makes the world go round.

I loved you in Homebodies earlier in the year. I thought that was the most beautiful story. After having worn so many hats for Bump, how is it coming back to primarily acting roles?

Oh, look, it's pretty delicious because a huge amount of responsibility and planning and hard work comes off my shoulders and I get to ride on other people's coat-tails. There's so much work that happens before everyone comes on set and so much work that happens after a production wraps and I don't have to be a part of that.

Even though they're very creative and gratifying phases, it's also nice to just be given a call sheet, learn some lines, join a team and be very grateful and gracious and all care, no responsibility. I love it. I really love it.

It's great, too, because I can ask questions whereas before I'd seen what was under the hood because of my work in pre- and post-production. Now I can say, "How did this story come up in the room?" or "What are you looking for in this scene?" It helps me perform better.

Claudia Karvan and Luke Wiltshire play mother and son in Homebodies. (Supplied: SBS)

I believe this is your first time working with Hugo Weaving since 1999's Strange Planet. How was this experience compared to 27 years ago?

Yeah, well, 27 years ago Emma-Kate Croghan directed us in a sex scene, and she was fantastically awkward and she declared herself as being very awkward.

There were no intimacy coordinators and Hugo and I did a really clumsy, embarrassing sex scene and then Emma-Kate a week later went, 'Well, that was really terrible. Can we do it again?' So, Hugo and I had a laugh about that.

But we see each other a lot socially and I'm very familiar with Hugo's work and it was beautiful just getting to the ease of working with him, it made the relationship so accessible.

Alice Garner, Claudia Karvan, and Naomi Watts in Strange Planet. (Supplied: IMDB)

It's been 25 years since The Secret Life of Us. Have you had a chance at all this year to look back on how impactful that series was for you? And for a lot of Australians.

Oh, absolutely. I mean, Deb Mailman, she just keeps going from strength to strength, what a privilege it was to have been her flatmate all those years ago.

We've done podcasts and there's lots of stuff online. It's still finding new audiences, which is wonderful.

It's still relevant to people in their 20s, which I find amazing. We wouldn't have known that back then. It was such a lucky job.

Do you ever think it could be remade today? Reboots are all the rage.

I would love them to do what they finally plan to do. They had a whole ending at the end of series three, which they never got to film. I definitely have sent messages to [screenwriter] Judi McCrossin and [producer] Amanda Higgs and said, "Look, why don't we just write a feature film, and we get to do what you guys always envisaged for the end of Secret Life of Us."

Wouldn't it be great? But that's their bag, their show. I'm just going to cross my fingers.

The Secret Life of Us cast in 2002: Deborah Mailman, Spencer McLaren, Claudia Karvan, Sibylla Budd and Samuel Johnson. (Getty Images: Patrick Riviere)

And the campaign starts today! You have such a huge career. Is there a role that you would really love to go back and experience again, knowing what you know now?

Oh, that's a good question. I think I was probably not as brave or, like, more wary, protecting myself a lot when I was younger.

So, I'd probably revisit all my younger roles and just embrace the team a lot more and trust the team a lot more and not be as reserved or guarded. So pretty much, I'll just redo my first decade.

Well, that folds into my next question beautifully. How do you think your 10-year-old self would react if she could see your career now?

Oh, wow. What a great question, my 10-year-old self. I think she'd be pretty surprised. I think she wouldn't know me. She'd be like, "Who's that person? Why didn't you become a lawyer?"

Claudia Karvan (right) on the set of her first film, Molly, in 1983. (Supplied: Claudia Karvan)

As someone who's been in the public eye since childhood, what's the most important thing you've learnt about maintaining privacy when you need it?

Just being kind to yourself. Knowing when to protect your boundaries and not judge yourself. Know when to power down. Learning how to say no. Self-care, that learning came to me very late in life.

While I was watching Airport Chaplain, I couldn't help but think of how much I would love a Tobias just for my own personal life. Where do you think you could use a chaplain?

In the ocean when I'm swimming or when I'm surfing. Or when I'm bushwalking and I think I'm going off track. Yeah, out in nature.

My final question for you. What is the change in the Australian screen industry that you most appreciate in 2026 compared to when you were first starting out?

Intimacy coordinators.

They choreograph the scenes. They make them more significant. They're like an on-set chaplain, actually, because they assist you through the uncomfortable conversations, they hold your hand, they connect people, they make you feel safe.

The Airport Chaplain premieres Wednesday, August 26 at 8:30pm on SBS and SBS On Demand.

World.title: Meghan set to star in Netflix series on return to UK
World.content:
CultureTV & radioMeghan, Duchess of Sussex Meghan set to star in Netflix series on return to UK India McTaggart , Lily Shanagher and Victoria Ward August 22, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Duchess of Sussex is set to star in a Guy Ritchie Netflix series when she moves to the UK. The Telegraph understands that the Duchess is in advanced discussions to join the cast for the third series of The Gentlemen. It is unclear how many episodes she will be appearing in. The Duchess of Sussex, pictured in Australia in April 2026, is set to return to acting. Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP The action series stars Theo James as a British aristocrat who inherits his family’s estate and discovers it is home to an underground cannabis empire. News of the Netflix role comes after entertainment sources told news.com.au on Thursday that the former Suits actress had been offered a part in an upcoming project based in Britain, which sources close to the Sussexes have not denied.



The Telegraph revealed on Wednesday that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were returning to the UK later this month, with their children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, already enrolled at a British school before September. Related Article Analysis

Royal family For Harry and Meghan, going home might just reopen old family wounds It is understood the offer of the role, which was only made recently, formed part of the decision-making process in the family relocating to the UK but was not the sole reason. The Duchess worked as an actress before meeting Prince Harry, and was best known for her role as lawyer Rachel Zane in seven seasons of the US legal drama Suits. In 2017, she went on an acting hiatus and told the BBC that she viewed her career break as “a new chapter”.



She returned to acting for the first time in nearly 10 years, playing herself in the upcoming comedy Close Personal Friends, starring Lily Collins and Brie Larson. Meghan finesses a sponge cake with her make-up artist, Daniel Martin, in her Netflix series With Love, Meghan. The family intends to relocate from the US to a private, non-royal residence thought to be outside London later this month. The Duke and Duchess’s status as non-working royals and private individuals will remain unchanged. It is understood that the King was not aware of the move until last Sunday, but he is said to be pleased his younger son is coming home and is looking forward to spending more time with him and his family.



The Telegraph understands Harry – who misses the UK and wants to be closer to his wider family – hopes to regain the King’s trust by no longer discussing private family matters in public or giving television interviews. Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK. Who will keep them safe? Prince Harry has spent years revealing details about the monarchy and his personal life. However, the couple plan not to expose their children to the public eye and British media organisations have been urged by the regulator not to disclose the location of the new family home or the children’s school. The Duke, whose own private security team claimed he was the focus of six terrorist plots, has long fought to be guaranteed police protection, but this has so far been rejected by the courts and the Home Office committee responsible for such decisions. But the family’s return is set to prompt a review of taxpayer-funded security.



Two senior government sources told The Telegraph that the Royal and VIP Executive Committee, the body that determines the security arrangements of high-profile figures, was likely to review the couple’s security arrangements in light of their plan to return to Britain, and that it might be easier to arrange protection when they are in the UK full-time. Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said on Thursday that the Duke and Duchess’s security was a “private matter”, despite the potential cost for taxpayers if their security were reinstated. No. 10 sources said Burnham’s comments reflected the fact that the Sussexes were private citizens, not working royals, and that their security in California was privately funded. The couple will retain their homes in Montecito, California, and Portugal, while the Duchess will continue to run her US-based lifestyle brand As Ever – which sources insist is thriving – from their new base. Despite her hiatus from acting, the Duchess has worked on a number of commercial projects with Netflix under her and her husband’s company Archewell Productions.



The Sussexes had a five-year $100 million deal with the streaming service, which imploded last year amid reports published in Variety that the relationship between key executives in the company and the couple had soured. Related Article Royal family Prince Harry, celebrities ordered to pay $18m – but final court bill could be higher During that time, the couple produced a six-part documentary on their life, a polo documentary and a lifestyle show named With Love, Meghan, that failed to make the top 1000 most-watched programmes on the streaming platform. In 2021, Andrew Morton, a royal biographer, said the late Queen had told the Duchess she was not obliged to become a full-time member of the royal family when she married Prince Harry, and could continue with her acting career should she wish. “[The Sussexes] were given a degree of latitude,” Morton told the Royally Obsessed podcast.



“They did say to Meghan: ‘If you don’t want to embrace royal duties full time, please be our guest and continue your acting career.’ Those opportunities were open to her.” The Telegraph, London Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: There’s good news for your super – but a big hole remains for retirees
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementSuperannuation Opinion There’s good news for your super – but a big hole remains for retirees Bec Wilson Money contributor August 22, 2026 — 5:09am

August 22, 2026 — 5:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Finally, the government has made its move on financial advice. And there’s plenty for us everyday people to be happy about. But there’s also a big hole in the middle that we must discuss because, ultimately, I want Australians to be able to get the help they need to make good retirement decisions. Daniel Mulino has announced the most significant changes to the financial advice regime and superannuation since the Albanese government came to power. Dominic Lorrimer Yet finding help without strings attached can be really difficult. It might be tied to the institution that already holds your money. Or it might come from an adviser with a centrally determined preferred or approved product list. Or you might find an adviser willing to give you retirement advice, but only if you also 



Because for many people, that’s when the big questions come in thick and fast: should I stay with my super fund? Should I move super funds? What type of retirement product is really right for me (versus the one my fund offers)? When should I start drawing an income stream? How does the age pension fit into my plans? And how much can I really afford to spend? Sometimes you just need someone independent to help you make some of these big decisions well. The big question is whether these reforms will finally make that kind of advice commercially attractive for advisers to offer consumers, and affordable to buy, or whether the advice industry has already moved towards a business model built around ongoing advice and investment management. The government is trying to shut the door on fear-based sales funnelling that can drive people to switch their super into dodgy schemes. Assistant Treasurer and Financial Services Minister Dr Daniel Mulino presented the government’s next stage of financial advice reforms at the National Press Club on Wednesday, with two big focuses. The first takes aim at super spruikers, lead generators and dodgy super switching – practices that have formed part of the chain of misconduct exposed by the devastating Shield and First Guardian collapses. And we should applaud these moves.



The government plans to ban unlicensed real-time communications about super. What that means is that an unlicensed super spruiker or lead generation company won’t be allowed to cold-call you, jump on a live online chat or otherwise engage you in real time to convince you to move your super. Editor's pick Opinion

Financial planning Why getting simple super advice has become an expensive nightmare Bec Wilson Money contributor These are the high-pressure interactions that happen where someone typically tells you your super is underperforming, you’re missing out or your retirement savings are at risk. Then, not long afterwards, they offer to introduce you to an adviser, or you’re told there’s a better place for your money, which ultimately leads to your super switching into high-risk, often poorly understood investments. In other words, the government is trying to shut the door on fear-based sales funnelling that can drive people to switch their super into dodgy managed investment schemes. But he’s also putting much more responsibility on the big institutions that run investment platforms. Under the reforms, ASIC will have the power to direct a super trustee, or a platform trustee, to begin compensating members if an investment option fails and there is reasonable suspicion the trustee hasn’t met their obligations.



And if the trustee is found to have breached those obligations, it will have to compensate members for 100 per cent of their capital losses. APRA will also have the power to require trustees offering higher risk investment options to have the capital backing to meet those obligations. Then, after the door to dodgy players was closed, Mulino moved onto part two – the part of the package we were all waiting for, and the one that will affect most Australians: how we actually get financial advice. There’s some good news here for almost everyone. The government is finally going to move on its long awaited Delivering Better Financial Outcomes (DBFO) reforms. Super funds will be able to reach out to members with “nudges” or prompts that encourage them to seek help. And it will become easier for funds to provide and charge for simpler types of financial advice. The cumbersome statements of advice that have helped make even quite straightforward advice expensive will also be streamlined.



And, the government will allow a new class of adviser to be offered by APRA-regulated super funds and life insurers. The goal of this is to provide a lower-cost form of advice that is within institutions that are already subject to strong regulatory oversight. There will be limits on the types of advice these advisers can provide, but they should be able to help consumers with some of the straightforward questions that, rather absurdly, super funds have struggled to answer under the current rules. Super funds will soon be able to provide more comprehensive advice to members. Dominic Lorrimer And I think that’s a superb thing. We desperately need more affordable help and support in the system. But there’s an obvious limitation. Your advice is coming from the institution that your money is already with, so while they may be able to help you make better decisions within their fund, they are not there to independently shop the market for you and tell you whether another super fund or retirement product might be better for you.



And that’s a pretty important distinction. If I’m approaching retirement, I don’t just want to know which retirement product in my existing fund might suit me next, I also want someone to tell me whether I should be in that fund at all. And if I go to an external adviser, I want to know they really are looking across the market for me, rather than being constrained by a centrally determined preferred or approved product list, designed at least in part, to make the advice business more efficient. These lists can play an important role in due diligence and risk management for advice businesses, and make providing advice more efficient. But efficiency for the advice business doesn’t always translate into a fair breadth of choice a consumer might expect when they are paying for advice. What I want is someone sitting on my side of the table, looking at my options without a predetermined destination for my money. And increasingly, I don’t know where you go to find that any more. To be fair, Mulino may have identified this problem too. Buried in Wednesday’s announcement was a commitment to reform the best interests duty to make it easier for advisers in the wider sector to provide what’s called “scaled advice” – essentially, allowing them to focus on the specific problem you’re asking about, rather than take your entire financial life into consideration.



This could be the most important part of the reforms for people approaching retirement, but the detail of the legislation will matter a lot. Because changing the rules doesn’t mean advice businesses will offer it. Another perspective Opinion

Loyalty programs Is CBA’s revamped rewards scheme worth it? Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor And there’s another piece of the puzzle that hasn’t been solved: Centrelink. Because when you’re approaching retirement, you don’t make your super decisions in isolation. You need to understand how your super and the age pension will combine to deliver you a retirement income. Mulino was asked on Wednesday whether Centrelink and super funds should be able to share information so that funds could provide more comprehensive retirement guidance. He acknowledged there was a real opportunity here, saying that funds could provide better guidance if they had a basic understanding of someone’s broader financial position. And that rather proves my point – retirement advice is a lot more than super advice alone. Your super, the age pension, your other assets and your home all come together at retirement, and difficult decisions need to be made to optimise your situation. We need to make these easier to navigate.



So, while I applaud these reforms for getting the ball rolling, I think there’s a hole right in the middle. We’re making it easier to get help from the super funds that already hold our money today. And we’re making it safer to get advice by shutting down some of the very worst practices. But the real test will be whether these reforms create a market for impartial, affordable advice that consumers can buy without having to buy an investment product or sign up to an ongoing management relationship. Because at retirement, many people aren’t looking for someone to manage their money for 20 years – they just want to pay a fair and transparent fee for someone to help them make the next few decisions well. World.title: Dear Prime Minister: Are you really going to let Kiwi kids best us?
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingFinancial literacy Opinion Dear Prime Minister: Are you really going to let Kiwi kids best us? Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor August 22, 2026 — 5:01am

August 22, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dear prime minister (and come to think of it, all state and territory leaders), I write for urgent action on something that appears to have fallen off the government’s agenda: the nous of our children when they are released into the financial “wilds” at the end of their schooling. We used to have a national financial literacy strategy. This lapsed pre-COVID. We used to have the Australian Government Financial Literacy Board. This was abandoned around that same time. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon at the Parliamentary Friends of Financial Capability event at Parliament House this week. Rohan Thomson Governments here – of both flavours – used to take Australia’s collective money smarts seriously. After all, it’s make or break stuff for our lives. But let me get back to that. In 2022, responsibility for financial literacy was transferred from ASIC – which I believe was doing a bang-up job reaching many children via its lesson plans for teachers – and shifted to Treasury.



Sure, there have been some commendable efforts from the ATO. The Tax, Super + You high school competition is of special note, as is the portal’s curriculum-aligned digital learning platform and simulation games. But it is not enough. Some 70 countries now have an active financial capability strategy. And many of these have begun teaching money as a mandatory part of the school curriculum, often delivered in social sciences all the way up to year 10. Yet 8.5 million Australian adults – nearly half of us – lack basic financial literacy. We are talking Ireland, Finland, 30 states in the US, and the United Kingdom from 2028. Goodness, even New Zealand is doing it from January next year. Yet, there is no official, top-down move to fix this for Aussie kids. Don’t get me wrong, there are many excellent initiatives by many independent bodies and charities, designed to help. But there is zero guarantee that a child will receive these.





What’s more, it is becoming widely understood that financial and mental health are heavily related. Indeed, there’s now a documented bi-directional link: one can cause the other, and it can go both ways. It’s not just wealth, it’s wellbeing. And it impacts relationships and families. Yet 8.5 million Australian adults – nearly half of us – lack basic financial literacy, says new UNSW analysis of the 2016 Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia Survey (HILDA). But I was heartened by, and honoured to speak at, the first-ever Parliamentary Friends of Financial Capability event at Parliament House this week. The event was convened by Labor senator Richard Dowling and Liberal senator Jessica Collins to bring together some 200 people who believe this is a neglected issue, and never before have I been in a room where there was such agreement about the outcome needed, if not the path there. No, it’s not as simple as it is in New Zealand to introduce mandatory money lessons into schools here – we have federation, and national curriculum changes take agreement between six states and two territories. But it is now vital.



It’s not like when many older generations graduated – when the cash was gone, the cash was gone. Today, young people are the targets of technology designed to assist/relieve them of money. Indeed, until roughly 15 years ago, it was only credit cards that presented an overspending challenge, but now there is a proliferation of buy-now-pay-later and early pay services and more, amid a cost-of-living crisis. Dare I open the housing can of worms? Adding financial education to the curriculum is a no-brainer. Aresna Villanueva Our kids need help. How are they to know how to forge themselves a secure future otherwise? Because many parents feel ill-equipped to, and even anxious about, imparting these skills themselves. Please, Mr Albanese, lead the charge to get the states and territories to agree to a revised national curriculum that elevates money lessons to be mandatory. Practical, relatable, real-life ones.



Further, I ask that you urgently implement an – appropriately updated – national financial capability strategy. And I would suggest re-engaging ASIC to steer it. Of course, there needs to be funding. But surely, with the bipartisan support demonstrated at Parliament House this week, the country’s money smarts is worth it. And why would we let NZ kids get an edge on ours? Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram.
