World.title: Dear Prime Minister: Are you really going to let Kiwi kids best us?
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingFinancial literacy Opinion Dear Prime Minister: Are you really going to let Kiwi kids best us? Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor August 22, 2026 — 5:01am

August 22, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dear prime minister (and come to think of it, all state and territory leaders), I write for urgent action on something that appears to have fallen off the government’s agenda: the nous of our children when they are released into the financial “wilds” at the end of their schooling. We used to have a national financial literacy strategy. This lapsed pre-COVID. We used to have the Australian Government Financial Literacy Board. This was abandoned around that same time. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon at the Parliamentary Friends of Financial Capability event at Parliament House this week. Rohan Thomson Governments here – of both flavours – used to take Australia’s collective money smarts seriously. After all, it’s make or break stuff for our lives. But let me get back to that. In 2022, responsibility for financial literacy was transferred from ASIC – which I believe was doing a bang-up job reaching many children via its lesson plans for teachers – and shifted to Treasury.



Sure, there have been some commendable efforts from the ATO. The Tax, Super + You high school competition is of special note, as is the portal’s curriculum-aligned digital learning platform and simulation games. But it is not enough. Some 70 countries now have an active financial capability strategy. And many of these have begun teaching money as a mandatory part of the school curriculum, often delivered in social sciences all the way up to year 10. Yet 8.5 million Australian adults – nearly half of us – lack basic financial literacy. We are talking Ireland, Finland, 30 states in the US, and the United Kingdom from 2028. Goodness, even New Zealand is doing it from January next year. Yet, there is no official, top-down move to fix this for Aussie kids. Don’t get me wrong, there are many excellent initiatives by many independent bodies and charities, designed to help. But there is zero guarantee that a child will receive these.





What’s more, it is becoming widely understood that financial and mental health are heavily related. Indeed, there’s now a documented bi-directional link: one can cause the other, and it can go both ways. It’s not just wealth, it’s wellbeing. And it impacts relationships and families. Yet 8.5 million Australian adults – nearly half of us – lack basic financial literacy, says new UNSW analysis of the 2016 Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia Survey (HILDA). But I was heartened by, and honoured to speak at, the first-ever Parliamentary Friends of Financial Capability event at Parliament House this week. The event was convened by Labor senator Richard Dowling and Liberal senator Jessica Collins to bring together some 200 people who believe this is a neglected issue, and never before have I been in a room where there was such agreement about the outcome needed, if not the path there. No, it’s not as simple as it is in New Zealand to introduce mandatory money lessons into schools here – we have federation, and national curriculum changes take agreement between six states and two territories. But it is now vital.



It’s not like when many older generations graduated – when the cash was gone, the cash was gone. Today, young people are the targets of technology designed to assist/relieve them of money. Indeed, until roughly 15 years ago, it was only credit cards that presented an overspending challenge, but now there is a proliferation of buy-now-pay-later and early pay services and more, amid a cost-of-living crisis. Dare I open the housing can of worms? Adding financial education to the curriculum is a no-brainer. Aresna Villanueva Our kids need help. How are they to know how to forge themselves a secure future otherwise? Because many parents feel ill-equipped to, and even anxious about, imparting these skills themselves. Please, Mr Albanese, lead the charge to get the states and territories to agree to a revised national curriculum that elevates money lessons to be mandatory. Practical, relatable, real-life ones.



Further, I ask that you urgently implement an – appropriately updated – national financial capability strategy. And I would suggest re-engaging ASIC to steer it. Of course, there needs to be funding. But surely, with the bipartisan support demonstrated at Parliament House this week, the country’s money smarts is worth it. And why would we let NZ kids get an edge on ours? Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. Expert tips on how to save, invest and make the most of your money delivered to your inbox every Sunday.

World.title: ‘Still Kelly country’: Life in Porepunkah after Dezi Freeman, as locals pick up the pieces
World.content:
It was those tactical police, with their big guns, who told Kompe that Freeman had shot and killed two police officers and injured another when they’d gone to his home to serve a warrant in a child sexual abuse investigation. Freeman, 56, had stolen a police pistol and vanished into the trees down by the Buckland River, and he was still on the run.

Almost a year ago, on another misty day like this, it was the police who came checking on Kompe. They were looking for a man he once knew well. Kompe first met Desmond Filby down by this river in the 1980s, and began teaching the long-haired teenager bushcraft. Forty years on, Filby was living in his own solar-powered retreat, off-grid, just a few kilometres up the hill, but he had taken a new name: Dezi Freeman.

Ray Kompe, who knew Dezi Freeman, at his off-the-grid hut in the Buckland Valley. “I’m a bit of a recluse these days,” he says.

When we arrive, the former gold prospector has just hoisted a huge new lithium battery onto the roof. It weighs more than he does. “The neighbours did have to check I hadn’t done myself in,” grins Kompe. He emerges from behind his little hut’s screen door with a torch still aglow on his beanie and the sleepy look of a miner stumbling back into the light.

It was built more than a century ago in Victoria’s high country, so close to the Buckland River in Porepunkah that you can hear the water rushing past under the wind. Back then, that river still gave up lumps of gold like Easter eggs. But today, you might think the hut long abandoned, if not for the patchwork of solar panels wired along its roof. They were put there – using an elaborate “Batman-style” abseiling rig – by its reclusive yet nimble 73-year-old inhabitant, Ray Kompe.

There is a little hut at the foot of the mountain, just minutes down the road from where Australia’s biggest-ever manhunt began.

Well before COVID, though, Kompe had had enough of Dezi. “He fell in with that conspiracy crowd. He was watching these violent WWII videos … of Japanese torture. Sickening stuff. I just thought: ‘Why am I here with this weirdo?’ ”

“Well, he wouldn’t be welcome here any more,” says Kompe. For decades, he’d put up with his fixations, his rants against the government, as they explored the bush and its hidden mineshafts and waterfalls together. But the idealistic teenager who loved photography and attended hippie festivals had undeniably grown into a bitter and angry man. Even before the pandemic, he’d become a fanatical adherent of the pseudo-law peddled by so-called “ sovereign citizens ”, those who don’t recognise the authority of government – who drive under fake licence plates and change their names to Freeman (free man).

Inside Kompe’s hut, we squeeze past a bicycle in the hall and a shower in the kitchen. He apologises for the mess while his white chihuahua Luna darts around our ankles. Kompe watched the police comb through it all a year ago – the start of hundreds of raids on properties across the high country in search of Freeman and those who helped him. They flew a tiny drone “the size of two cigarette packets” straight through his place, politely weaving between towers of books and cassette tapes, into cupboards. Officers even shone a light down into the outside dunny. No Freeman.

I’ve come to see Kompe because I’m trying to understand how someone could survive in the wild here – or at least how they could be smuggled out of it under the noses of what felt to locals at times like half the state’s police force. But then there’s so much more to understand about what happened in Porepunkah than that, especially for the families still mourning and the remote community still divided by the violence at its door.

It would be another seven months before police caught sight of him again – when he emerged, wrapped in a doona, from a shipping container at a remote hideout more than 100 kilometres away near the NSW border. After a three-hour standoff, Freeman dropped the doona to fire that stolen revolver and was shot dead by the tactical snipers calling for his surrender.

Them meaning the “cookers”, the sovereign citizens – especially the ones who hate being called sovereign citizens. “You know, the nutjobs,” says Wendt.

Thompson also knew Freeman. He’d gone along with the other nine officers serving the warrant that day because it was hoped that he might be able to reason with the conspiracy theorist. He’d spoken of Freeman in the weeks prior, Thompson’s best friends Andrew “Crouchy” Crouch and Dirk Wendt tell me over a beer back in Melbourne. “Thommo was thinking: ‘We’ll sort it. I’ll talk him down again,’ ” says Crouch. “I didn’t realise then how big a stronghold that area’s become for them.”

Detective Thompson, known as “Thommo”, knew this country well, and how treacherous it can be beyond the tourist bubble of Bright. This is not the Australian bush as seen in dusty, outback noir: stray from the path and the scrub is thick and wet, threaded with blackberries and secret tunnels. Riverbanks can suddenly burst and turn whole clearings into marshlands.

Neal Thompson (left) and Vadim de Waart-Hottart (pictured with a painting done for him by someone he helped through a mental health crisis) were remembered as adventurous and kind. “Thommo” was known for his silly Macgyver fixes out bush, but singular focus on the job. And both he and de Waart-Hottart (“the romantic”) were still adored as family by their former partners.

Those who knew the two officers killed – including local police not authorised to speak publicly ahead of an inquest into the deaths – say problems between police and the “cookers” in the hills had been brewing before the shooting. “But we didn’t know what we were walking into,” says an officer who was there when it happened.

The night Freeman murdered seasoned local detective Neal Thompson, 59, and 35-year-old rising star, Vadim de Waart-Hottart, snow fell on Mount Buffalo. A battering blizzard of rain and lightning howled down the spine of the tourist road as scores of heavily armed police scoured the forest for the fugitive.

Instead, that Tuesday, Crouchy heard news of the Porepunkah killings over the police radios. Thommo, his best friend since he was 12, the cop who was always first through the door, had been shot dead. Crouch’s unit, the dog squad, was called up to the high country to hunt for the killer.

“He was finding it harder than I expected, harder than I did, giving it up,” says Crouch. “But we had real adventures planned for retirement.”

Secretly, though, he was chuffed. And a little overwhelmed. He’d joined the force barely out of his teens and he liked the swagger it gave him around town. He liked helping people. He still wore the same long, black detective’s coat he’d always worn, chasing crooks through wheatfields, crashing police cars, as if he’d rocketed straight out of a 1980s cop drama. His favourite crook in town called him “The Don”.

Thommo and Crouchy were supposed to retire together. Two cops working at opposite ends of Victoria, they’d grown up together in Bendigo, and now they’d lined up their final shifts to fall within days of each other. Thommo always had to be first through the door, “like a bull at the gate”, Crouch says, so, of course, Thommo was retiring first, too. A party was planned that Friday, though Thommo was worried his station in Wangaratta would do a guard of honour “or some nonsense”, and had a sly idea to nip off to the pub early.

When I arrive in Bright on the first night of the town’s popular winter festival, my accommodation host explains: “People come here for the peace. But some people come here to hide. Especially out there. Who are you here with again?”

This March, his parents returned to Australia and to the same police chapel to commemorate the Russell Street bombings that killed another young officer in Melbourne 40 years ago. Beside them was Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush, as he had been during Vadim’s funeral.

It rained for days after the Porepunkah murders, every day for nearly a fortnight. But, on September 5, the day of de Waart-Hottart’s funeral, the sun broke through the stained-glass windows of the police academy chapel in Melbourne, as the young constable was being laid to rest. His mother Carolina smiled, raising her hands to the light. She’d told those gathered at the funeral that her son would live on in nature, and now here he was, her Vadim, making everyone smile again.

The lobby was packed full of flowers and tributes for de Waart-Hottart and Thompson at the Wangaratta police station in the weeks after the shooting.

“We’ll have to clear all this out soon,” says Vogels, staring at the photographs of Thompson and de Waart-Hottart still on display on the little white table in the foyer, children’s drawings pinned to the wall behind. “We’re going to do something special for them.”

A permanent memorial is now being hewn out of rock outside the station for Thompson alongside de Waart-Hottart – the “gentle giant” from Belgium who had been excited to explore the Alpine wilds on his new secondment from Melbourne. A female officer, who narrowly escaped the shooting herself when the homemade shotgun Freeman turned on her jammed, has been fundraising with her son for a similar memorial outside the Bright station, ahead of Victoria Police commemorations on August 26.

At Wangaratta police station in those early days, there were so many flowers piled in the entryway, the doors could barely close, says Senior Sergeant Luke Vogels. People brought slabs of beer too, though sadly, policy dictated the tinnies had to be turned away. Nothing like this had ever really happened before.

He couldn’t tell them then, but, while they gathered, officers were analysing surprise new intelligence about the whereabouts of their son’s killer. Detectives had thought Freeman already dead – months of searching had failed to turn up a single, useful lead. Now suddenly they had one, and it led to a remote property in the state’s north.

De Waart-Hottart’s mother and brother at his funeral (left), and Andrew Crouch helping carry Thompson’s coffin during his service days later in September 2025. Eddie Jim; Justin McManus

Three days later, when Freeman was found there and shot dead, de Waart-Hottart’s parents were the first people Bush called. Today, police are piecing together how he got there, and who they believe helped him. Multiple people have been raided and arrested. No one has yet been charged.

But “sov-cit” ideas are growing in these hills and beyond, locals say. All elections, from councils to federal parliament, have seen an increase in sov-cit protest votes. Even some of Thommo’s friends, people he got to know out hunting and fishing, would later turn out to be sympathetic to Freeman’s anti-government cause, as conspiracy theorists lionised the fugitive online. They called Freeman the modern-day Ned Kelly. Porepunkah is, after all, they said, just 80 kilometres from Glenrowan, where Kelly made his last stand against police 150-odd years ago.

“This is still Kelly country,” says Freeman’s close friend, Bruce Evans, adjusting a velcro strap on his camouflage pants. It’s a common refrain.

Bruce Evans says he misses his good mate Dezi Freeman, but adds: “I know he shot those cops.” Jason South

In Bright, where the hills cast shadows of green velvet, the murders split the community. Some rallied around Freeman’s Filipino wife Mali, well-liked but left homeless and adrift with their children after he fled. Others tied blue ribbons to lamp poles to honour the officers shot.

Leanne Boyd, who once employed Mali at her popular cafe and helped fundraise supplies for her, says she fell somewhere in the middle. She was no fan of her friend Mali’s odd husband, but the strain of people pulling in both directions left her exhausted. Either Freeman was a monster or an outlaw hero. Either Mali was his Lady Macbeth accomplice or “a f---ing saint”, as one friend of Freeman’s hisses at me down the phoneline.

It’s the morning rush at Boyd’s cafe and a pen wobbles in her long, blonde hair; a tremulous, load-bearing look about it. These days Mali is rarely seen around town, though prosecutors have dropped talk of charging her over the shootings. “Mali always asks, ‘What’s going on in the outside world?’ ” sighs Boyd. “She just wants peace. I think we’re all sick of thinking about it.”

Leanne Boyd says “the kindness came from everywhere at first” as locals rallied around police – and Freeman’s young family left behind – after the shootings. Jason South

I understand. Four months ago, when Freeman was shot dead, I’d driven up this mountain and stood on this street and asked the same questions. One in a parade of journalists periodically crashing over the town like the tide and then retreating, with business cards tucked in the crooks of doors and letterboxes. Bright had been all bustling colour then, orange leaves trodden underfoot in the final hours of the Easter weekend. There was hope that, with Freeman gone, the tourism that powered the town would come roaring back to life.

Some businesses are still recovering from the manhunt lockdown that choked off the rare, bumper snow season of 2025, even with government assistance grants. Boyd says she lost $28,000, back when her only customers were the undercover cops in town (“They dressed too well to be locals or ski bunnies”).

“Magic town”: tourists and locals enjoy the start of Winter Fest in Bright in late July. Jason South

Still, today there is fake snow on the air, and fairy-lights overhead and the town is once again heaving with out-of-towners for the winter festival. Over Boyd’s shoulder, I watch a couple struggling to fit armfuls of hire skis – and their gigantic, grinning Samoyed – into the back of a hatchback.

Only the year before the shooting, the property that borders the farm where it happened was taken over by a film crew for production of Netflix movie War Machine. “People with guns were running around then, too, fighting imaginary aliens,” says local Gary Monshing. “So we’ve had a bit on around here.”

Gary’s daughter Georgia and her partner Ben now run the family ski gear shop in Porepunkah. It’s one of many competing ski shops on the tourist road – at least two of them guarded by near-identical border collies – and the Monshings are exactly the kind of genuine, postcard-friendly people that make tourism agencies breathless to remind the public that, yes, Bright really is the same honey-gold snow town it’s always been, thank you very much.

Georgia Monshing and Ben Kaye (pictured with their daughter Milla) didn’t want to complain about the manhunt lockdown choking off business (though they made a good trade in snowchains for police cars), but say they are relieved the area’s now bouncing back. Jason South

But while many locals are eager not to be defined by the tragedy, others seem just as eager to stress that they don’t believe “the official story”. Some trust police even less than before. And the question of who helped Freeman on the run – and who might have helped turn him in – is still there too, on the air.

When Freeman was killed in March, his eldest son posted a plea online for people not to celebrate. “That’s still my father,” Koah wrote.

Josh Roose, a researcher who advises police and governments on extremism cases, calls the high country “strange country”, where the modern, online phenomenon of sov-cits collides with old bush mythology of the outlaw. You’ll find people in rural poverty, off-grid in makeshift shelters or huts like Kompe – once living rough by the river and still hesitant to use the heating until after dark, until it’s really cold – while, next door, luxury Airbnbs sit empty half the year.

As police hunted Freeman, drones buzzed in the night, but properties were too vast to properly surveil, and phone taps quiet. (“Everyone knew they were listening,” says Boyd.) Some locals even refused to serve police coffee, Roose recalls. “It’s a closed shop up there. They might get tourists but the locals are the locals. That’s their defining borderline between us and them.”

The thing to remember about the Freeman case, Roose tells me, is that “Dezi was not only deeply embedded in a network of anti-government types” – though he was, he was up to his neck in them the way you can find yourself up to your neck in blackberries in the scrub. But Freeman was also “just embedded in his local community in a way most people don’t understand”.

When the sun sets behind the mountain, an underground network of two-way radios crackle to life. Among those listening is Bright blacksmith (and one-time bikie) Stephen Mallett. As the head of Australia’s main “doomsday prepper” Facebook community, he’s met many of those at the other end of the line. Sometimes it’s someone on the roads needing help. Sometimes it’s someone like Freeman. Mallett knew him before the shooting as another local preparing for catastrophe – whatever flavour of civil war, foreign invasion or asteroid collision you preferred. “But the day of the shootings,” says Mallett, “the radio waves all went dead.”

He was one of the first of Freeman’s associates raided (and cleared of helping him). When he opened his door in the howling rain to find red lasers pointed at his chest, he considered racing for his back fence and the forest behind – that forest of old mines, forgotten huts and hidden waterfalls. Mallett is perhaps the 20th local to tell me that police, in their months of searching, didn’t cover even half of it. But Mallett didn’t run.

Stephen Mallet, pictured with his dog Tucker. Eddie Jim

“Nothing to hide. And I was afraid they’d shoot my dog,” he says as he shows me his camouflage “bug-out bag” or emergency pack. The thing to grab in case of apocalypse. He wouldn’t take the huge knives he makes, custom, for “hippie chicks” online if he was running. He’d pack light. And he’d keep moving, through the pine plantations, the wineries, stealing off fruit trees or going up the waters Freeman used to kayak, which all rush north to the Murray River, near where he was discovered. “They’d never find you.”

Friends remember Freeman pointing out his prepper stashes on the mountain and disappearing into its trees for weeks at a time to hunt. Beth Knights says he knew how to live off the land even back in their 20s, when they met at the hippie festivals in these hills, cooking over campfires and swimming naked in the river. He still went by his family name Filby then, and his hair was long. There was no electricity for a bush-doof rave, but there was a magic idealism on the air; people coming together in little tribes.

Freeman wasn’t like the city folk with whom Knights hitched a ride from Melbourne. He was a local, “with a thick, bogan accent”, but warm and fun and generous then. He knew how to build a fire break, and he’d catch fish with his hands from the river, the water coursing past his legs. Life went rushing on, of course, as it does, and dragged them apart. Knights, today a TV writer in Castlemaine, wonders what dragged Freeman under. A particular conspiracy? A personal tragedy?

Dezi Freeman (right) at a Rainbow Gathering hippie festival in the hills in the 1990s.

She remembers a bitterness in Freeman when she saw him again, at a music festival in the 2000s. “Or maybe it was just sadness. It’s like he couldn’t fit anywhere. He only made sense out there.” Something about him left an impression, though. “I always wanted to know where he ended up. I was just horrified when I realised it was him.”

For the Filbys, Freeman’s ravings had been a problem without a satisfying explanation for years. He lived off welfare support while hating the government; he made fun of “flat-earther” conspiracists, while his own biblical delusions intensified. Freeman had been deeply affected by a series of deaths in his family, though most of the Filbys left were estranged from him by the shootings, including nephews Luke and Joe. Luke remembers his uncle destroying cassettes of Metallica, once his favourite band, because he’d declared them satanic. “Dez was always the oddball uncle,” says Joe. But he was also the uncle who took a young Joe hiking when he was depressed in his teens and offered support. “We never saw anything like this coming. It’s been devastating.”

Around the time of COVID, Freeman’s attempts to arrest a local magistrate and help privately prosecute then-premier Daniel Andrews made him infamous.

But by August 2025, he was facing serious allegations of child sexual abuse, and his brother and wife finally convinced him to see a psychologist. He had an appointment booked on the day of the shooting. He never made it.

The track that leads to the Porepunkah property where Freeman shot dead the police officers. Eddie Jim

Ten minutes out of town, the old, converted bus where the Freemans lived is still there. It sits in one corner of a sprawling chestnut farm, next to the Buckland River. Under the tarp of Freeman’s makeshift kitchen, he hung a sign for the Buckland and a picture of the Virgin Mary.

You can see the property from the hills near the airfield, but it’s easy to miss the turn-off – a narrow gravel track through a tunnel of forest with a metal gate at the end. Exclusion zone, warns a handwritten, cardboard sign. No trespass. There is a strange, fairy-tale feeling to the trees here; lit gold in the sunlight, but, as the sky darkens, they lean too close.

The converted bus and living space where the Freemans lived, in one corner of the Swift farm. Jason South

Freeman’s landlords, Andrew and Rebecca Swift, still live behind this gate, in a red-roofed farmhouse with their daughters. Others live here too, “a little community”, according to neighbours and friends. But few people get past the gate.

Freeman made it himself, an elaborate early-warning system of security codes and solar-powered cameras, with more hidden throughout the trees. He always had eyes in the bush, locals say. He’d construct elaborate “hides” from which to watch his neighbours, strap cameras to his chest and don camouflage suits that made him look like Chewbacca. When child services and police surrounded the bus more than once in the years before the shooting – out of concern for the Freeman children – their approach was picked up by this ring of CCTV.

The Swifts aren’t answering the phone, but the gate’s warnings grow more strident the further I read. Offenders will be prosecuted and fined a minimum of ten thousand dollars.

They’re well-liked in town, the Swifts, though fiercely private. Rebecca in particular is known for her anti-government views. The Freemans moved onto their farm four years ago, after a string of fallings-out between Freeman and his former landlords had left them homeless. People speak of Freeman’s terrifying temper, of his obsession with guns and a mysterious marijuana crop that sprung up at one property in Myrtleford. Most of all, Freeman hated female cops. But the shootings in August caught the Swifts by surprise. “They’re peaceful people,” says friend Bruce Evans.

Police had decided a specialist sniper squad wasn’t needed that day to serve the warrant, hoping to keep Freeman calm. Instead, they sent 10 officers, including two of their best: Thompson the veteran and de Waart-Hottart, formerly of the city’s public order response unit.

In Andrew Swift’s own account of what unfolded when Freeman barricaded himself in the bus with Mali and their toddler – as told to a YouTuber who runs wellness festivals, not “the mainstream media” – Swift says he never heard Freeman warn police he had a gun.

Freeman shot Thompson first as the detective climbed in through the bus window. Then de Waart-Hottart.

A preliminary hearing for the upcoming inquest heard that Freeman stole de Waart-Hottart’s gun and used it to shoot Thompson a second time, where he lay on the ground. “Can you hear us Thommo?” called one of the other officers now taking cover. “F---ing scum, die in hell,” said Freeman.

At Thommo’s favourite cafe, run by close friend Anita Cook, a plaque by one bench now reads “Neal’s corner”. “He was kind of the man in my life that I depended on,” says Cook, who saw Thompson as usual when he stopped by before work the day of the shooting. “He’d always sneak in early to surprise me. I’ve only just stopped looking up expecting to see him.” Jason South

Roose gave expert testimony at the inquest into the 2022 Wieambilla shootings – when Christian extremists murdered two police officers and a neighbour at a remote Queensland property. That should have been a routine missing-person check. But, like Freeman, the Train family hated police, and called them “devils”.

Since the Porepunkah shootings, Freeman’s image has started appearing on posters at far-right rallies throughout Australian cities. Yet, in the regions where these ideologies are also brewing, mental health services and other supports remain painfully thin, says Roose – a knife’s edge. “We have to wake up to this as a serious threat.”

Sunday in Bright, and under the soaring timber beams of the Our Lady of the Snows church, Father Tony Shallue is delivering a sermon on the dangers of misinformation. The Freemans came here most Sundays, including two days before the shooting, though Father Tony worried about Freeman’s strange slide into doomsday fanaticism, his ravings about the Antichrist.

“In this world of information, not all of it is wisdom,” the priest tells his flock now. It’s a sermon so on theme I wonder if my cover is already blown, having just strolled in off the street to find the congregation in a late Mass. The singing had drawn me in. A black dog is tied up out front.

Father Tony briefly pauses his sermon warning of technology coming between people to wrestle with a malfunctioning microphone. But it’s not all bad, he continues, if it brings us together.

The main farmhouse at the Porepunkah property where the shooting happened, pictured during the manhunt. Joe Armao

We check back on Ray Kompe at his hut, where the only real technology is the solar panels and the gadgets he fashions himself. Kompe apologises again for the mess, but the closer I look, the more I sense an order to the clutter. His dog’s vet records hang, neatly labelled, on one wall. On another are framed drawings from his neighbours’ children, the neighbours who check on him.

People tried to check on Freeman, when they knew something had taken him under. Others seemed happy to draw him deeper and deeper into the whirlpool of pseudo law and conspiracies.

In the past year, Kompe says he’s lost interest in making gadgets entirely, though he’s not sure why. “Everyone’s just on their phones now,” he offers, half-heartedly, but he’s looking across the field, towards the hill where the boy he knew as Desmond Filby shot three men.

“I mean, the world doesn’t ever really go away, does it?”

World.title: ‘Anger’s not something that women have been allowed to have’: Why Myf Warhurst is done playing nice
World.content:

This story is part of the August 22 edition of Good Weekend. See all stories .

Think of Myf Warhurst and the word “bubbly” might spring to mind. With everything she does – from Spicks and Specks, the Eurovision Song Contest or her documentary The Truth about Menopause – Warhurst is the ray of sunshine; the nice one. But she’s no longer playing nice. She’s taken on the patriarchy in a new book, Middle Rage (out August 25). And she’s mad. When I heard you’d written a book on rage, I thought maybe it was about you shaking your fist at climate change or losing it over smaller things, like parking tickets. But this book is really serious – about tackling patriarchy head-on. What does the patriarchy mean to you and why did you decide to focus on it? Initially, it was going to be this funny book about all the things in middle age that annoyed me. But because [with menopause] you have this great awakening, you lose your oestrogen, and all of a sudden it’s like you’re overcome with a laser focus. You can see everything clearly. You see the inequality everywhere. And rather than just getting sad about it, I was feeling furious, and then I looked into that and realised, “Oh, anger’s not something that women have really been allowed to have over the years.” Girls are encouraged to play nice, keep it small, don’t be too expressive. There’s all this conditioning that has got us here, and it all leads to one thing, and that is the patriarchy. That’s an easy thing to jump to and say, “Oh, you know, it’s the patriarchy’s fault,” but it’s a system by which we live, and it’s a very clear system that advantages one over the other. It also disadvantages men, because little boys aren’t allowed to become the full human beings that they could become by showing their emotions, and they’re forced into a system that kind of makes them go to work and do shitty jobs for everyone who’s making the money at the top. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Squealing on the inside’: Myf Warhurst on her surprise teen-crush co-star I’ve also had a couple of relationship experiences whereby I realised my own conditioning allowed me to put up with certain behaviours that I shouldn’t have ... I’m terrified of [releasing the book] because people aren’t going to expect it from me, but I’m also really proud of it. What makes you terrified? Girls, especially, learn how to people-please because they realise it makes them safe in an environment. So it’s very hard to strip back all those layers of conditioning and know I might disappoint some people with this book and know that some will think I’ve changed or lost my mind. But this person has always been there. I just hadn’t shown that side of my personality until now. ‘I never thought it could happen to me because I’m a very well-educated, very privileged white woman.’ Myf Warhurst You also talk directly to men in the book, don’t you? The thing is, I grew up with great men, and maybe that was a luxury and a privilege. My brothers are fantastic; they’re creative, they’re very emotional, they respect me, as do my male friends. But I think it’s probably having had good experiences that led me towards not questioning other men who have come into my world in the same way, because I just trusted a little bit blindly. And I think it’s a Gen X thing, too; the way that generation was brought up. We were brought up on love stories and romances, where the ending was always tied with a neat little bow, and you got married, and then the story stopped.



The book went to some dark places, particularly when discussing one of your exes around the time of COVID-19. You describe it as an unhealthy relationship that left you financially in debt. You wrote that things got so dark that there were nights you went to sleep hoping you didn’t wake up. What was that like? Well, fortunately, it was a long time ago, so now I can talk about it. But also, writing the book allowed me to work through it myself. I haven’t included anything particularly salacious, but I think it was important to note that when you get caught up in relationships that are unhealthy, it can really lead you down a dark path because you feel like there’s no way out, especially if you’ve been manipulated to believe that you’re the problem. But it was also important for me to note that if I don’t say these sorts of things, then other women will be frightened to do so. I never thought it could happen to me because I’m a very well-educated, very privileged white woman who exists in a world full of kind people. How did it happen to me? It does because you’re not looking for it. What are the top few things you’d recommend to women about recognising controlling behaviour? Just look for patterns, look for repeat behaviours – patterns like denying your reality when you say something happened or how you felt. If they say that’s not how it was, or you’ve remembered it incorrectly, then that’s a huge red flag. Your interpretation of a moment is your interpretation. There is nothing wrong with it. They could also, in the same breath, say they love you, which is confusing and can be quite manipulative. So, look for the patterns, and once you see them, you have every right to just get out in those early days. You don’t have to make it work … Women, especially of my generation, Gen X, were brought up in a culture where we’re taught to believe we are the ones that make it work, regardless of how difficult it is. Related Article Good Weekend Rachel spent five years ‘quiet quitting’ her marriage. Her husband didn’t see it coming How do you reflect on that relationship now? You go through all the emotions. You go through the lows. It wasn’t great and I wasn’t great. For me, it was incredibly educational. It’s taken me until 50 to really see these kinds of behaviours for what they are, and I’m disappointed about that. I wish I’d known [about them beforehand], and I do think younger generations know this stuff a lot earlier than we do, or we did. So, I am genuinely, weirdly grateful because finally it all makes sense, and I’m able to look at this next chapter, whatever the hell it may be – who I can become – without worrying about whether or not I have to have a relationship. I grew up with all those thoughts of feeling “less than” because I never managed to get relationships right. Now, it’s like, “Well, it’s not working now, I can see it. I don’t want that any more.” I see it as fortunate now. I can write a book like this because I’ve got the time. Because I haven’t got kids. You’ve talked in the book about calling out bad behaviour more now because you’re at this stage of your life. Can you give me an example of that? Look, the theory is real. The practice is harder and I think it’s going to take time to really stand behind everything I’ve written. It’s not like I’m walking around being furious all the time. But I’m a bit more straight-up. I’m not writing those emails any more that say “just checking in”, “no worries if not”. I still do it sometimes, and I check myself … You don’t change inherently as a person. It’s just understanding that you are allowed to be direct, and you are allowed to say what you want or need, and if that disappoints someone, then that’s OK. It doesn’t mean becoming a Karen, either – I use the term in the book, the ladies with the can-I speak-to-the-manager haircuts. Like, that’s entitlement, that is patriarchal behaviour. Related Article Investigation

Good Weekend Isolated, scared, forlorn: The heartbreaking final months of Virginia Giuffre’s life It’s interesting there’s no male equivalent to “being a Karen”. There was a news story a couple of years ago where you were in a dispute with a neighbour about a fence. Do you feel like you were depicted as a “Karen” in that situation? That was over legal boundary issues, of which I’m certainly not an expert, and I wasn’t actually involved in that argument – I was in the house at the time. I think the media are always very quick to portray women in a negative light. It gets clicks. It’s the algorithm. I do think there’s this resistance to women speaking up about anything and having an opinion, and that is, again, the last gasp of the patriarchy just trying to put women back in their place. But similarly, for men, they’ve been allowed anger but have had to suppress other emotions. We are allowed as women to cry – I mean, I do it all the time – but men aren’t. And so many men I’ve spoken to while doing this book say that they haven’t cried for years.



What really struck me in the book was the experiences you’ve had with creepy men, like the guy who kept texting you while you were on the radio saying that he was on his way in to see you from the country. How scary was that for you? That’s pretty normal when you’re in the media, though. And my experiences are very similar to most women who are in the public eye. Actually, I’ve probably gotten off pretty lightly compared to women who are very vocal online today and are very vocal in the media. I’ve also realised that what we were taught, which was not to call it out, not to cause a fuss by responding, meant you’re feeding the beast. I actually think maybe staying silent is not the answer. What would you like people to take away from this book? This book might disappoint some people who pick it up and go, “Oh, that’s not what I was expecting.” But I hope that they can keep an open mind and see it as a way to reconnect with understanding how broader systems work and how that affects all of us, and I think that’s where we need to look right now. Because a lot of women are feeling very frustrated at the moment, and I think it’s important to understand why. How many women were killed by their intimate partner in the last week here in Australia? It was five. A week before that, it was four. Like, what is going on? Things need to change, and I think this book might help people want to change things around them and to help younger generations learn so they can have a safer and more productive time of it, and to make choices that are better for all of them, not just for a system that works against them. Middle Rage by Myf Warhurst is published by Hachette Australia on September 8. If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: The property premium Sydney families are paying for the right state school
World.content:
Exclusive PropertyNewsSydney house prices The property premium Sydney families are paying for the right state school Robyn Willis August 22, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Choosing the right school for your child can often come at a cost, but new data reveals just how much some parents are prepared to pay – and it has nothing to do with school fees. Data from Cotality shows that the median value of homes in some Sydney catchment zones is significantly above that of properties immediately beyond their borders, suggesting families are prepared to pay a premium to ensure their child has a place at a specific school. Some Sydney school zones command premium property prices. Peter Rae The report, which focused exclusively on high schools, compared property values within the catchment with those in the rest of the suburb based on data to June 2026. Children living within state school catchment zones are guaranteed a place at those schools, according to the NSW Department of Education.



The divide was most obvious in the Randwick/Rose Bay and Killara/Lindfield zones, where median property values were $1 million greater inside the zone than properties beyond the boundary. In the Rose Bay/Randwick catchment zone, for example, the median house value within the catchment was $4,339,810 compared with $2,783,174 outside the zone, while in Killara/Lindfield, the median value inside the zone was $3,805,422, while beyond the boundary it was $2,763,611. Rose Bay Secondary College, Epping Boys High School and Killara High School remain among the highest ranking non-selective state schools in NSW for ATAR scores. Demand from families is not news to Ray White Upper North Shore sales agent Jessica Cao, who works in Killara and Lindfield.



“I have been doing this for over 10 years, and it is always the case [that buyers want to be in the catchment area],” she said, adding that buyers often plan ahead. “With a lot of the families, the kids are in later primary school years [when they buy],” she said. “It is a very family-oriented area and families stay for a long time.” While for families of high school-aged children the focus is on the ATAR result, demand is also strong among parents of primary school children, although their reasons differ. Elizabeth and Sam Newton admit they paid a $400,000 premium so that their son and daughter could live near Boronia Park Public School, which enjoys a reputation among locals as a close-knit community with a nurturing environment.



“We sold for $1.8m [outside the catchment] and bought [near the school] for $2.2 million eight years ago,” Elizabeth said. Elizabeth and Sam Newton wanted their children to be able to walk to school and foster local connections. George Chan “[We loved] the fact that the kids could grow up independent and have the freedom to walk to the school and the local shops. It’s pivotal to their development,” she said. McGrath Hunters Hill sales agent Matt Ward said that interest in the school had increased among local families in recent years. “People were not talking about it five to 10 years ago, but in the past year or two, good news travels fast and people are spreading a positive message about that school,” he said.



In areas such as Hunters Hill, where parents regularly opt for private schooling when their children reach high school, a school-friendly address is more complex than catchment zones. Related Article NSW residential property More Sydney properties are being passed in. This is what happens to them “If you live in Sydney, 95 per cent of people would have a car, but at the same time, particularly [for students] in high school, people live busy lives, and if you can have kids getting on the bus to get to school [that’s an advantage],” Ward said. Cao said that for some families, a catchment-zone property allows them to sell for a premium when the time comes, as well as providing a “back-up” state school. Cotality quantitative analyst Irene Kang said that while the report found the difference in values remained even after the influence of proximity to the coastline or waterways was removed, other factors such as accessibility to public transport could not be discounted.



However, buying into an area for its catchment zone has risks too. Related Article Auctions Family buys $3.5m inner west house that would have cost $3.8m earlier Catchment areas can change over time, a spokesperson for the Education Department said, and they are informed by factors such as new housing activity and demographic changes as well as enrolment projections and planned housing development. Cotality’s executive research director, Tim Lawless, said that school catchment areas are not considered a strong driver of price growth because they are subject to change. “Changing rules and regulations are a risk in the property market,” he said. “If the school zone is changing, it will have a marginal impact along the boundary.”



For the Newtons, the school commute is about to get a little longer. The family is moving to a waterfront property to further their 10-year-old daughter’s interest in sailing, a sport the whole family is passionate about. They have put their home on the market. “I told friends I am not leaving this house unless it is for waterfront or in a coffin because the [local school] community is incredible,” Elizabeth said.

World.title: An unloved South American city is home to the perfect sandwich
World.content:
Almost every visitor to Peru goes to Callao, though, most don’t hang around for long. The country’s main international airport is located in this port city, which has been effectively subsumed by Lima, the capital. For the most part, Callao is the sort of gritty, unloved part of the world that most people are more than happy to leave. It’s a far cry from the beauty of Lima’s tourist hubs of Miraflores or Barranco.



That lack of interest in Callao, however, is a shame because so many people miss La Punta, the finger of land in Callao’s far west.

Callao’s upmarket coastal district of La Punta. Alamy

This is an upper-class neighbourhood originally settled by a migrant Italian community, and you can still feel that influence at one of its most cherished, historic restaurants, Don Giuseppe.

The charming owners here, Juan Hernandez and wife Lidia Siles, have an Italian background, but their food at this no-frills diner is distinctly Peruvian, with home style dishes such as sandwiches and seafood soups, served with the sort of warm hospitality that will have you hankering for a Don Giuseppe visit long after your Peruvian adventure is over.

World.title: I order a weak long black. Is my cafe overcharging me for my other drink?
World.content:
Q: I ordered a weak long black and a strong flat white at my local cafe, which then charged me for the additional shot of coffee for the strong flat white. Logic says there should be no additional cost since I’m receiving one less shot in the weak long black. Am I being unreasonable? T.C., Mosman, NSW

Photo: Simon Letch

A: I ran your question past my daughter. She studied film and TV at uni, works as a neo-soul singer-songwriter, and lives in the northern hipster suburbs of Melbourne, so she knows everything there is to know about being a barista. She thought you make a reasonable enough point and, if you asked politely, most cafe workers would probably cancel the charge for the extra shot because most cafe workers aren’t paid enough to give a stuff (although some of the more pedantic baristas might refuse, maybe even leaving a couple of fronds off your latte-art fern to demonstrate their deep contempt for your three-shot pettiness).

Personally, I’m not sure I follow your coffee logic. If a long black is a set price, why should you expect to pay half-price if you only want a one-shot version of it? That’s like buying a double-size bedsheet and expecting it to be half-price because you’ll only be putting it on a single bed. Nobody wants to be known as a three-shot whiner, so maybe the simplest solution is to amend your order.

World.title: Warriors forward Shakira Baker's double life
World.content:
Though she tried to keep it hidden from her students, Shakira Baker's second job was never going to stay secret for long.

The Manurewa High School teacher and Warriors forward saw her two worlds collide earlier in the season when the school's league team played curtain-raiser to the Warriors women, officially blowing her cover.

"I kept it quiet for a little bit, but they came down to the Hamilton game against the Knights. They were all screaming on the sideline, so it was really cool to have them there and that support."

Being exposed as a Warrior has, of course, seen her become much more popular at the school.

Baker admits balancing teaching with professional sport can be difficult, but she said being in the classroom helps keep her grounded throughout the NRLW season.

However, she is hopeful rugby league will eventually become a full-time profession for women.

"It's about having that going outside of rugby league, having that outlet. Being semi-professional is tiring but I can see where they're trying to take it in the long term and hopefully in the coming years we see it become a full-time competition."

In her second year at the Warriors after a decorated career in rugby union, the former Black Ferns Sevens star said the side was just beginning to gel after a tough run of injuries early in the year.

"It's been up and down a little bit, we're trying to get consistency. We've taken the learnings and just want to put our best foot forward."

Still a relative rookie in league, Baker knows she still has plenty more to learn.

"Having that first season, knowing what to expect, knowing what the body is gonna feel like and things like that. I'm still enjoying it, still loving being a part of this club and I am understanding the game a little bit more but still a lot to learn as well."

With the Warriors securing some big name signings in 2026, including Stacey Waaka and Mele Hufanga, Baker said they felt the expectations on the side grow.

"Their knowledge and the energy that they've brought in really sort of amped us ones coming in from last year. I'm not too sure if that put a target on our club or not. But we're really lucky to have that experience and their knowledge amongst us."

Baker says expectations on the side have grown. DJ Mills

Though not a veteran in league, Baker brings 17 years of experience herself as a professional sportswoman.

Having started her career at 19 with the Wellington Farah Palmer Cup side, Baker went on to earn 13 test caps as well as Commonwealth Games and Rugby World Cup gold medals in Sevens.

She has no desire to return, however.

"Once I hung up the rugby boots and put my rugby league boots on, that was the decision I made, that I want to see that through long term. There's no thinking I want to make a switch back."

While leadership doesn't come naturally for her, Baker is a natural mentor for the team's younger players.

"I've been involved in sport for a very long time but I'm sort of a person of few words so I just go out there and do it and if it rubs off on them, it rubs off on them. They keep me young."

She also understands the sporting journey is not all smooth sailing, having also faced her fair share of adversity.

In 2013, Baker was diagnosed with Long QT syndrome, a heart condition which brings an increased risk of fainting, seizures, or sudden death during physical activity.

With her playing future under threat, Baker underwent surgery and has fortunately continued her career without incident.

"I was signed off by the cardiologist and I don't have to take medication and things like that, I still have the condition but it's non-symptomatic so it's all fine."

However, Baker must always have a defibrillator close by, though it is now largely precautionary.

World.title: MBIE backs council ruling that Christchurch Airbnb owners need to get consent or stop
World.content:
The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) has ruled that Christchurch unit owners have to ask for permission to offer the property as an Airbnb - or stop.

Christchurch City Council sought a determination from the ministry because it felt the owners, named in the determination as T Denman and K Suter, had changed the use of the unit from its consented use as a household unit, by making it available for short-term accommodation.

The unit, on Gloucester St, was issued a code compliance certificate in May 2025 as a multi-unit dwelling.

It is on the ground floor with a separate unit above.

The council told MBIE that it did not have evidence the unit had ever been used for its consented use and had been advertised online as visitor accommodation. The unit could be booked for one group at a time and one night or more.

The council contacted the owners in March telling them that the unit had changed from a residential classification to accommodation.

They had breached two requirements of the Building Act, in that they should have given notice of change of use, and that they could not change the use of the building unless the council gave them written notice that the new use would comply with the relevant provisions of the building code.

It issued a notice to fix, which said the owners should notify the council of the change, supply required documentation, and receive written notice that the new use would comply with the rules as required.

Alternatively, they would have to stop using the building for accommodation and return it to its residential use.

The owners said they had sought advice from the council before they started letting the unit and were told it would not be considered a change of use.

They had told the council they wanted to make it a short-term rental so they could use it as a holiday home.

MBIE principal adviser determinations Rebecca Mackie said there was no dispute the council had not approved a change.

There was also no dispute that the multi-unit residential building was consented as sleeping residential.

The question was whether the use had changed.

Mackie found that it had, because the unit was advertised at a nightly rate.

"In this case, the unit is not occupied as the exclusive home or residence of a household... The unit is made available to members of the public as short-term accommodation through an online accommodation platform, with different occupants able to stay on a nightly or weekly basis. That pattern of occupation is transient, rotational and commercial in character. Although each booking may involve only one person or one group staying at a time, there is no continuity of occupation by any particular household.

"The purpose of the use is to rent the unit out as temporary accommodation. That use is materially different from the purpose of the Housing category.... nor do I consider the low level of services provided is determinative of the use of the unit."

Mackie said the unit's use group had changed and there were additional or more onerous building code requirements with the new rules.

"The owners did not provide written notice to the authority under section 114, and the use was changed without written notice from the authority under section 115 that the building in its new use complies to the extent required, in contravention of these sections of the Act. Therefore, there was a basis to issue the notice to fix under section 164."

She upheld the council's notice to fix.

Consultant Mike Blackburn said the determination was relevant to apartments in other developments that were used predominantly as short-term accommodation.

"Where Council determines that a change of use has occurred, the Building Act process can also bring additional Building Code requirements into consideration. In this case MBIE specifically identified requirements relating to access and facilities for people with disabilities as an example of requirements applying to the new use. For developers, designers, property owners and operators involved in this part of the market, Determination 2026/026 is therefore one worth being aware of."

World.title: Hamilton man Jason Monkley charged childcare firm $2900 to fix van - then torched it
World.content:
A man who was trusted to repair a childcare van instead drove it to Hamilton Gardens and set it alight, only to be caught by his own CCTV footage.

Jason Paul Monkley had spent months fixing the Ōtorohanga-based Kiwi Kids Club van.

The owner had shelled out $2900 for materials, but after telling her the work was done and he would take it for a warrant, Monkley instead drove the van to Hamilton Gardens in the dead of night and torched it.

His actions led to a charge of arson, and this week Monkley appeared in Hamilton District Court for sentencing before Judge Stephen Clark.

Court documents state Monkley twice denied any involvement in the blaze. However, his movements were tracked to the minute by the city council, BP and his own CCTV system.

The court heard the victim had arranged for Monkley to fix her company van in mid to late 2024. Over the following months, she paid $2900 for the work to be completed.

By 13 May, 2025, the van was ready to be picked up. Monkley contacted the victim and said he needed to take it for a warrant of fitness.

However, at 3.02am on 15 May, Monkley was spotted on his CCTV system leaving his house with a red petrol container in his Ford.

He was caught on CCTV at BP Whitiora 20 minutes later, before he returned home.

At 4.46am, he was seen putting a bike and a clear plastic container into the back of the van before driving off.

He drove through Gate 1 at Hamilton Gardens at 5.32am and parked the van near the main car park. He set it on fire soon after and then rode his bike home.

Police received a call about the fire at 5.51am from a member of the public.

When spoken to, Monkley denied any involvement and said the van was stolen from outside his house.

He was questioned a second time and told officers he had left it outside an associate's property, from where it was stolen.

Monkley, a sickness beneficiary, had earlier accepted a sentence indication, and his counsel Glen Prentice said nothing in a pre-sentence report suggested he was unsuitable for home detention. He had been on bail with no issues, and he could immediately pay the reparation of $3400, which included a $500 insurance excess.

Judge Clark read excerpts from the victim impact statement in which she said she had trusted Monkley.

She ran the childcare programme in Te Kūiti and Ōtorohanga "with little to no support from the community" and was "flabbergasted" by his actions.

While Monkley's motive was not discussed in court, the victim said he could have told her he was "having issues".

"She says she was somewhat stunned and disappointed, and you could have worked it out as she described you as a family friend."

Judge Clark said he could not see anything in his pre-sentence report that would warrant further credit, except perhaps the fact Monkley had offered to pay the reparation in full.

For that, and his plea, the judge sentenced Monkley to nine months' home detention from a starting point of 19 months' jail.

The judge ordered the reparation be paid within 14 days.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: East Coast conservationist rescues emu chicks after feral cat attack
World.content:
An East Coast conservationist has become a surrogate dad to a couple of emu chicks, rescuing them after a feral cat attacked their nest.

Ruatoria man Graeme Atkins took the chicks in after inadvertently scaring away their real father.

"I was down the beach collecting firewood for a birthday celebration and scared the dad off the nest," he told Checkpoint.

"It was a bit of a bummer that that happened," he said, explaining that male emus look after the eggs and raise the chicks.

After a restless night spent worrying about the birds, he returned to the nest and saw a feral cat had attacked.

"Out of the five chicks I saw the day before only two were left," he said.

So he took action, taking them in despite "a little bit of trepidation about what we were getting into".

The chicks have made themselves at home on Atkins' property. Supplied

Raising them was similar to raising puppies, he said, as the chicks squeaked beside him.

"We've got so much advice from people who know emus.

"They're pretty endearing as a pet, they grow on you," he said.

The chicks are three weeks old now, and spend their days following Atkins around. He has created a warm home for them in a fenced-in enclosure outside his house.

"Because it's been so cold I put them inside a box that's got wool matting, and then some dry grass."

They have quickly made themselves at home - and developed a taste for some of the rare plants on Atkins' property.

"In six months they could be up to five feet tall," he said.

World.title: ACT to campaign on Paul Henry's 'Starship for cancer' proposal
World.content:
The ACT Party wants to build New Zealand's first dedicated national cancer centre, turning a musing from new candidate Paul Henry into a campaign promise.

ACT would establish a philanthropic foundation to attract some of the funding, and get rid of a cap on donation tax credits - the same cap that put one National MP at odds with his party.

When he announced his candidacy in July, Henry said he wanted a world-class cancer hospital in New Zealand, but admitted it would cost "multiple billions" of dollars.

"I think you could easily get a group of wealthy New Zealanders to stump up with about 10 billion, easily. The rest of it we would borrow, but that would be an investment in New Zealand's future," he said at the time.

Now, the party has confirmed it is pressing ahead with the idea, unveiling a plan to build a "Starship for Cancer" with campuses in Auckland and Christchurch.

"Starship showed what New Zealand can achieve when we concentrate talent, technology, generosity and national ambition around a single mission. ACT wants to do the same for cancer," Henry said.

Henry said Starship Children's Hospital in Auckland showed what the country could achieve when it concentrated on a single mission. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

The former broadcaster confessed he had announced the policy "on the fly" last month, and had expected to be pulled aside and discouraged.

"Instead I was told, 'we think you might be onto something'," he told an audience in Christchurch.

ACT expected around $2 billion of capital investment would be required.

"When I mentioned this out of the blue standing next to David Seymour at the press conference, I suggested we might be looking at a figure close to $10 billion, so ACT's involvement has already saved the country $8 billion," Henry said.

ACT would legislate to establish a not-for-profit, independent National Cancer Centre Foundation with charitable status.

To attract donations, ACT would remove the cap on donation tax credits.

The cap was criticised by National MP Greg Fleming on Thursday, who said work was underway to "fix" it, but revenue minister Simon Watts has insisted there are no plans to change it.

A policy document explained the centres would be funded through a combination of public-private partnership financing, charitable donations, existing Crown health investment, and other private capital "where appropriate".

The Department of Cancer Sciences at the University of Auckland and the Christchurch Cancer Foundation would work on business cases for the campuses.

Henry admitted he announced the policy "on the fly". RNZ

Health New Zealand would be a "major customer" of the centre, with ACT expecting it would relocate its existing cancer services in Auckland and Christchurch to the new campuses.

The Crown's ongoing financial liability would come through Health New Zealand purchasing the clinical services and using the facilities.

"This expenditure, to a significant extent, would otherwise need to occur elsewhere in the health system. In the future, medical

tourism from overseas could help subsidise the Centre's operations," the document said.

Henry said the campaign policy was "aspirational" but insisted it was realistic and practical.

"Comprehensive cancer centres are the gold standard internationally because they bring researchers, clinicians, universities, private providers and philanthropists together with world-class treatment, technology and clinical trials," he said.

World.title: Lawyer convicted of assault on his 12-year-old son which left him hospitalised
World.content:
A lawyer has been convicted and granted name suppression following a serious assault on his son that required him being hospitalised.

The lawyer, aged in his 50s, appeared in the Timaru District Court on Friday before Judge Campbell Savage where he was sentenced to supervision after pleading guilty to a charge of assault on a child.

The judge said the case, which began in 2022, had moved at "glacial pace".

"One's led to the inescapable conclusion that you've done just about everything in your powers to frustrate the process, including avoiding the service of summons. It seems that you've used your knowledge of the system to duck and dive attempts to get it set down, and then you've counterpunched with a flurry of meritless pre-trial applications."

Court documents obtained by RNZ detail the offending which occurred in April 2022.

The summary of facts said the lawyer and his son were boxing on a concrete area at the rear of their address.

The lawyer was a "fully grown man and the victim is a small built, 38kg 12-year-old child," the summary said.

Both were wearing boxing gloves.

The lawyer struck the victim's head causing him to bleed.

"The victim said 'please stop. I am serious'.

"The defendant then struck the victim in the face followed by the stomach. This caused the victim to cry. He went to the ground.

"The defendant continued to punch the victim on the ground. Eventually the victim said he could not breath and the defendant stopped. The victim then jumped the fence to get away."

The victim was taken to hospital and was initially diagnosed with a suspected fractured cheekbone and perforated liver, however after scans this was not the case.

He sustained extensive bruising to his head and ears and a cut above his eye.

He was admitted to hospital for three nights to allow observation and investigation of his possible injuries.

The lawyer declined to comment to police.

At sentencing the man's lawyer, Michael Sandom told the court the lawyer appeared before the court as a defendant and as a practicing lawyer.

The lawyer was convicted at Timaru District Court. (File photo) RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Sandom said he was appearing among many of his colleagues and peers, which brought a level of "embarrassment and shame".

"[He] is not a perfect person, but none of us are.

"He knows the mistake that he made, he is remorseful for what occurred and in my submission shame for what occurred is an important theme for this sentencing."

Sandom said the offending would stay with the lawyer "for the rest of his life".

The offending was "distressing and repugnant" to the lawyer.

"He's ashamed for what occurred. He can barely face it, can barely talk about it, can barely engage with it at all."

Sandom said the lawyer was a "kind and generous person" as well as an "advocate" in the criminal jurisdiction.

He accepted it was "serious" offending.

Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae said the Crown opposed the lawyer's application for a discharge without conviction and said his affidavit for name suppression did not meet the threshold.

Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae. (File photo) Stuff / Pool / Alden Williams

Judge Savage said the matter had passed through the court system "at glacial pace", with the first hearing in April 2022.

The lawyer pleaded guilty during a trial after the victim had given evidence. Judge Savage said the lawyer's claim he did not see his son's statement until trial was "implausible".

"One's led to the inescapable conclusion that you've done just about everything in your powers to frustrate the process, including avoiding the service of summons. It seems that you've used your knowledge of the system to duck and dive attempts to get it set down, and then you've counterpunched with a flurry of meritless pre-trial applications."

Judge Savage said it was "charitable" to say the lawyer's guilty plea came at the 11th hour.

"It came as the clock was striking 12."

He said he had no doubt the lawyer loved his son "with all your heart".

In terms of aggravating factors, the judge pointed to the victim's age and the breach of trust.

Judge Savage declined to discharge the lawyer without a conviction, but did grant final name suppression.

He said he did not see the lawyer as a risk of re-offending.

The lawyer has been practicing for more than a decade. The New Zealand Law Society register does not say whether he holds a practicing certificate.

RNZ asked the New Zealand Law Society how the lawyer was able to continue practicing while the matter was before the court.

A spokesperson said the Law Society took any concerns regarding criminal offending by lawyers "seriously".

"Personal conduct by a lawyer may be considered under the complaints and disciplinary framework in the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006 (the Act) in certain circumstances.

"However, a lawyer who holds a current practising certificate and admits to, or is found guilty of, criminal offending is not automatically suspended from practice."

The spokesperson said concerns or complaints must first be considered by independent Standards Committees who may refer matters to the New Zealand Lawyers and Conveyancers Disciplinary Tribunal, if the conduct was "sufficiently serious".

"In addition, section 40 of the Act provides that a lawyer who has applied to renew their practising certificate may continue to practise while the application is being considered. This may include cases where proceedings are ongoing."

Asked if a lawyer could be suspended pending a complaint, the spokesperson said only the tribunal could make an order that a lawyer be suspended from practice, including for an interim period while any disciplinary process is underway, or strike a lawyer off the roll of barristers and solicitors following referral from a Standards Committee.

The Disciplinary Tribunal is administered by the Ministry of Justice.

Asked why the register did not have the expiry date for the lawyer's practising certificate, the spokesperson said the Society was unable to comment on individual cases for privacy reasons.

"Speaking generally, practising certificates have an expiry date of 30 June each year."

Ministry of Justice acting group manager of National Service Delivery Louisa Carroll said the Ministry could not comment on the circumstances of any individual lawyer or active court proceedings.

Asked about the lawyer receiving legal aid clients, Carroll said legal aid providers must meet and maintain approval requirements and comply with the Legal Services Act, their legal aid provider contract, and professional obligations.

"Legal aid providers are also required to notify the Ministry within five working days if they are charged with, or convicted of, an offence punishable by imprisonment."

"Where the Ministry becomes aware of concerns about a provider, it may consider those concerns through its complaints, audit, quality assurance and provider approval processes."

Carroll said depending on the circumstances, the Ministry may take a range of actions, including imposing restrictions on a provider, modifying or cancelling their approval to undertake legal aid work, or referring matters to the New Zealand Law Society.

"Approved providers remain eligible to receive legal aid assignments unless their approval is changed, restricted, suspended, or cancelled.

World.title: Healthline calls in reinforcements amid biggest flu outbreak in 10 years
World.content:
Healthline calls in reinforcements for flu surge Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Healthline has called in reinforcements to cope with a deluge of calls amid the biggest flu outbreak in years.

Flu-related hospitalisations are at a 10-year high in Auckland, with national infection rates at a four-year high and rising.

Health NZ chief executive Dale Bramley earlier said the entire health system was under pressure, with the spike being driven by influenza A along with cases of RSV, cold viruses and some Covid-19 cases.

The chief operating officer of Wakarongorau Aotearoa, which operates Healthline, Brian O'connell, told Checkpoint the service was handling about 20 percent more calls in the past seven days compared to July.

He said a normal day would see about 1000 calls but this was now up to 1200 to 1300 a day.

Healthline had increased resourcing by about 10 percent, he said. This meant at any time there were about 25 nurses and paramedics on and the current wait time was 10 minutes.

"When people are calling Healthline they're connected with one of our nurses or paramedics and can talk through concerns and then our team will work with them about how urgently they need to seek health advice or give advice to keep themselves well at home."

Out of every five people Healthline spoke to, O'connell said only one would be diverted through to hospital or calling 111.

He said Healthline could be especially helpful at the moment for any parent who was worried about a sick child.

"Speaking to our clincial team can really help give you that reassurance and make sure you're not going to the wrong place."

About 30 percent of the calls Healthline received were for children under the age of 5.

As a result, O'connell said Plunket had been helping out by putting on more nurses who could take calls relating to young children.

Plunket told Checkpoint in a statement, it was taking an extra 200 calls a day as it helped to support Healthline with addressing demand.

It said some whānau might experience longer wait times than usual.

How can the flu outbreak be addressed?

Should people be masking up as flu outbreaks surge? Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

University of Otago professor of Public Health Dr Michael Baker told Checkpoint, more needed to be done sooner in the future, including stronger advice about masks.

"The problem is when we're at this stage of the epidemic curve we've left it too late because we're already overwhelming the health system. It's hard to change the trajectory."

Professor of Public Health Dr Michael Baker. (File photo) Supplied / Department of Public Health

He said a graded response to dampen down transmission would be a good idea along with continuing with vaccination.

"But now we're stuck in this situation and I hope we can do better in future.

Winter respiratory infections usually went from May to October, Baker said, with the intensity varying greatly year-to-year.

Baker said we needed to get better at rapidly ramping up control measures including mask use in enclosed environments and additional precautions in high risk settings like public transport and waiting rooms.

Employers could also get more active at discouraging workers from coming to work sick, he said, and encourage working from home.

There were also additional RAT tests available now that could test for influenza, RSV and Covid-19, Baker said, which were tools available to be used in strategic ways.

"Some countries do have systems for communicating the level of respiratory risk in the community. We don't have a graded system in place to know when to issue those warnings - a system like this needs a bit of design work, working with community groups, Māori and those that are particularly vulnerable to get a sense of the kinds of warnings they would appreciate.

"We've published work in the past about having a graded system on this for seasonal infections...it's quite a well established approach but we do need that willingness from our political and health leaders."

World.title: Report on Mt Maunganui landslide risk unread: Tauranga City Council
World.content:
Tauranga councillors had report outlining landslide risk Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Tauranga councillors had a detailed report showing there was a high risk people could die if their local campground got hit by a landslide but no one read the report.

The council said that despite the report being in an August 2025 council agenda, it was not read and the meeting never happened.

Five months after the meeting was cancelled, six people were killed in a landslide as debris came off Mount Maunganui and covered a large area of the campground.
